No. 1. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Reveived September 9.) 
(No. 257.) | 
My Lord, Therapie, August 25, 1849. 


STATEMENTS unfavourable to the Hungarians have obtained credit 
here since the arrival of the post from Vienna yesterday. Advices from 
Bucharest had previously reported the arrival of General Dembinski, with 
two or three ae distinguished fugitives, at Orsova. More recent com- 
munications from Vienna and Belgrade are said to assert that the Austro- 
Russian forces have gained a decisive victory near Temesvar, and that a 
considerable number of prisoners and several pieces of artillery have 
fallen into their hands. Long before this despatch can reach your 
Lordship, the truth, whatever may be its character, will no doubt have 
found its way to Her Majesty’s Government, and therefore | abstain from 
entering into particulars, which, however probable in substance, rest on no 

“certain foundation, though the Austrian Minister very naturally exerts 
himself to accredit and circulate an impression that the cause of Hungary 
is completely lost. sae 

Meanwhile the want of any recent intelligence favourable to the 
Hungarians, the approach of the main body of the Austrian and Russian 
forces towards Transylvania, and the dissatisfaction expressed at the 
Porte’s endeavours to maintain a neutral attitude, encourage those who 
are adverse to Reshid Pasha’s administration, and who look forward to 
the triumph of Russia as a good opportunity for effecting his overthrow. 

The Grand Vizier and his friends are evidently apprehensive of an 
impending crisis, with respect not only to the possession of ministerial 
power, but to the still more important question of external policy. ‘The 
former of these dangers may be deemed to have received a temporary 
check by the arrest of two persons suspected of being engaged in a plot 
for the restoration of Reshid’s adversaries, and more particularly of Riza 
Pasha, to the Sultan’s favour, 1am assured that the examination of their 
papers has furnished proof of the intrigue, and that the chief agent in 
carrying it on was employed as a spy by the Russian Legation. But the 
Sultan appears to be accessible to secret information, and he is always 
more or hese fearful of Russia. Nor does the fairness with which he has 
‘ately acted towards his Ministers afford any strong security against the 
sudden changes to which an undecided character is liable in critical 
circumstances. Any joint demand addressed to His Majesty by the 
Cabinets of Vienna and St. Petersburgh, while their armies, flushed with 
victory, remain in the nalekhouvhaod of Turkey to perpetuate the submis- 


sion of the Hungarians, would be ues to find advocates here, and a timid 
[43] 


2 


course of policy adapted to base interests, and supported by artful coun- 
sels, would be but too likely to prevail. 

l have the Grand Vizier’s personal assurance that no departure from 
the principles so often declared to me by the Porte is yet in contemplation, 
and therefore my object in addressing your Lordship on this occasion is 
mainly prospective. Events, however, press on with so much rapidity in 
the present. state of Europe, that what is now a matter of speculation 
may easily prove to be one of reality before I can receive your Lordship’s 
answer. ‘The general impression and indeed the apparent probability is, 
that the Emperor of Russia will not be inclined to withdraw his troops 
before he obtains some guarantee for the maintenance of Russian interests, 
as well with respect to the permanent repression of free principles of 

overnment as to the extension of his influence over the population of 
Solavic origin settled under various names between the confines of his 
empire and the eastern shore of the Adriatic. The future position of 
Austria is also viewed with uneasiness. Not only is it feared that the 
obligations contracted by that Power will entail upon it the necessity of 
serving Russian interests, with little regard to any other consideration, 
but in the opinion of some, the territories of the Sultan may not impos- 
sibly be looked to as affording the sole convenient means of compensation 
due from Austria to her northern auxiliary. 

Indications of an endeavour to get up a case of complaint against the 
Porte are not wanting. The Austrian Minister has been of late particu- 
larly active in calling for decided measures with respect to the refugees in 
Wallachia. To-day he has presented a strong official note* to Aali Pasha, 
containing a formal protest against the Porte’s unwillingness to act 
according to his requisitions, and demanding the extradition of all refugees, 
Poles and Hungarians, without entering into any distinction of political 
and criminal offences. ‘The Russian Envoy has occasionally seconded the 
Internuncio’s remonstrances, and it is emphatically given out that his 
Court is greatly dissatislied with the conduct of the Turkish Cabinet, 
antl particularly of the Grand Vivier, 

Vour Lordship need not be teld that if the Porte were eventually 
eonvicted of having been slow to execute any stipulations of her treaties 
with Austria as to the extradition of fugitives, she would have much to 
plead on the score of humanity, of the manner in which she has been com- 
mitted against the Hungarians by the Russian forces in Moldavia, and 
of the manifest dilference between a whole nation in arms and a band of 
marauders or deserters. In point of fact, however, the Porte’s neutrality 
has been sacrificed in a far greater degree to the military operations of 
Russia and the unfortunate necessities of \ustria, than to any partiality 
which her Ministers may have entertained for a people having many 
traditional claims to their sympathy and good will. 

The Ottoman Government has never been remarkable for the clear- 
ness or consistency of its proceedings, and its natural desire to combine 
a fair regard for its own interests with a proper attention to the claims 
of humanity and to the obligations of treaty, may possibly have betrayed 
it into some occasional irregularities. But its constant endeavour, on 
the whole, has been to maintain that neutral position which under your 
Lordship’s instructions | have uniformly recommended, and in aid of 
which the French Minister has more than once joined with me in per- 
suading the Porte to pursue a course prescribed by the same prineiple. 
Under these circumstances I only anticipate your Lordship's opinion, 
when | submit that the Ottoman Ministers are fairly entitled to support in 
continuing to carry out a principle which it has been my duty, and to all 


appearance that of General Aupick also, to inculcate with reference to, 


the war in Hungary. 
The probable and almost inevitable results of any marked disa 
potatoes in that respect must be as clear to your Lordship as to myself, 
n the new state of things consequent on the supposed reduction of Ban. 
gary to the condition of an Austrian province, by means of Russian inter- 
vention, the Porte will find it difficult enough to maintain the degree of 
independence which it has hitherto preserved. If its Ministers be left to

M. le Comte, Vienne, 14 Aodt, 1849. 

EN réponse aux rapports de votre Excellence du ler Aodt, concernant 
la conduite de la Porte 4 l’égard des rebelles Magyares qui le 26 Juillet 
ont été foreés de se réfugier en Moldavie, j’ai 'honneur de vous faire 
connaitre ce qui suit, 

__ la Porte, dans l'instruction donnée au mois de Février A son Com- 
missaire, Muad Effendi, a déclaré qu'elle considére les Ma yares comme 
des rebelles. Elle a également reconnu que des individus en état de 
rébellion contre Vautorité légitime de Sa Majesté l'Empereur d’Autriche 
ne doivent pas se soustraire aux mains de la justice, en passant sur le 
territoire Ottoman, et que si quelques uns d’entre eux devaient franchir la 
frontiére, ils ne pourraient pas étre admis, d’aprés la teneur de l'Article 
AYVIIT du Traité de Belgrade. Nonobstant tout ceci, la Porte fut d’avis 
que si de pareils individus trouvaient moyen de se sauver sur gon terri- 


toire, ils devraient ne pas étre renvoyés mais seulement désarmés et 
éloignés des frontiéres, 


B 2 


La contradiction dans laquelle elle tombe ici avec elle-méme, saute 
aux yeux, et nous ne pouvons de notre cété que protester de la maniere 
la plus formelle contre une pareille ligne de conduite survie envers les 
iisunees Magyares ou Polonais qui se réfugient sur le territoire Ottoman. 

utre Article XVIII du Traité de Belgrade, nous pouvons alléguer 
en notre faveur la circonstance, que le droit de jurisdiction sur les sujets 
Autrichiens dans les Etats Ottomans est exclusivement réservé, en vertu 
des traités, A la Mission et aux Consulats de Sa Majesté Impériale. C’est 
pourquoi le Gouvernement Ottoman se rendrait coupable aussi_d’une 
violation manifeste de ce droit, s'il cherchait A s’opposer 4 une mesure 
‘udiciaire que les autorités Autrichiennes jugent nécessaire d’employer 4 
bégard de leurs nationaux compromis. 

Vd existence de ce droit So quneriction consacré par les traités, il serait 
de toute impossibilité A la Sublime Porte, ainsi qu'on a eu derni¢rement 
occasion de le lui faire observer, de chercher A faire valoir la théorie des 
réfugiés politiques nouvellement surgie dans quelques Etats de l'Europe 
Oceidentale. Nous la rendons encore une fois attentive aux consequences 
qui découlent en derniér résultat d'une pareille théorie, ainsi qu’a la 
nécessité of se sont trouvés méme des Gouvernemens Républicains, tels 
que la France et la Suisse, d’avoir recours aux mesures les plus sévéres 
contre d’aussi dangereux intrus, 

Or. les inconyéniens que la présence des réfugiés politiques a fait 
naitre dans les pays se feraient sentir infailliblement et avee encore plus 
de célérité en Turquie, of les mesures de police sont si défectueuses, et ou 
il ne se trouve déja que trop d’élémens de trouble et de soulévement 
parmi les. différentes nations qui en forment la population, 

Dailleurs, ceux des insurgés Valaques qui ont eure i la téte de la 
derniére révolte ont été exilés hors du pays, tandisque dans le cas présent 
Yon voudrait transférer dans l'intérieur du pays des rebelles provenant 
d'ufi’ Etat étranger, tans le but de ne point les livrer 4 leur autorité ; 
nouvelle contradiction, digne de figurer @ cété de la précédente. 

Enfin la Porte ne saurait non plus s‘autoriser de la conduite tenue 
par l’Autriche 4 l'égard des fuyards arrivés du territoire Ottoman, car il 
est généralment conn ur due. les autorités Impériales sur la frontiére de la 
Croatie, ob la question du traitement & faire subir 4 ces réfugi¢s a été le 
plus souvent agitée 4 cause des troubles fréquens de la Bosnie, ont 
toujours regu Vordre de repousser des fronti¢res ceux parmi les Bosniaques 
que se seraient trouvés en état de révolte armée contre leur Souverain, eb 
auraient cherché un refuge chez nous uniquement pour échapper a la 
punition méritée. 

Votre Excellence aura donc, en s’étayant des argumens qui précédent, 
A insister auprés de la Porte sur l’extradition de tous les rebelles 
Magyares ou Polonais, et surtout de leurs officiers, lesquels ont déji passé 
ae territoire Ottoman ou y arriveraient par la suite. 

Vous voudrez bien nous faire connaitre, M. le Comte, par la premiére

No. 3. 


Viscount Palmerston to Sir Stratford Canning. 


(No. 229.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, Seprember 24, 1849. 

1 HAVE received your Excellency’s despatch No. 257, of the 25th 
ultimo, containing observations on the effect likely to be produced at 
Constantinople by the late successes of the Austrian and Russian forces 
in Hungary; and I have to state to you that it is not unnatural that the 
Turkish Government should entertain the apprehensions which you have 


5 


mentioned, as to the use which Russia is likely to make of the military 
success which her armies have gained in Hungary; but Governments 
may sometimes fall into error by being over suspicious as well as by not 
being so enough, 

it would indeed be blindness not to see that the success of the Russian 
arms in Hungary must give to Russia for much time to come, a consider- 
able degree of political ascendancy over the Government of Austria; but 
there does not seem to be any reason for supposing that the Emperor of 
Russia means to take at present any undue advantage of the position in 
which the.termination of the Hungarian war has placed him; and the 
circular which has lately issued from the Russian Government, and of 
which a copy was inclosed for your Excellency’s information, in my 
despatch No. 220, of the 6tl instant, announces that the Russian troops 
are to retire without delay into the Russian territory. The Turkish Go- 
vernment, however, must feel that the advice which has been invariably 
given to it by Her Majesty's Government, to remain strictly passive and 
to preserve a neutral position between the contending parties, was sound 
and wise; for if the Turks had given way to their natural impulse, and: 
had manifested an active partiality for the ‘Hungarians, while on the one 
hand they would not have turned the scale in favour of Hungary, they 
would, on the other hand, upon the defeat of the Hungarians, have remained 
exposed to the well-founded resentment of the two impstial Governments. 
As it is, the Turkish Government has only to pursue the same steady 
course which it has hitherto followed, and it can have no cause to fear 
attack either from Austria or Russia. 

lam, &e, 
(Signed) PALMERSTON. 


No. 4, 


Viscount Palmerston to Sir Stratford Canning. 
(No. 230.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, September 24, 1849. 

WITH reference to the despatch from Prince Schwarzenberg to 
Count Stiirmer, of which a copy is inclosed in your Excellency’s despatch 
marked confidential, of the 25th ultimo, and wherein the Austrian 
Government demands from the Porte the extradition of the persons who 
have lately come from Hungary to take refuge within the Turkish domi- 
nions, | have to observe to your Excellency that even if the AVITIth 
Article of the Treaty of Belgrade, of which a copy is annexed, did pro- 

ae apply to the officers and soldiers of the Hungarian army who might 

e driven to seek shelter within the Turkish territory, that Article does 
not contain any engagement on the part of the Porte to give such persons 
up to the Austrian Government; and the utmost that could be demanded 
would be that they should not be allowed to reside permanently in the 
Turkish Empire. : 

But the XVIL[1Ith Article of the Treaty of Belgrade obviously relates 
to cases of a very different kind from that of the war which has just 
ended between Austria and Hungary; and it would be a strained inter- 
pretation of that Article to construe it to apply to the officers and soldiers 
of the Hungarian armies who have been fighting for the constitutional 
Denes of Hungary against the armies of Austria and Russia, Such 
officers and soldiers cannot be deemed to be the persons intended to be 
described by the expression “ces sortes de gens,” or to be classed with 
*voleurs et brigands.”’ 

It is to be observed, however, that the demand of the Austrian 


Government was made before the surrender .of Georgey to the Russian 


General-in-chief was known at Vienna; and the demand seems to have 
referred principally to the Hungarian detachment which was driven 
into Wallachia from Orsova on the 17th of August; and it is to

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Recetved September 26.) 


(No. 262.) 


My Lord, Therapia, August 27, 1849. 

AT an audience which took place this morning in the Palace of 
Beylerbey, I had the honour to present Her Majesty's reply to the Sultan's 
letter. ‘The Sultan gave me a most gracious reception, and expressed his 
earnest wish to draw still closer the bonds of amity which unite the two 
countries. 

I availed myself of the opportunity to enforce the terms of Her 
Majesty’s letter, and to encourage the Sultan in a steady adherence to that 
line of policy which under your Lordship’s instructions | have uniformly 
recommended ; I am the more solicitous on this point, because any appear- 
ance of change in the Sultan’s inclination would greatly promote the 
suceess of those intrigues which, helped on secretly by Huseian agents, 
are directed to the overthrow of the present Ministry. 

just and benevolent system of administration extending to all 
classes ; a careful selection of public functionaries ; the punishment of those 
who, like Nejib Pasha, dare perseveringly to act in opposition to the 
Sultan’s commands ; a continued and more active attention to all improve- 
ments productive of general prosperity and national strength, together 
with the encouragement of commerce on principles of well-considered 
liberality, are the leading points which L represented as tending more than 
any others to promote a cordial understanding not only between the Sove- 
reigns of Great Britain and Turkey personally, but also between their 
respective Governments and nations. I gave the Sultan to understand 
that in proportion as these views were carried out with effect and consis- 
tency, the sympathies which already operated so favourably on the rela- 
tions of the two countries with each other, would acquire new force, and 
increase the power of Her Majesty's Government to realize, in case of 
enistgency, those friendly sentiments which they never cease to entertain 
towards the Turkish Empire, 

With respect to the Porte’s foreign policy and the military operations 
on its north or north-western frontier, 1 expressed a hope that with the 
preservation of peace would be combined a firm maintenance of the Porte’s 
neutral position, and a generous regard for the just claims of humanity. 

In alluding to recent occurrences, though | confess that my approval 
as to several proceedings of late is little more than comparative, I thought 
it best for future objects to intimate a favourable opinion of Reshid 
Pasha’s administration, and | was happy to observe that my remarks in 
that sense appeared to be agreeable to the Sultan; nor is it necessary to 
add, that the Grand Vizier, on learning their tenor from Aali Pasha, who 
was present, expressed to me the most grateful satisfaction, 


There is more goodness of feeling and right-mindedness, than energy, 
quickness, or grasp of understanding in the Sultan's character, nor has: 
nature endowed His Majesty with an easy elocution, But m spite of 
personal disadvantages, he conveyed to me by his manner, countenance, 
and language, the impression that for the present at least his policy conti- 
nues to be that of a friendly intimate connexion with England, and that 
whatever may be the necessities of the present anxious Period. or the 
compliances which may be extorted from him by intrigue an intimidation, 
he looks eventually to Her Majesty’s Government for support in the hour 
of need, and wishes meanwhile that the relations between his Minister 
and Her Majesty’s Embassy should be those of real confidence and cor- 
diality. He listened with every appearance of interest and assent to my 
remarks concerning the internal administration of his empire, and assured 
me emphatically that the sentiments which I had expressed were to their 
full extent identical with his own. ; 

Referring to the Queen’s visit to Ireland, the Sultan manifested a 
marked degree of pleasure on learning with what enthusiasm Her Majesty 
had been weleomed to that part of her dominions, and a lively hope that 
Her Majesty’s presence there would be followed by a return o prosperit 
as useful to Her Majesty's Government as to Her Majesty's Iris 

ion, 
Hopes I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received September 26.) 


(No. 267.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 3, 1849, 

THE discomlfiture, by defeat, surrender, or dispersion, of so large a 

rt of the Hungarian armies, anticipated as a probable final result, but 
in fact most unexpectedly sudden, has brought a number of refugees into 
the Ottoman dominions, and given importance to the claim of extradition 
which had already been raised by the Austrian Cabinet. The distin- 
guished names of Kossuth, Dembinski, Bem, Perezel, and Mezzaros, stand 
out from among the crowd of exiles, and make it difficult either for the 
Porte to give way or for the two Imperial Governments to forbear. The 
whole number of compromised individuals, Hungarian and Polish, who 
have escaped from the seat of war and entered Wallachia by Orsova, 
amount to upwards of eighty. They were amicably received by the 
Turkish authorities, and they were su Becton) forwarded under escort 
to the fortress of Widdin, where they still remain, with an exception or 
two, awaiting the Porte’s decision as to their ulterior destination. ‘The 
leaders are detained on their parole, and the others, as | am informed by 
a young officer just arrived from Widdin, are left almost entirely to 
themselves. 

The Russian and Austrian Representatives both here and at 
Bucharest continue to insist on the extradition of the whole number 
respectively ; though it is probable that they would be satisfied if the 
more distinguished individuals were given up to them. The Internuncio 
rests his demand on the XVIIIth Article of the Treaty of Belgrade. 
The Russian Envoy appeals in support of his claim to the IInd Article 
of the Treaty of Rainardji It is remarked that in point of tone’ and 
language the Internuncio is the more peremptory of the two. 
On grounds of humanity not unmixed with considerations affecting 
the Porte’s character and future policy, | have not hesitated to advise a 
decided resistance to the Aran of extradition. I have further endea- 
voured to dissuade the Turkish Ministers from pledging themselves to 
any measure of restraint not clearly preseribed by the terms of treaties, 
and from contracting any engagement not leaving a certain latitude of 
action for the future.

I was happy to learn from General Aupick that his view of the 
matter was entirely similar tomy own, and we have m consequence acted 
upon the same line and received assurances of the same tenour from the 
Grand Vizier and Aali Pasha. 

We should have been better pleased to take even a higher position, 
and to recommend a more generous treatment of the unfortunate exiles; 
but the treaties, though vsfied beyond the strict letter of their obligation, 
and the example afforded on other occasions by the claimants themselves, 

ive, nevertheless, a certain degree of weight to the Austrian and 
Russian demands, taken in their more limited extent, and impose, for the 
sake of peace, a necessity of acting with much prudence and considera- 
tion for these Powers, 

While this question was still pending I saw the Grand Vizier in 
private, and left him disposed to take a right course on the main point of 
extradition. 

The Council met on the 30th ultimo, and decided that the Porte 
could not without dishonour give up the refugees, though in maintaining 
its refusal every practicable exertion would be made to assuage the 
resentment which that Wate might create, Aali Pasha, in sending 
me a message to this effect, added, that in a few days a vessel would be 
sent to receive the refugees on board at Varna, and convey them to some 
island in the Archipelago, Rhodes for instance, or Candia, most probably 
the latter, 

I have reason to believe that in case of being urged to give up the 
refugees by pressing and reiterated demands, the Porte with ultimately 
make an appeal to the leading Powers, and abide by their opinion. 

There are persons, my Lord, who apprehend that the Emperor 
Nicholas having obtained such complete success in Hungary, and having 
his armies in movement from one end of Russia to the other, will strike 
into a bolder line of policy than heretofore, and take some decided 
step towards realizing that scheme of aggrandizement which has long 
been a favourite though distant object of ambition at St. Petersburgh. 
Her Majesty’s Government are the best judges of this probability. . I 
will only take the liberty to remark that the conjectures founded many 
months ago on the attitude assumed by Russia, as indicative of muc 
larger views than the mere occupation of the Principalities, have been 
fully realized by the event; that no slight degree of trickery as well as 
of dictation has been employed to obtain the partial concurrence of the 
Porte; that the Court of St. Petersburgh, entertaining a fixed aversion 
to free principles of government, professes to aim at the restoration of 
order disturbed throughout Europe by the propagation of those prin- 
ciples; that the movement manifested among the Sclavonic population 
out of Russia threatens to operate as a check on Russian influence, if not 
appropriated in time to Russian purposes; and that the credit of securin, 
a national compensation for so many sacrifices required from his people 
and army, may fairly be presumed to have its natural place in the 
Emperor's calculations. On the whole, it is but reasonable to expect 
that the present successes will be used to pevaiats the great objects of 
Russian policy throughout the East, and that endeavours will be made 
under the impressions created by victory, to draw the Turkish Govern- 
ment into a more complete subserviency to the ipoliicel views of that 
Power. How far the Cabinet of Vienna may be disposed or obliged to 
act as an auxiliary to Russia in earrying out these views; whether, as 
some believe, the question of extradition has been raised for sinister 
purposes; and what measures of intimidation or aggression may follow 
upon the Porte’s continued refusal to give up the refugees, the course of 
events will best serve to show. But I should fail in my duty if I did 
not again solicit your Lordship's attention pointedly to this subject, and 
declare my conviction that, with every exertion on the part of Her 
Majesty's Government and Embassy, it will henceforward be more 

difficult than ever to keep the Sultan and his Ministers in that course 
of policy which they have lately pursued with tolerable pretensions to 
steadiness in their wey and further, that without stronger guarantees 
than any I have heard of as already existing, it will hardly be safe to 


overlook the inducements which, naturally enough in the present state 
of Europe, may prevail with the Russian Cabinet to vo the Porte into 
its views by force, if persuasion fails, even in defiance of public opinion 
elsewhere. 

ra The importance of pee Her ide Government for the 
worst ig so evident, that I hope to be excused for adding on this occa- 
sion, that notwithstanding the mild tone of M. de Titoff’s ostensible 
notes, indications of impatience and resentment have lately appeared 
in the language of the Russian Ministry and of its agents; nor can it 
be concealed that the striking change of opinion throughout these 
countries in favour of Turkish principles of government, as compared 
with those of Russia, must be in no small degree mortifying and even 
alarming to the Cabinet of St, Petersburgh. 

I have, &c.

_ AALI PASHA has commu icated to me confidentially the draft of 
his answer to M. de Titoff’s note respecting the refugees from Hungary, 
with a request that I would suggest an amendments that might occur to 
me on perusing It. Inclosed herewith is a copy of the draft, with my 
suggestions in the parallel column, such as they have been adopted b his 
Excellency. Had the Pasha entirely followed my advice, he would ave 
omitted, or at least recast, the concluding paragraph. But he thought it 
necessary for conciliation ; and as it now. stands, my objection lies more 

ainst the form than the substance. I need not remark to your Lord- 
ship, that in counselling a Turkish Minister when there is any immediate 
danger of Russian resentment, | am obliged to take ply into 
account the character of the client as well as the merits of the case. 
Aali Pasha will no doubt ele me a complete copy of his note, when 
approved by the Sultan an given in to the Russian Envoy. The most 
sauintactory art of it is perhaps that which shows in how many 
instances both Russia and Austria have declined to give up_refugees 
claimed by the Porte. ‘he answer to M. de Stiirmer’s note will of course 
not differ materially from that addressed to M. de Titoff. I have not 
however seen it; and I may take this opportunity to state, on Aali 
Pasha’s authority, that the allusion made by Prince Schwarzenberg, in his 
instruction communicated by Count Stiirmer, to certain assurances 
received from the Porte in the commencement of the late operations in 
Wallachia, is founded on a complete misapprehension of what really 
passed on the occasion.

‘No. 270.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 5, 1849. , 
LATE the night before last I learnt from Aali Pasha that Count 
Stiirmer, at his own particular request, was to have an audience of the 
Sultan next morning, in order to receive from His Majesty's own lips an 
assurance that the refugees should be “ internés” and “ surveillés” b the 
Porte. This arrangement took me by surprise. The concealment of the 
proposal from me till after it had been settled was not entirely in keeping 
with the confidence professed towards me by the Grand Vizier, and | saw 
in it much actual awkwardness and eventual embarrassment for the 
Sultan, I consequently sent Mr. Alison next celts to Reshid Pasha, 
with directions to make known my impressions to his Highness, to ascer- 
tain more exactly the nature of his views in obtaining the proposed 
audience, and to persuade the Sultan, through him, not to commit him- 
self beyond some general expression within the terms of the note proposed 
as an answer to M. de Titoff’s application. The Grand Vizier excused 
‘himself by saying that Aali Pasha had been directed to acquaint me with 
Count Stiirmer’s request, and that he hoped the audience would prove a 
facility to the acceptance by Austria and Russia of the Porte’s intended 


‘course of prosersiine as to the refugees. He consented at ihe same time 


that Mr. Alison should see the Minister for Foreign Affairs before Count 
Stiirmer’s audience, with a view to advising the Sultan to confine his 
answer to a general assurance that the refugees would be removed from 
the frontier and prevented from Sone any further harm. Mr, Alison 
was in time to communicate with Aali Pasha at the Palace, and he had 


‘reason to believe that a suitable intimation was submitted at once to the 


Sultan. 

At an early hour yesterday an Austrian steamer arrived from the 
Danube, It was saluted by one of the Russian vessels of war lying off 
the residence of the Russian Envoy at Buyukdery, and having hoisted a 
‘Russian flag at the fore, with the Austrian colours as usual, proceeded 
‘down the Bosphorus. | learnt ata later hour that Prince Michel Rad- 
-givil was on board, with a letter from the Emperor Nicholas to the Sultan, 
and that, accompariied by M. de Titoff, he had waited on the Grand 
Vizier, where ANE Pasha had subsequently arrived to take part in the 
conference. . 

This morning, by my direction, Mr. Alison saw the Grand Vizier, and 
M. Pisani saw Aali Pasha, in order to ascertain from those Ministers the 
precise nature of what had passed at Count Sturmer’s audience and at 
the Russian conference at Reshid Pasha’s. 

With some slight shades of difference in the two reports, it appears 
that the Sultan declared himself to act, with respect to the refugees, on 
the sole ground of humanity, intending to send them into the interior, and 
to order that care should be taken to prevent their doing any kind of 
harm to Austria or Russia. It further appears that Count Stirmer had 
endeavoured to persuade the Sultan that principles of humanity did not 
apply to pareone who, like these refugees, had occasioned so much dis- 
order and bloodshed. 

With respect to the Russian communications, it appears that they 
are couched in very strong language. 

‘The Emperor's letter announces the conclusion of the war in Hun- 
gary, and demands the extradition of the refugees. 

Count Nesselrode’s instruction requires an immediate and categorical 
answer as to the refugees, declaring that the future relations of the two 
empires with each other will depend upon its purport. 

In addition to those communications, M. de Pitott and Count Stirmer 


have declared that the escape of a single refugee will be taken for a 
declaration of war.

No. 16. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmeraton.—(Received October 1.) 


(No. 276.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 10, 1849. 


HIE, General Council which sat the day before yesterday at the Porte 
on the subject which at present almost exclusively occupies the attention 
of the Turkish Government, came to no final decision. Though Reshid 
Pasha was supported in his view of the question, which continues to be 
unfavourable to the Russian demand, by most of his colleagues, and par- 
ticularly by the Sheik-ul-Islam or Grand Mufti, he ex erienced such 
opposition fori others, influenced probably by the hope o overthrowing 
his Ministry, that he thought it advisable to obtain an adjournment of the 
meeting. it was therefore agreed that the Russian Envoy should be 
‘nvited to an interview by Aali Pasha or the Grand Vister, anc that before 
the Council adopted any final resolution, the Porte’s objections to the 
proposed extradition should be fully stated to his Excellency. 

Reshid Pasha and M. de Titoft met in consequence last night at the 
former's house. A statement explanatory of the Porte's sentiments respect- 
ing the question at issue was made by the Grand Vizier. The Russian 
Kinvoy, after listening for some time to lis Highness’ explanation, abruptly 
broke in upon it by exclaiming, “ The Porte then intends to refuse!" Reshid 
Pasha, in reply, disclaimed the inference, and urged his right to expect 
that the Pot ze’s well-founded objections should be submitted to the candid 
consideration of the two allied Emperors. M. de Titoff retired, after 
having said that he would talk the matter over with his colleague the 
Austrian Internunclio. 

in the course of this afternoon another meeting of the Council took 
place; and no further communication having been received from either of 
the Imperial Envoys, it was decided that a direct representation should be 
made to the Emperor himself at Warsaw, and that neither the assent nor 
the refusal—the “ yes” or “no” demanded by Russia—should be given to 
Prince Radzivil. 

I am assured that the difference of opinion exhibited at the previous 
meeting of the Council was no longer apparent, On that oceasion the 
Sheik-ul-Islam reprobated the required act of extradition as a breach of 
liga opposed to the law of Mahomet. The opposition originated 
with the Hekkim-Bashee, the Sultan’s state physician, who is a member of 
the Ulema, and accused of being deroe Russian interests, 

I] have, sc. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

No. 17. 
Sir Stralford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received October 1.) 
(No. 277.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 13, 1849. 
HE Porte has adopted secretly the intention of sending Fuad 
Effendi with a letter of explanation from the Sultan to the Emperor of 
Russia, and of addressing an explanation of similar purport to the Emperor 
of Austria through its Representative at Vienna, his attempt to depre- 


cate the resentment which its refusal to give up the refugees may pecasion, 
was not suggested by me, though it may possibly be the result of my 


~ 


ao 


general recommendation to accompany a firm adherence to the principles 
of humanity and honour with every suitable demonstration of will 
and friendly deference. The Porte, in sending Fuad Effendi to Warsaw. 
exposes itself to the risk of having him sent back without being received : 
but the advantage of manifesting a readiness to explain its objections, of 
putting Russia more completely in the wrong as to public opinion, and of 
gaining time, appears to outweigh in its conception the fear of that humilia- 
tion. It is hoped that the Emperor of Russia will be conciliated by a 
mission bearing in some respects the character of a complimentary tribute 
to the successes of his army in Hungary. 

Prince Radzivil is to have his audience of leave on the 15th instant 
and to take his departure on the ensuing day. He will be the bearer of a 
formal answer from the Sultan to the Emperor, referring to the more 
explicit letter which Fuad Effendi is charged to present to His Imperial 
Majesty. 


T have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING, 


No. 18. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston,—(Received October 1.) 
(No. 279.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 16, 1849. 


THE pending question between Russia with Austria on one side 
and the Porte on the other, has assumed not only a serious aspect, but a 
character of immediate urgency, It would seem that the former two 
Powers are determined to obtain possession of the refugees with the 
intention no doubt of consigning the most illustrious among them to 
the executioner, or at least that their Representatives are prepared to go 
the full length of diplomatic intimidation, in order to force the hands of 
the Porte. Count Sttirmer and M. de Titoff, after expressin their 
regret at the decision of the Council and their hope that the * urkish 
Ministers had well considered its consequences, and after havin endea- 
voured to undermine the firmness of Aali Pasha and the Grand Vizier by 
the insinuations of their secret agents, have sent in official notes repeatin 
their previous peremptory demand of the extradition of the refugees, an

more immediate approach of a danger against W ‘ch there is little security, 
and that of a precarious or contingent nature. Your Lordship will not be 
surprised to learn that, under these circumstances, the members of the 
Council are again divided in their opinions ; that the Sultan himself is per- 
pee and that the Grand Visier and his more ‘mmediate friends in the 
FJovernment are doubtful of the result and anxious to obtain all possible 
support from the British and French Representatives. 

Persuaded as | am that in this instance the Porte could not, without 
diseredit, give way to anything short of palpable necessity, especially at 
a moment when the Sultan’s direct appeal to the justice aud friendly sen- 
timents of the Emperor of Russia is actually on its way to Warsaw, I 
have no hesitation in adhering to the o ‘nions which have hitherto eruiclen 
my advice to the Porte. I have not hurried to press them again upon 
the Turkish Ministers and their Sovereign, because [thought it better to 
show confidence in their steadiness, to ayoid raising &ny unnecessary 
excitement, and to, abstain without urgent motives from volunteering 

ledges which it might be difficult to redeem. ‘The principal members of 
the Government, and indeed the Sultan, who is finally the Government 
itself, were already in possession of my sentiments. should have thought 
myself highly to blame if I had concealed from them my conviction that 
they were bound by no specilic engagement of treaty to give Up the 
refugees to Russia and Austria; that in offering to send them out of the 
country or to place them in the interior under guard, they did all that 
could be fairly expected of the Porte; that by submitting to the imperious 
demands addressed to them in 80 dictatorial a form, they would dishonour 
themselves and their country, violate the common principles of humanity, 
and entangle themselves in & system of policy of which they had hitherto 
struggled to keep clear, and which they could hardly adopt without chil- 
ling the sympathy of their friends and gradually estranging their most 
cordial supporters. 

These opinions, taking them as a whole, are not entertained by me 
alone. ‘They are singularly prevalent among all classes of persons, whether 
native or foreign. 1 have mors particularly found them where I felt most 
interest to look for them,-—in the language of my colleague the French 
Minister; and L kaow that his Excellency has not been backward on his 
side in conveying them to the knowledge of the Grand Vizier and other 
leading members of the Government, I may venture indeed to state that 
on more than one oceasion I have found General Aupick inclined to stimu- 
late my exertions, though at the same time declaring his readiness to follow 
rather than precede me in the course preseribed by humanity and sound 
consistent policy. 

Though several attempts were made in the course of yesterday to 
learn my sentiments as to what was considered to be a new stage of the 
pending queation, it Was not till a very late hour last night that received 
a direct application from Aali Pasha, ‘The purport of his Excellency’s 
message was that the Council was to deliberate to-day on the question

the French Minister. OF this paper a copy is herewith inclosed, together 
with copies of my answers and of the instruction which I addressed this 
morning to the interpreter charged with conveying them to Aali Pasha.

Sir Stratford Canning to M. Pisani. 


Sir, Therapia, September 16, 1849. 


AT a late hour last night.1 received from his Excellency Aali Pasha 
the paper of queries annexed to this instruction, with a request that I 
would communicate it to the French Minister, and return him an early 
answer this morning. 
I have in consequence had an interview with his Excellency General 
Aupick, and the accompanying paper contains the answers which we 
to return to the questions proposed to us by the Ottoman Secretary 
of State. 
This paper you will conve 
Aali Pasha, and in consigning it to his Excellency’s hands you will say 
that, althouch the menace of suspendin the dinlorianie relations of the 
Russian and Austrian Legations with the Porte was among the contin- 
gencies to be foreseen, and makes no real difference in the question of 
extradition, | have not hesitated to reply as cistiice ye the circumstances 
of the moment permit, to his inquiries ; and I trust that the Sultan's Minis- 
ters, ready, as they doubtless are, to provide for the essential object of 
extradition by other less objectionable means, and having referred irectly 
to the Emperor of Russia himself will not depart from their previous 
decision, involving the highest considerations of humanity, honour, and 
poucy: without the most mature and comprehensive deliberation. I mean 
y “comprehensive,” that which embraces the future position of the Porte 
as to its relations of confidential policy: and a knowledge of the opinion 
entertained on the point at issue by other friendly Governments. 
You will proceed from Aali Pasha’s house to the Porte, and keep 
yourself in readiness to communicate with his Excellency, and to inform 
me of the result of the Council with the least practicable delay. 


Tam, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Monsieur, Varsovie, le 4} Aodt, 1849. 


NOUS venons de recevoir la nouvelle que les réfugiés Polonais, Bem, 
Dembingki, Wysochi, et Zamoyski, qui ont joué un réle si important dans 
Vinsurrection Magyare, voyant aujourd hui cette cause définitivement 
perdue, se sont hatés de se sauyer en Turquie pour se soustraire au 


chatiment qu ils méritent. 


Nous avions lieu de nous attendre A cette fuite; car c'est lA la 
maniére d'agir que pratiquent invariablement dang tous les pays ces 


=i | 


27 


champions de anarchie, qui, apres avoir attisé les passions révolution- 
naires, fait éclater I'émeute ou la guerre eivile dans quelque contrée ou 
sous quelque prétexte que ce soit, ont toujours soin, A l'heure de la défaite 
de mettre leurs personnes en sireté, abandonnant a leur triste sort les 
malheureux qu’ils ont entrainés par leurs excitations. 

En intérét de morale, de bon ordre et de justice, engage 'Empereur a 
prescrire a votre Excellence d'exizer de la Porte avec énergie, que non 
seulement elle n’accorde pas asyle dans ses Etats aux réfugiés Polonais 
ci-dessus dénommés, mais encore qu'elle les fasse immédiatement arrater 
et livrer a nos autoritts militaires dans les Principautés du Danube. 

Ces individus sont des sujets de I'Empereur, qui, aprés s’étre rendus 
coupables de révolte envers lui, viennent de se compromettre de nouveau 
de Ja maniére la plus grave, en prenant le commandement des forces mili- 
taires d'une insurrection formidable, qui a mis non-seulement en danger 
l'existence de Empire d’Autriche, mais qui, par le projet avoué d’étendre 
la guerre et la sédition a tous les pays dont se composait l’ancienne 
Pologne, menagait également la sécurité et le repos de nos propres 
POSSESSIONS, 

Ein réclamant extradition des individus dont il s’agit, votre Excel- 
lence aura soin de formuler cette demande de maniére a faire comprendre 
de prime abord, qu'il n'entre pas dans les intentions de !'Empereur d'engager 
une controverse sur les principes de fausse philanthropie que la Porte 
s'attache 4 professer 4 l'égard des réfugiés politiques. Ces principes, au 
sujet desquels nous nous sommes plus d’une fois franchement expliqués 
envers le Cabinet Ottoman, sont d’ailleurs, comme le démontre l'évidence 
des faits récens, genre nent abandonnés en pratique par celles des 
Puissances Européennes qui en ont fait le plus parade. Ce que nous 
dlemandons & la Porte, c'est une détermination nette et décisive; il s'agit 
d'un oui ou d’un non. : 

Votre Excellence est invitée 4 poser la question en ces termes, et a 
mettre le Gouvernement Ottoman en demeure de se prononcer; elle aura 
seulement soin d’engager les Ministres du Sultana péser avec maturité 
les graves conséquences qu’entrainerait un refus opposé a la légitime 
réclamation de I'Empereur, refus qui, vd la haute importance que Sa 
Majesté attache 4 obtenir la satisfaction qui lui est die, réagirait néces- 
sairement de la_maniére la plus préjudiciable sur l'avenir des relations 
politiques de la Russie avec la Porte. 

Agréez, &c. 
(Signé) NESSELRODE.

NOUS avons examiné les notes qui ont éte données par les Légations 
de Russie et d'Autriche, portant que si on ne leur donnait pas une réponse 
favorable, leurs relations diplomatiques avec la Sublime Porte devaient 
atre considérées comme rompues. Or, dans notre Conseil c'est li une des 
éventualités que nous avons prévues et acceptées. Il n’y a done pas lieu 
de changer de décision ct “Wintention; d’autant plus que les réponses 
et les assurances de MM. les Représentans de la Grande Bretagne et 
de France, 4 l'occasion des questions qui leur ont été adressées, ont été 
considérées par nous comme prouvant que la raison est du cété de la 
Sublime Porte. C'est pourquoi nous avons unanimement jugé convenable 
de persister dans notre résolution précédente,

IT is my duty to inform your Excellency that diplomatic relations 
are formally suspended between the Porte on one side and the Russian 
and Austrian Legations on the other, in consequence of the ‘Turkish 
Government not having complied with a peremptory demand for the 
extradition to these Powers Fespeenyey of the Hungarian and Polish 
subjects who in considerable numbers have taken refuge in Turkey, It 
ia difficult to say where this difference aay stop, considering the very 
delicate nature of the point at issue, invo 
humanity and honour; nur would it be prudent for any Government whic 
takes an immediate interest in the independence and welfare of this empire, 
to be unprepared for those contingencies to which 80 precarious a state of 
things may immediately lead. ‘The Porte is engaged, while maintaining 


ving as it does a question of 


31 


its position, to remove by suitable explanations any adverse feelings whi

No, 25. 


Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston—(Received October 3.) 


(No. 285. Confidential.) 


My Serer = ain Therapia, September 19, 1849. 

; ALLED upon the Gran izier yesterday, and in a private inter- 
view submitted to him the importance of taking ache Lear 
nee in the present state of the Porte's relations with Russia aa 

ustria, on the principle of providing for the worst without giving way to 


exaggerated apprehensions, or attracting evil by a calles of preparation. 
| urged him in particular to remove the refugees from Widdin at once, and 


to make a safer disposition of the Turkish troops in Wallachia. 1 told 


him that clea os an immediate declaration of war appeared to be out of 
the question, if justice, reason, and established uasge were still to be 
respected by Russia, an attempt to seize the refugees by force, or to take 
more complete possession of the Principalities, might possibly be resorted 
to in a moment of disappointment and irritation; and that on this account 
+t was desirable that the Porte should diminish the chances of collision b 
an early adoption of suitable measures in the least offensive manner. It 
would be preferable, | said, to remove all the refugees without exception ; 
but if that were too inconvenient, it was at least necessary to remove those 
who were more particularly marked for vengeance by t eir eminent ser- 
vices in the defeated cause. 1 recommended that they should be removed 
by land at least as far as Adrianople, if not into Asia, but I observed that 
their removal to Candia, as originally intended, might create a suspicion of 
escape which it would be imprudent to hazard at pee 

With respect to the forces in Wallachia, which Reshid Pasha reckons 
at 20,000, I suggested that half should be at once brought into Bulgaria, and 
that the remainder, excepting only a portion necessary to support the police 
at Bucharest, should be stationed near Giurgevo, with means of conveyance, 
in cuse of emergency, across the Danube to Rustehuk. I further advised 
that those measures should not be adopted clandestinely, but that a com- 
munication, simultaneous with their execution, should be made to the 
Russian local authorities, with an assurance as to the refugees that their 
removal into the interior was intended as an additional security for the 
public peace, and that it would make no difference as to the question of 
their ulterior disposal ; and with respect to the army, that the change of 
positions had no other motive but a desire to diminish the expenses of the 
oceupation; and that it was to be hoped, without pretending to preseribe any 
rule of conduct to Russia, that the same consideration, a ded to the resto- 
ration of quiet in Transylvania and the advanced period of the season, 
would-be no less appreciated by the Court of St. Petersburgh than by the 
Porte itself. 

The Grand Vizier, as the French Minister had done before, agreed 
with me in this view of thesubject, and he is to take the sense of the Council 
upon it to-day. He had indeed asked my opinion respecting the Wal- 
lachian army several days ago; and the removal of the refugees into the 
interior had been pressed upon him at a much earlier period, and even 
before their arrival in Turkey, so as to occasion surprise respecting the 
cause, whatever it may have bea of his neglecting so obvious a measure of 
precaution, | 

In the course of my conversation with the Vizier I learnt with satis- 
faction that the intention of the Sultan and his Government is to maintain 
the present position throughout; that he has staked his official interests 
upon the question; that having gone so far, he feels the necessity of 
striving once for all to emancipate the Porte from its moral dependence on 
Russia: and that the means at his disposal are sufficient, even in the as 
yet improbable case of hostilities, to defend the capital and frontier against 
the immediate impression of a first attack. 

{ need not add that although it may be argued, not without trath, 
that the Porte would stand higher in general estimation and European 
sympathy, by resisting on a question of humanity and honour till over- 
come by physical force, so great a hazard could not be incurred with any 
prospect of ultimate success except under a well-founded expectation of 
timely assistance from abroad, 

‘he usual Turkish squadron is still at anchor in the Bosphorus, and 
between 40,000 and 50,000 troops, the Grand Vizier says 60,000, are 
quartered in this immediate neighbourhood, 

The Sultan has deferred an excursion which he contemplated in 
company with a part of his fleet to the Archipelago; and a grand review 
which was also to have taken place about Hp time is dropped for the 
present. 


Upon the whole I venture to hope that in the perilous contingencies 


So 


which now threaten the Porte, a. more than usual degree of prudence, as 


well as of firmness, may be reasonably counted on; but the final issue, 


whether it be one of emancipation or of increased submission with its 
riecessary consequences, will mainly, if not entirely, depend upon the 
degree of support and eventual assistance to be expected from England 
and France, and more especially from England. 
| L have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—( Received October 3.) 
(Private and Confidential.) 


My dear Lord, Therapia, September 19, 1849. 

WHEN Fuad Effendi’s instructions were forwarded to him under the 
impression that he would find the Emperor of Russia at Warsaw, I wrote 
to Colonel Du Plat, conceiving that the Turkish Commissioner, or rather 
Ambassador, for such is the character with which he is invested, might 
derive some advantage from communicating with that officer on terms af 
confidence. The letter which I addressed for this purpose to Her Majesty’s 
Consul explains concisely the state of the affair which has taken Fuad 
Effendi to Warsaw, and I have now the honour to inclose a copy of it for 
your Lordship’s information, though, if it be true that the Emperor has 
returned to St. Petersburgh, no. use can be made of it. | 

One of my colleagues has just informed me, on the strength of some 
expressions which dropped from one of the Russian Attachés in his hear- 
ing, that the Russian Legation is greatly embarrassed by the Porte’s 
resistance; and this appearance, for it is no more than an appearance, 
tends to confirm the prevailing impression, which | have difficulty in 
entertaining, that in the late proceedings here, M. de ‘Titoff has been rather 
pushed on by Count Stirmer than Austria by Russia.

Inclosure in No. 26. 


Sir Stratford Canning to Colonel Du Plat. 
(Confidential,) 


Sir, Constantinople, September 14, 1649. 


THE Sultan's Commissioner in Wallachia, Fuad Effendi, proceeds to 
Warsaw charged with a letter from His Majesty to the Emperor of Russia. 
lt is by him that I propose to forward this letter to you. Lt may be 
desirable, I think, for you to make his acquaintance, and to know what is 
the immediate object of communication between the two Sovereigns. 

Prince Radzivil, of whose mission you are probably informed, has not 
succeeded in obtaining the Sultan’s consent to the extradition of the 
Polish refugees. ‘The Sultan and his Ministers are unanimously of opinion 
that with every sentiment of deference and goodwill towards the Emperor 
of Russia, they cannot with any degree of honour or humanity accede to 
His Majesty's demand, ‘To the Austrian Internuncio, who has applied 
for the surrender of the Hungarian refugees, the same reluctant objections 
have been made, 

lt is not easy to conceive how they could have taken an other 
course, ‘They are hound by no treaty, with respect to political offenders 
received in Turkey, to do more than to send them away or to remove them 
from the frontier. One of these two things they profess themselves ready 
to do, and if so, after the complete overthrow and submission of the 
Hungarian insurgents and the dispersion of their leaders, the two Imperial 
Governments can hardly be supposed to have any motive derived from 


mM 


40) 


their own safety for insisting on the extradition of the refugees. As an 
example, the execution of those unfortunate men would be superfluous. 
Their utter discomfiture, flight, and exile, scem to suftice for that purpose. 

Surely the Porte eannot be expec ted to set aside every consideration 
of honour, humanity, consistency, and regard for the prevailing opinions 
of the greater part of Europe, in order to gratify a spirit of vengeance 
with which she has.no sympathy, or to enter into a system of policy which 
would change prejudicially the position she has hitherto studied to main- 
tain. . She fad adopted the resolution of not giving up the refugees before 
Prince Radzivil’s arrival here; and the means of intimidation which have 
been since employed to frighten her Ministers out of that resolution, could 
only have succeeded with a Government lost to every sense of its own 
dignity and independence. No discussion was to be allowed; no objec: 
tions were to be heard, the demand of surrender was peremptory; a 
© ¥os" or a “No!” Observe, too, that a manner of proceeding so dicta. 
torial and humiliating is fast becoming a habit with Russia in its dealings 
with this country; a habit not easy to reconcile with that solemn recogni- 
tion of the Sultan’s rights and deference for his dignity and independence 
declared by the Treaty of 1841, to which the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh 
was a party in common with the other Great Powers of Kurope. 

It may be hoped that the Emperor of Russia is too just and too 

nerous to persist in trying to force the hands of the Porte on a point 
rom which its principles, ‘fa sentiments, and its interests alike forbid it to 
recede, Even if His Majesty were not to be satisfied with the explana- 
tions offered by the Sultan, it is difficult to conceive that he would [eel 
himself justified before Europe in adopting any measure involving an act 
of hostility, or even an interruption of the usual diplomatic relations. 

‘At all events [ am anxious to do what little depends upon me 
favour the chances of a satisfactor solution, by putting you into personal 
communication with Fuad Effen i, whom on several oceasions I have 
found worthy of confidence, and whose firmness in the present instance 
may be put to severe trials. He has long been on terms of friendly and 
confidential intercourse with Her Majesty's Consul-General at Bucharest. 
Whatever may be the result of his visit. to Warsaw, I need not urge the 
importance of my being made acquainted with it as soon as possible, 
Her Majesty’s Government will also be anxious to have earl information 
upon the subject. My impression, I cannot say more on this oceasion, 18 
that they will enter fully into the Porte’s insuperable objections to extra- 
dition, and see with deep regret any important change in the friendly 
relations subsisting between Russia and Turkey. 1 have had no commu- 
nication whatever with my Russian and Austrian colleagues on the pend- 
ing question, Prince Radzivil paid me the compliment of # visit, which I 
returned: but-we have not met, and I understand that he has his audience 
of leave to-morrow, and gocs away on the following day, with a letter of 
compliment to the Emperor of Russia, in return for the one whieh he 
brought. I have, &e. 

(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Sir, Foreign Office, October 5, 1849. 

I HAVE received your despatch No. 48 of the 14th of September, 
containing copies of the correspondence which has passed between you 
and Fuad Effendi, respecting three Englishmen detained by the author- 
ities at Widdin ; and: I have to acquaint you that I approve of your 
proceedings in this matter. 

British subjects serving in the Hungarian army, would, if taken 
prisoners in Hungary, of course be liable to be kept and dealt with as 
prisoners of war, either by the Austrian or by the Russian troops, but 
there is no ground whatever upon which either the Austrian or Russian 
Government could require the Porte to deliver up to them British subjects 
who are within the Turkish territory,

Sir, Foreign Office, October 6, 1849. 


YOUR Excellency’s despatches to No. 285 of the 19th ultimo inclu- 
sive, have been received at this office and have been laid before the Queen; 
and | have to signify to you the entire approval of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment of the conihick which you have pursued in regard to the discussions 
which have taken place between the Porte and the Ministers of Austria 
and of Russia, on the subject of the demands made by the Austrian and 
Russian Governments for the surrender of the Hun arians and Poles, 
who, after the termination of the war in Hungary, have taken refuge 
within the Turkish territory. 

The Austrian and Russian Governments found their demands upon 
the Treaties of Passarovitch in 1715, and of Belgrade in 1739, between 
Turkey and Austria, and upon the Treaty of Kainardji of 1774, between 
Turkey and Russia. But it seems clear from the Articles of those Treaties 
which relate to refugees, and of which I annex copies, that the Porte is 
not bound to catanly with these demands. The XIVth Article of the 
Treaty of Passarovitch, and the XVIIIth Article of the "Treaty of Bel- 

rade, make no mention whatever of any mutual surrender of refugees ; 
and the lind Article of the Treaty at Kainardji gives the choice of an 
alternative, leaving it optional for each Party either to deliver up refugees, 
or to expel them from its territory. ‘The rorte has it seems taken this 
view of the engagements contained in these ‘Treaties, and deeming itself 
under no treaty obligation to deliver up the persons who have been 
claimed, it has mafused to do so; conceiving that to give them up without 
being obliged by treaty 80 to do, would be an act inconsistent with the 
laws of hospitality, repugnant to the feelings of humanity, disgraceful to 
the Turkish Government, and derogatory to the honour, the dignity, and 
independence of the Sultan's Throne. ‘The Turkish Government appears 
to have asked your Excellency and General Aupick, whether you con- 


curred in the interpretation whieh they had placed upon the treaties.

ference which has arisen between the Russian and the Turkish Govern- 
ments, upon the subject of the application made by Russia to ‘Turkey for 
the surrender of the Poles, who, upon the termination of the war in 
Hungary, took refuge in the Turkish territory, and threw themselves 
upon the protectin ospitality of the Sultan. 

The ‘Turkish Government not having, at the date of the last accounts 
which we have received from Constantinople, succeeded in satisfying the 
Russian Minister at that Court that the Sultan could not, without dis- 
honour, comply with the application which had been made to him ; ant 
the Russian Minister having thereupon officially declared that he must 
suspend his diplomatic intercourse with the Porte, the Turkish Govern- 
ment, distressed at the unfriendly tone of the Minister of a Power which 
has hitherto professed so sincere & desire to maintain the integrity and 
to uphold the independence of the Ottoman Empire, have addressed them- 
selyes to Her Majesty’s Government, to request the assistance and sup- 
sort of Great Britain, in the painful situation in which the Porte has thus 
yeen placed, 

Her Majesty's Government, sincerely anxious that the difference 
which has thus arisen, should not lead to further estrangement between 
two Powers, in the maintenance of whose friendly relations with each 
other Great Britain takes a deep interest, have readily determined to 
comply with the request of the Porte; and | have in consequence to 
address to you the present instruction. 

Her Majesty’s Government understand that the grounds upon which 
the Russian Government has applied for the surrender of these Poles, are 
the stipulations contained in the llnd Article of the Treaty concluded on 
the 10th July, 1774, between Russia and Turkey, at Kainardji. 

Now Her Majesty’s Government readily admit that the stipulations 
of that Article entitle the Russian Government to make the application 
which they have made; but Her Majesty's Government ea ber to 
submit, for the friendly consideration of the Government of Russia, that 
this same Article distinctly gives t0 the Sultan an alternative which he in 
equally entitled to choose; for by the stipulations of that Article cach of 
the Contracting Parties is at liberty either to surrender refugees, being 
subjects of the other Party, or to expel them from its own territory. Tt 1s 
clear, therefore, that the Sultan «= not bound by treaty to comply with 
the application made to him by the Russian Minister at Constantinople 
for the surrender of the Polish refugees; and that he would fulfil to the 
very letter the obligations of the Treaty, by requiring those Polish 
refugees to depart from his dominions, 

This being the case, the question arises, whether the Sultan is called 
upon by international usage or by the duties of good neighbourhood, to 
do that which he is not obliged by treaty to do. 

Now if there is one rule which more than another has been observed 
., modern times by all independent States, both great and small, of the 
eivilized world, it is the rule not to deliver up political refugees, unless the 
State is bound to da so by the jositive obligations of a treaty ; and Her 
Majesty's Government believe that such treaty engagements are few—if 
indeed any such exist, 

The laws of hospitality, the dictates of humanity, the general feelings 
of mankind, forbid such surrenders ; and any independent Government, 
which of its own free will were to make such a surrender, would be 
deservedly and universally stigmatized as degraded and dishonoured, 

lt appears then to Her Majesty’s Government, that the Sultan, being 
bound by no treaty engagements in this respect, was compelled by a due 
regard for his own honour and for the dignity of his Crown, to decline to

has hitherto and for a long course of time been considered as one of the 
firmest and staunchest allies of the Ottoman Empire, have addressed 
themselves to Her Majesty’s Government to request the assistance and 
support of Great Britain in the painful situation in which the Porte has 
thus been placed, 

Her Majesty's Government, sincerely anxious. that the difference 
which has thus arisen should not lead to further estrangement between 
two Powers. in the maintenance of whose friendly relations with each 
other Great Britain takes a deep interest, have readily determined to 
comply with the request of the Porte, and [have in consequence to address 
to your Excellency the present instruction, 

[t appears that the application for the surrender of these Hungarians 
18 founded upon the stipulations contained in Article XLV of the Treaty 
between Austria and Turkey at Passarowitz on the 2ist July, 1718, and 
upon Article XVIII of the Treaty concluded between those same Powers 
on the 18th September, 1789, at Belgrade. 

Now Her Majesty's Government would beg to submit to the con- 
sideration of the Government of Austria, that those Articles of those 
Treaties contain no engagement whatever by which either of the Con- 
tracting Parties can be required by the other to surrender persons of any 
kind who have taken refuge in its territory. Those Articles contain no 
engagement for, mutual surrender of fugitives or refugees, though they 
do contain other stipulations as to the manner in which such persons are 
to be dealt with. 

It is clear therefore that the Sultan is not bound by Treaty to comply 
with the application made by the Austrian Minister at Constantinople for 
the surrender of the Hungarian refugees. 

This being the case, the next question which arises is, whether the 
Sultan is called upon todo so by international usage and by the duties 
of good neighhourhood. 

Now il there is one rule which more than another has been observed 
in modern times by all independent States, hoth great and small, of the 
civilized world, it is the rule not to deliver up political refugees, unless the 
State is bound to do so by the positive stipulations of a treaty; and Her 
Majesty's Government, believe that such treaty engagements are few,—if 
indeed any such exist, 

The laws of hospitality, the dictates of humanity, the general feelings 
of mankind, forbid such surrenders; and any independent Government, 
which of its awn free will were to make such a surrender, would be 
deservedly and universally stigmatized as degraded and dishonoured. 

lt appears then to Her Majesty's Government, that the Sultan being 
bound by no treaty engagement in this respect, was compelled by a due 
regard both for his own honour and forthe dignity of his Crown, to decline 
to comply with the application which was made to him for the surrender 
al the Hungarians, 

But the Sultan has duties of good neighbourhood to fulfil towards 
Austria: and those duties require that he should not permit his territory 


49 


of the case impose upon him in this matter towards the Emperor of 
Austria, To require from the Porte more than this would be to infringe 
upon the independence of the Sultan; but Her Majesty’s Government think 
too highly of the sense of justice which must animate the Austrian Govern- 
ment, to vclieve that Austria can desire to impair that independence ; and 
Her Majesty's Government are persuaded that the Cabinet of Vienna 
cannot think that it would be sound policy for Austria to do 80. 

It was indeed no longer ago than the month of July 1841, that 
Austria in conjunction with France, Great Britain, Prussia, and Russia, 
recorded and proclaimed to the world, in the preamble of a solemn treaty 
concluded between the Five Powers and the Sultan, her desire and deter- 
mination to respect the inviolability of the Bovereton rights of the Sultan. 
> Her Majesty’s Government cannot believe that the sentiments and 
thé policy which then guided the Austrian Councils in regard ‘to Turkey, 
‘do not equally prevail at Vienna at the present time; and Her Majesty's 
Government therefore confidently hope, that as the Sultan has expressed 


his intention of making such arrangements in regard to these Hungarian 


-refugees, as must relieve the Austrian Government from uneasiness on 


-their. score, the Cabinet of Vienna will not press upon the Porte any 


demands which could not be complied with consistently with a due regard 
to the honour of the Sultan and the independence of his Throne. 

As the best mode of conveying, these sentiments and wishes of Her 
Majesty's Government to the Government of Austria, your Excellency 
will read this despatch to Prince Sebyvarzenberg, and you will give him 
a copy of it.

stipulations of the Treaty of Koutschouk Kainardji, the letter of which,

considered at that time, he judges to be favourable to the Russian claims, 
when she might have drawn a better argument and a recent precedent 
from the refusal of Austria to give up Prince Ypsilanti, at the demand 
of the ‘Turkish Government, during the Greek revolution, alleging, with

put forward no separate and independent claims on the Turkish Govern- 
ment, and can only participate in such concessions as the Power which

allered rebellion having been directed, not against the Russran, but: . 


against the Austrian Government.

ments, but 1 thought it mi ht be interesting to your Lordship to know 
the opinion of a foreign Minister on this question, who, though of no 
rreat diplomatic experience, has made his way entirely by his own 
abilities, and has had the advantage, ‘nasmuch as that bears on the 
subject, of a long residence in the East.

D'APRES létroite liaison et lamitié qui existent entre ma Sublime 


Porte et l'illustre Cour d’Autriche, la durée de la prospérité et lintégrité 
de votre empire ont de tout temps été l'objet des vouux les plus ardens de 
mon Gouvernement et de ma nation. Tout ce qui peut y porter atteinte 
nous fait une peine extréme, comme tout ce qui peut les consolider nous 
cause une vive satisfaction. 

Par conséquent, les grands ¢yénemens qui ont fait disparaitre les 
traces des troubles et des divisions des Etats de votre Majesté Impériale, 
m’ont comblé de joie, et je m’empresse de vous en féliciter. 

Je prie de tout mon coeur le Maitre de l'Univers de faire que désor- 
mais vos Etats soient en paix et heureux sous votre autorité légitime, et 
que votre régne soit pour votre empire et pour vos sujets une nouvelle 
ére de repos et de tranquillité, 

J'ai chargé mon Ministre auprés de votre Majesté Impériale d’entrer 
en détail avec votre Ministére sur le parti que j'ai pris de garder, de 
maniére 4 ce que dorénavant ils soient dans l'impuissance d'intriguer et 
de former des projets séditieux, les quelques individus qui par suite de 
la cessation de la lutte en Hongrie se sont réfugiés dans mes Etats, et 
sur mes raisons pour me dispenser de les rendre. | 

Je prie votre Majesté Impériale, au nom de lancienne amitié qui 
existe entre les deux Cours, au nom de |'honneur de la souveraineté qui 
doit yous @tre cher aussi, d'écouter en toute confiance et d'une maniére 
favorable, les communications que mon Ministre fera. 

J’ai l'espoir que votre Majesté appréciera équitablement mes justes 
excuses et mes intentions pures; et je saisis, &c.

for their immediate enlargement. The names of the individuals in

The Ottoman Secretary of State has returned a favourable answer; 
and as soon as the Sultan’s sanction can be obtained, I hope to receive the 
order for which I have applied, and to effect the release of those gentle- 
men with the least practicable delay.

59 


It is not antipathy to Austria, though so well merited at the hands 
of every Hungarian, but'a true conviction, which makes me say that even 
Austria has lost far more by her victory, gained through Russian aid, than 
she would have lost in merited defeat through honourahle arrangement. 
Fallen from her position of first-rate Power, she has now forfeited her 
self-consistency, and has sunk into the obedient instrument of Russian 
ambition and of Russian commands. 

Russia only has gained at this bloody game. She has extended and 
strenethened her influence in the East of Europe, and threatens already 
in a frightful manner, with outstretching arms, not only the integrity but 
the moral basis of the Turkish Empire. 

May it please you, my Lord, to allow me to communicate to your 
Excellency a most revolting condition which the Turkish Government, 
atthe suggestion of Russia, is about to impose on us poor homeless 
exiles. 

I, the Governor of unhappy Hungary, after having, I believe, as a 
gon eitizen and honest man, fulfilled to the last my duties to my country, 

ad no choice left me but between the repose of the grave and the inex- 
pressible anguish of expatriation. 

Many of my brethren in misfortune had preceded me on the Turkish 
territory. I followed thither in the hope that I should be permitted to 
pass to England, and there, under the protection of the English people— 
a protection never yet denied to persecuted man—allowed to repose for 
a while my wearied head on the hospitable shore of your happy island. 

But even with these views [ would rather have surrendered myself 
to my deadliest foe, than to cause an difficulties to the Turkish Govern- 
ment, whose situation ] well knew how to ap reciate, and therefore did 
not intrude upon the Turkish territories without. reviously inquiring 
whether 1 and my companions in misfortunes should willingly received, 
and the protection of the Sultan Hines to us. 

We received the assurance that we were welcome guests, and should 
enjoy the full protection of His Majesty the Padishah, who would rather 
sacrifice 50,000 men of his own subjects than allow one hair of our heads 
to be injured. 

It was only upon this assurance that we passed into the Turkish ter- 
ritory, and according to this generous assurance we were received and 
tended on our journey, received in Widdin as the Sultan's guests, and 
treated through four weeks, whilst waiting from Constantinople further 
orders as to the continuation of our sad journey to some distant shore. 

Even the Ambassadors of England and France, to whom I ventured 
in the name of humanity to appeal, were so kind as to assure me of their 
full sympathy. 

is Majesty the Sultan was also so gracious as to give a decided 
newative to the inhuman pretensions of our extradition set forth by Russia 
and Austria. 

But a fresh letter from His Mejeaty the Czar arrived in Constan- 
tinople, and its consequence was the threat and the suggestion sent to us 
by an express message of the Turkish Government, that the Poles and 

ungarians, and in particular myself, Count Casimir Batthyany, Minister 
of Foreign Affairs of Hungary under my government, and the Generals 
Messaros and Perezel (all present here), would be surrendered unless we 
chose to abjure the faith of our forefathers in the religion of Christ and 
become Mussulmans. 

‘And thus 5000 Christians are placed in the terrible alternative either 
oF facing the scaffold or of purchasing their lives by abandoning their 
sth. 

So low is already fallen the once mighty Turkey, that she can devise 
no other means to answer or evade the ‘Barua of Russia. 


Words fail me to qualify these astonishing suggestions, such as never 
have been made yet to the fallen chief of a generous nation, and could 
hardly have been expected in the nineteenth century. 

My answer does not admit of hesitation. Between death and shame 
the choice can be neither dubious nor difficult. Governor of Hungary 
and elect to that high place by the confidence of 15,000,000 of my coun-
