33 


60 


trymen, 1 know well what 1 owe to the honour of my country even in 
exile, Even as a private individual, | have an honourable path to pursue. 
Once governor of a generous country, I leave no heritage to my children, 
They shall at least bear an unsullied name. God's will he done. I am 
prepared to die; but as I think this measure dishonourable and injurious 
to Turkey, whose interests I sincerely have at heart, and as I feel it a ees 
to save my companions i exile if | can from a degrading alternative, 
have replied to the Grand Vizier in a temporizing manner, and took also 
the liberty to apply to Sir Stratford Canning and General Aupick for their 
generous aid against this tyrannic act. 

In full reliance on the noble sentiments and generous principles of 
your Excellency, by which as well as through your wisdom you have 
secured the esteem of the civilized world, I trust to be excused in inclosing 
copies of my two letters to the Grand Vizier and Sir Stratford Canning. 

1 am informed that the whole matter is a eabal against the Ministry 
of Reshid Pasha, whose enemies would wish to force him to our extra- 
dition in order to lower it in public estimation and render im oasible its 
continuance in office, It is certain that in the Grand Council held on the 
9th and 10th of September, after a tumultuous debate the majority of the 
Council declared in favour of our extradition, the majority of the 
Ministry against it. No decision was come to in consequence of the 
altercation which took place, hut notwithstanding, the Ministry thought 
fit to make us the revolting yt aati IT have named. : 

This mode of solving the ¢ ifficulty would not, Tam convinced, save, 
the Ministry, because @ protection only given in contradiction of the 
Sultan's generous feeling, at the price of 5000 Christians abandoning, 
their faith, would be revolting to the whole Christian world, and prove 
hardly calculated to win sympathies for Turkey in the event of war with 
Russia, which in the opinion of the most experienced Turkish statesmen 
is approaching fast. 

As to my native country, Turkey does, | believe, already feel the loss 
of the neglected opportunity of having given to Hungary at least some 
moral help to enable it to cheek the advance of the common enemy, But. 
in my humble opinion it appears to me that it would be a very ill-advised 
mode of gaining Hungarian sympathies by sending me to an Austrian 
scaffold, and foreing my unhappy companions to abjure their religion or 
accept the same alternative. 

No friends to the Turkish Government would spring up from my 
blood shed by her broken faith, but many deadly foes. 

My Lord, your heart will | am sure excuse my haying called your 
attention to our unhappy fate, since it has now assumed political 
importance. 

Abandoned in this unsocial land by the whole world, even the first 
duties of humanity give us no promise 0 protection, unless, my Lord, you 
and your generous nation come forward to protect 1s. 

‘What steps it may be expedient that you should take, what we have 
a right to expect from the well-known venerosity of England, it would be 
hardly fitting for me to enter on, 

[ place my own and my companions’ fate in your hands, my Lord, 
and in Aas name of humanity throw myself under the protection of 
England. 

Time presses. Our doom may ina few days be sealed, Allow me to 
make an humble personal request. I am a man, my Lord, prepared to 
face the worst, and | can die with a free look at heaven as I have lived. 

But | am also, my Lord, a husband, son, and father. My poor true- 
hearted wife, my children, and my noble old mother, are wandering about 
Hungary. ‘They will probably soon fall into the hands of those Austrians 
who delight in torturing even feeble women, and with whom even the 
innacence of childhood is no protection against persecution. 

l Sonus your Excelleney, in the name of the Most High, to pat ii 
stop to these crueltics by your powerful mediation, and especially ta 
aceord to my wife and children an asylum on the soil of the generous 
English people. | 


As to my poor, my loved, and noble country, mast she too perish for 


61 


Byer? Shall she, unaided, abandoned to her fate, and unavenged, be 
doomed to annihilation by her tyrants. Will England, once her hope, not 
become her consolation? The political interests of civilized Europe, so 
many weighty considerations respecting England herself, and ahiaky: the 
maintenance of the Ottoman Empire, are too intimately bound up with 
the existence of Hungary for me to lose all hope. } 

My Lord, may od the Almighty for many years protect you, that 
you may long protect the unfortunate and live to be the guardian of the 
rights of freedom and humanity. 

I subseribe, &e.

and subsequently an eye-witness of the mill ys Bares qistaton ol a

then ce the mountains from Transylvania into Wallachia with Generals

provided with an English passport) with the Hungarian and Polis! 
refugees by the ‘Purkish authorities at Widdin, Under these peer 
“staneca I consider it my duty to address a few remarks to your is ip

ave been unreservedly commanicated fo me. |. ton 
ha Ths fortitude displayed by M. Kossuth in this trying Bouse

67 


able, He distinctly perceives that the consequences of the shameful step 
recommended to him would be ruinous to the cause he has most at heart; 
but it demands’a longer experience of the corruption and fanaticism, or, 
what amounts to the same thing, the hypocrisy, which characterize so 
large a re of the governing class in Turkey, to appreciate the motives 
by which this offer has been dictated. ‘The whole affair may I believe be 
explained as follows 

The Grand Vizier finding he could obtain no positive pledge from the 
French and English Ambassadors, that in the event of war resulting from 
a resistance to the demands of the Emperor of Russia, the Porte might 
depend on the active support of their respective Governments, had then 
recourse to the Great Council of State. Here, however, he experienced a 
similiar disappointment; the dishonour involved in the extradition of Hun- 
garian and Polish exiles was by a large majority declared to be preferable 
to the alternative held out by the Emperor. Such a measure being appa- 
rently most repugnant to the feelings not only of the Ministers but of the 
Sultan himself, Reshid Pasha next adopted an expedient which he con- 
ceived must, as far as the Turks were concerned, overcome all opposition. 
He privately despatched a steamer with agents to Widdin, strongly urging 
the refugees to declare themselves Mussulmans, he felt connident in this 
case, that no Turk would dare to propose their extradition to the Russians. 
Now whether right or wrong in this conclusion, it is certain that with 
reference to csr, eke and the rest of Europe, he overlooked two important 
considerations. Suchan act of compulsory apostacy must excite universal 
diseust, and should hostilities ensue, Turkey instead of meeting support 
and sympathy, would be left to her own resources, without a friend or 
ally in all Christendom. And in the next place the influence of the men 
on whom he depends for enlisting on his side the people of Poland and 
Hungary, would be utterly annihilated. 

t happens most fortunately, therefore, and I rejoice that I can 
announce to your Lordship that the experiment has on the whole proved 
a decided failure. Out of more than 150 individuals belonging to the civil 
or military service of the late Hun arian Government, Ministers, Employés, 
Generals, and Officers, not more than fourteen have, to save their lives, 
consented to abjure their religion, Amongst these are Generals Bem, 
Stein, and Keinetthi, With respect to the first of these no one can fora 
moment suspect him of cowardice in becoming a Turk; he only seeks 
another chance of making war on Russia. Stein is a German, an able 
cone officer, but a mere mercenary and soldier of fortune, who never 
had the confidence of the Hungarians. Keinetthi isa brave but uneducated 
man, who has risen from the ranks of the Austrian army. [t would be 
unnecessary to mention the names of the remainder of this small band of 
proselytes: they have up to this time not been joined by a single private 
soldier, It remains now to be seen whether the Porte will accept of this 
limited number of conversions, and whether in ease it should do so, the 
Emperor of Russia will on these grounds be content to take a less number 
of victims. 

As in his autograph letter to the Sultan he ts said to have written 
that the escape of a single individual from Widdin would constitute a 
casus belli, it is more than probable that he will not abate an iota of his 
pretensions. General Bem must of all others be chiefly obnoxious to his 
displeasure, when it is hardly to be supposed that he will not insist upon 
his being given up with the rest. Should the Turks therefore refuse to 
comply with these demands, war would appear to be the inevitable conse- 
quence, and with this certaint before them, it would be folly on their part 
to surrender those of the refugees who had adhered to their Christian 
faith, and who would be precisely the agents who might be depended 
upon for exciting to arms and securing the Sopata oy of the inhabitants 
of Poland and Hungary. But the chances of the Porte, entering upon a 
war, if unsupported by the Western Powers, ainst Austria and Russia, 
are too precarious to dissipate the terrors which cast every day a deeper 

ioom over the devoted exiles of Widdin, ‘Their only reasonable hope of 
deliverance is founded on the prompt and energetic interference of Her 
Majesty's Government, alone or in concert with that of the French Re- 


ry 


| 


———aaee 


8 


ublic. They scarcely believe it oasible that they and the Sultan, who 
anid wist to eee the can be thus deliberately abandoned to their 
fate. It must ie evident'to all, that if, together with international law and 
the rights of humanity, the independence of the Ottoman Empire be thus 
trampled upon with impunity, Russia, with the footing she has newly 
acquired in the Danube, will henceforward obtain an undisputed sove- 
reignty at Constantinople, for there would seem to beno imaginable case in 
which the Western Powers would venture on a war to protect that 
i ndence. 
Me here ia every probability on the other hand, that the mere threat of 
hostilities would at once induce the Emperor to listen to reason In this 
affair; unless in consequence of the recent triumph of his arms, he is 
labouring under a delusion as to the military resources of hig empire, and 
inflated with the arrogance which has been usually observed to precede a 
fall, and which the “Burks, whom he treats so contemptuously, may be 
the destined instruments in the hands of Providence to chastise. The 
military resources of Russia have never been so much overrated as at this 
moment. She has gained a great prestige from the successful termination 
h yatjeae empaign, but if the truth were known, she would have lost 
rather than have gained ground in public estimation. She was indebted 
for her successes neither to the valour of her troops nor the skill of her 
generals. Notwithstanding the efficiency of the Russian artillery and 
superior discipline of the cavalry, the army asa whole was an unmanageable 
mass, the officers were notoriously disaffected, the soldiers spiritless and 
half-famished, and on all occasions ready to desert to the enemy. But the 
Hungarians were unfortunately on their side still more disheartened and 
demoralized; they never for an instant believed that they could make a 
successful stand against the combined forees of Austria and Russia ; with 
reater confidence in themselves, rough their armies were com 
chiefly of raw levies, and these very badly armed and officered, I do not, 
doubt that the result would have been widely different. At Temeswar I 
saw the allied army chased from position to position for the space of four 
hours, and it is certain that a decisive victory would have been gained by 
Generals Bem and Guyon if, by some fatal inadvertence, the whole of the 
ammunition had not been sent forward on the road to Arad. Could the 
Turks have been induced to send a small subsidiary force into Hungary @ 
few months ago, or even to furnish the Hungarians with a few thousand 
muskets, the scale might have been easily turned in favour of the latter. 
But they would now lind the task more difficult, not on account of any 
hysical inferiority, for though the Russians may have a better appointee 
artillery, the Turks, payee ly and morally too, are in better fightin 
order, they are much better fed, and animated with a better spirit. Still 
in any war which the Turks might wage alone against one or more Chris- 
tian Doweta, ‘t is not to be expected they would command the sincere 
sympathies of any Christian people, even of such as acknowledge the 
sovereignty of the Sultan ; for they naturally fear that the recovery of their 
former power might lead to the revival of their former oppression, But 
the alliance of England and France would be taken as a pledge that their 
rights and privileges would continue to be respected, and it Is ensanlehing 
how far such a security would go to rally the hristian populations roun 
the throne of the Sultan. 
I have, &c. |

(Secret.) 
My Lord, Paris, October 11, 1849. 

| RECEIVED on Monday morning the 8th instant, your Lordship's 
despatches to Vienna, St. Petersburgh, and Constantinople, on the subject 
of the recent differences of the Porte with Russia and Austria; also one 
directing me to communicate them confidentially to the French Govern- 
ment. ‘This instruction I proceeded immediately to execute. Since the 
first diplomatic rupture between those Powers was known here by the 
telegraph, I have felt it my duty to keep your Lordship informed almost 
daily of the views and sentiments of both the Ministers and leading men 
in France upon this complicated question, 

I therefore now consider myself dispensed from entering into man 
details which had the result been different I should have considered it 
necessary to put upon record; but as the eflect of my representations has 
been to induce, on the part of the French Government, the adoption of a 
line of conduct prectealy in accordance with the views of Her Majesty's 
Government, it will now suffice to state shortly some of the grounds on 
which in particular points there was hesitation on the part of some of the 
members of the French Government, the only effect of which, as the matter 
now stands, has been to delay a couple of days the further transmiss.on af 
some of the despatches. 

Upon the main point of the importance to this country of maintaining 
the independence of Turkey, no one has openly expressed difference of 
opinion, though no doubt the feeling as to the extent to which other 
dangers are to be risked for that object, is in many minds much influenced 
by the sense of their present internal difficulties. ‘The interest which at 
any other moment the leading men in France would have felt in the Hun- 
garian struggle, was much checked by the conviction of that close part- 
nership between all the revolutionists in Europe, of which they had proof 
in the case of Rome, and which they believed to be equally the mainspring 
of the insurrection, in a country of whose real state they know so little. 
Considering the dangers from which they hardly feel themselves to have 

et escaped, to be aggravated by the spread of this spirit, they certainly 
elt relieved by the termination of the war in Hungary. 

A quarrel which ostensibly had its origin in the safety of the chiefs in 
the late contest, therefore at first sight was viewed in connexion with a 
se different state of previous public feeling than that which had pre- 
vailed in England, However, upon second thoughts, the unheard-of 
nature of the demand made by Russia and Austria, and the political 
danger of submitting to it, had their due weight, and there seems to have 
been unanimity amongst those who have the conduct of affairs, that the 
line taken by the French Representative at Constantinople must be firmly 
supported. There then remained the practical question as to how this 
was to be done with the least chance of war, which in the present state of 
the country they think would now be an unexampled evil. ‘There were 
some who felt in addition, that should the contest. become general, the 
existence of France might be compromised, whilst England must remain 
in all essentials invulnerable. These considerations were all brought to 
bear upon the one practical and immediate point—the action of the fleet. 
"The areuments were few, but the voices were many by which it was main- 
tained that it was desirable in the first instance to try the effect of the 
verbal representations made at the two Imperial Courts; ‘that should 
these be unsuccessful, it would then be time enough to take a step, which, 
if in the quarter to which it was directed was not actual menace, indicated, 
“ they thought prematurely, an intention to go beyond purely diplomatic 
imits, 

[ should here add that some even of those who now thought, as the 


~ case was brought before them, they could not do otherwise’ than adopt the 


43 


Ou 


course we had already done, still regretted that before that step had been 
taken and orders sent, there had not been a regular official communication 
made to Paris. | reminded these in the frst ‘nstance that from the very 
moment the question was discussed between us, I had always given as my 
personal opinion that any diplomatic representation must in this case 
accompanied by such a naval demonstration, and | had never heard from 
any of the French Government with whom I conversed any objection ta 
auch a course; but I said that it was more important for them to recoliect 
that this was not a step originating in London, It was understood that 
Sir Stratford Canning who on the spot must be supposed to be the best 
judge of the present exigency of the case and of the importance of 
the. effect whieh would thas be produced, either in avoiding danger OT 
giving moral alate to the just resistance of the Porte, had himself 
ritten to Sir William Parker, on his own responsibility, to come Up 
to the Dardanelles, and the Admiral was only waiting for the conlirma- 
tion from London of that requisition, Under these circumstances the 
British Government would not after consultation have changed their 
-gesolve, and even the delay which would have been eaused by commu- 
-nications between Paris and London might have compromised the vital 
interests of the question. : 
But whilst the step had already been taken, the intention had been so) 
well concealed, that these despatches, whieh it was hoped would produce the : 
desired effect upon the Russian and Austrian Governments, would arrive: 


at their destination and might receive their answer before the approach of” 


the fleets could be known. I therefore urged most stron ly that our joint 
action should. not be in the eyes of Europe a bye-word, which wou d be 
the case if, whilst the English fleet moved up towards the Dardanelles, the 
Krench flect remained at Toulon. I said the real danger of war would be 
produced by such hesitation, which would of course be immediately re- 
ported to Vienna and St, Petersburgh; whilst in the cordial and ostensible 
inion of these two great Powers of the West, I saw the seat assurance 
for the peace of Europe. It ig unnecessary that I should dwell any longer 
upon the representations | made, or enter into any details of the quarter 
where these were most needed, as the Council yesterday decided (as | 
communicated at once in & few hasty lines) that the French fleet should 
be telegraphed to put to sra immediately, and the instructions were to be 
prepared and forwarded at once by & special steamer, with the hope that 
she might reach the squadron before it arrived off Naples. | understand 
those instructions are to be to the effect that the French Admiral is to 
bear up towards Smyrna, and put himself in communication with Sir 
William Parker. 

L have marked this “Secret,” as the French Government consider it 
of great importance, OF aceount of their Parliamentary difficulties, that 
this decision should not be known for some days.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston—(Received October 15.) 
(No. 295.) 
My Lord, 


Therapia, September 28, 1649. 
WE are not yet in possession of any intelligence calculated to throw 
light on the manner in which the Emperors of Russia and Austria may be 
expected to receive the Porte’s explanation of its motives for not comply- 
ing with their peremptory demand for the extradition of the refugees from 
Hungary. It appears that Fuad Effendi set out from Bucharest with the 
Sultan's letter on the 2Ist instant. But it is not clear whether he had 
obtained passports for entering within the Russian frontier, and it is 
rumoured that he has taken a circuitous route towards Warsaw, where he 
will pone) not find the Emperor. 

‘he prevailing impression here is, that M.de Titoff, influenced by 
Count Stiirmer, has exceeded the strict limits of his instructions in sus- 
pending his diplomatic relations with the Porte; but such a proceeding 
is by no means consistent either with the position of a Russian Minister 
or with the personal character of M. de Titoff, 

Tam assured that the Prussian Representative, though I have not 
seen him myself since the departure of Prince Radzivil, has expressed to 
Aali Pasha opinions decidedly favourable to the Porte’s view of the 

ending question. Nothing has occurred to indicate any relaxation of 
Bisiiiens on the part of the Turkish Ministers, The only member of the 
Council who persisted in showing any marked opposition to the line of 
conduct proposed by Reshid Pasha has been dismissed from office. 
I have, &e.

& exécution pour intérner les réfugiés dans une partie reculée de l'Empire 
Ottoman, ou bien les éloigner du territoire Turque, lorsque, A la douloureuse 
surprise de la Sublime Porte, un ultimatum collectif de Représentans de 
la Russie et de l’Autriche 4 Constantinople vint poser au Gouvernement 
Ottoman le cas d’extradition immédiate des réfugiés, avec menace de 
rompre les relations avec la Sublime Porte en cas de refus. Votre Excel- 
lence ne peut ignorer que cette menace a déja recu son exécution en pré- 
sence d'une sommation qu’aucun trailé ne justifie, que les usages diplo- 
matiques repoussent comme attentatoire 4 lindépendance des nations, et 
qui n'est pas plus fondée en droit et en justice qu'elle ne lest dans les 


formes consacrées. La réponse du Gouvernement Ottoman ne pouvait ¢tre 


douteuse: il a refusé de livrer les réfugiés, tout en maintenant sa déclara- 
tion préalable, 

Cette résolution, dictée par les principes éternels de 'humanité et de 
lhonneur, le Gouvernement du Sultan l'a prise, M. le Ministre, avec la 
conscience de sa gravité. Placé entre une faiblesse qui entrainait la 
déconsidération, et une résistance honorable bas¢e sur son droit, le Sultan 
et son Gouvernement ont reculé devant un acte de déloyauté. Mais en 
reculant ils se portaient par la pensée et par l'espérance vera cette noble 
France, la puissante et généreuse alliée de la Turquie, 

Je viens donc, M. le Ministre, au nom du Gouvernement du Sultan, 
demander au Gouvernement de la République lassistance morale et maté- 
rielle dela France. En faisant cet appel ala généreuse sympathie d'un 
grand peuple qui n’a jamais connu d'autre guide ni obéi & d'autre mobile 
qu’aux lois de I'houneur et de "humanité, jose espérer que je n’ai pas 
trop présumé de sa bienveillance traditionnelle envers la Turquie, et je 
m’en rapporte a lui avee pleine confiance., 

Veuillez, &e. 
(Signe) CALLIMAKI,

FUAD EFFENDI arrived here on the evening of the 5th instant, 
and his Excellency sent me on the following day a lettqx of which he was 
the bearer from Colonel Du Plat, inclosing one which SirStratford Canning 
had addressed to }ler Majesty's Consul at Warsaw, under the impression 
that Fuad Efendi would find the Emperor at that capital. The copy of 
your Lordship’s despatch to Sir Stratford Canning No. 230, of the I3th 
ultimo, transmitted to me in your Lordship’s despateh No, 243, of the 
28th ultimo, had fortunately just reached me, making me acquainted with 
the opinion of Eler Majesty's Government ses ine the demand which 
has been made by Austria at Constantinople, for the extradition of the 
persons who have lately escaped from Hungary into the Turkish territory; 
and I therefore determined to call upon Fuad Effendi, and offér him every 
support in the prosecution of the object of his mission, which [ could pro- 
perly afford him without instructions from your Lordship, by availing 
myself of the knowledge which I possessed of the views of Her Majesty's 
Government on the merits of the question at issue between the Austrian 
and the ‘Turkish Governments, : i; 

[ consequently wrote a few lines to his Excellency, of which I annex 
a copy, proposing to wait upon him on the following day; and 1 received 
the reply of whieh a copy is also annexed, 

When L called at his Excellency’s hatel on Sunday the 7th instant, he 
expressed his great gratification at my kindness in COME to him before 
he had paid his visits to the Diplomatic Body, which he said he understoo 
it was contrary to etiquette that he should do until he had been receiver 
by the Emperor, After some other preliminary remarks, we entered upon 
the subject of his mission; and he evinced some anxiety to learn from me 
the feelings produced here by the refusal of the Porte to deliver up the 

litical refugees, stating that as far as civility on the part of the Impe- 
rial authorities could be taken as evidence of their dispositions towards 
Turkey, his reeeption promised to be more satisfactory than he had at one 
time ventured to expect, He then said that he was to see Count Nessel- 
rode the next day, the 8th, and that he hoped his audience of the Emperor 
would also shortly take place, | ‘ 

In replying to his Exeelleney | said to him that I could not pretenc 
to offer him any decided opinion upon the persistence which might be 
shown in prosecuting the demands of Russia; but that, as far as I had 
yet been able to form my judgment, | was inclined to hope that the Porte's 
refusal to give up the refugees would not be made a serious grievance 
against Turkey. Lacquainted his Excelleney with your Lordship's view 
of the case with respect to the pba en of Austria; and I said that L 
was ready, if he thought it would advance his interests, to have some cons 
fidential conversation on the subject with Count Neaselrode, in anticipation 


a | 


of any instructions which | might eventually receive from your Lordship. 
To this he replied that until he had himself seen Count Nesselrode and 
perhaps even the Emperor, he thought it would be premature for me to 
take any step in support of the object of his mission; that the Sultan did 
not wish, if possible, to discuss the question of right, und had addressed 
himself rather to the generosity of the Emperor, inting out to him the 
impossibility of a Mussulman Sovereign violating the rights of hospitality, 
on which the refugees had reckoned, without legrading himself for ever 
in the eyes of his own subjects ; and his Excellency said that such a com- 
munication from one Sovereign to another had better be made without an 
appearance of his Envoy's acting in concert with others. His Exeellency 
said, however, that if [ would in the meantime ascertain General de 
Lamoriciére’s ideas on the subject, he would be obliged to me, and that he 
would eventually avail himself with gratitude of any support which the 
French Minister and Her Majesty's Legation might be able to afford him, 
should his hope of receiving a satisfactory answer to the letter which the 
Sultan hac addressed to the Emperor prove unfounded, He evidently 
trusted that this would not be the case; and he evinced an opinion that 
the Austrian Government was likely to prove more unwilling to accept the 
explanations of the Porte, than His Imperial Majesty. 


Such being his Excellency's views, [ left him with the expression of a” 


hope that he would be able to acquaint me with his prospects of success 
before the departure of my messenger who leaves St. Petersburgh 
to-morrow, 

_I then called on General de Lamoricidre, and after informing him of 
Fuad ffendi’s arrival, | made him acquainted with all that | knew myself 
upon the subject of his mistion and of the recent events at Constanti- 
nople—Fuad Effendi having mentioned to me the cessation of diplomatic 
relations between the Austrian Mission and the Porte, 

General de Lamoriciére replied that he had not received a line from 
Paris on the subject ofthe refugees, since he had announced the de arture 
of Prince Radzivil from Warsaw: but he expressed a conviction that the 
opinions of his Government would coincide with those which | believed 
to be entertained by that of Her Majesty; and that therefore, as far as 
unofficial support could be of use to and Effendi, he was willing to afford 
it to his Excellency, 

As Count Buol, the Austrian Minister, had arrived on the previous 
evening from Vienna, and as it was probable that his arrival was not 
unconnected with the late events at Constantinople, General de Lamori- 
ciére, after [ had left him, proceeded to the Austrian Legation, where he 
had a long conversation with the Count, during which, availing himself of 
the information which I had given him, he pressed M. de Buol very hard 
upon the unjustifiable pretension of Austria to foree upon the Porte an 
interpretation of the XVILIth Article of the Treaty of Belgrade, which it 
was impossible for any Mussulman Sovereign to admit, saying that the 
French in their dealings with the Arab tribes of Africa were obliged to 
respect the sacredness of the asylum granted to refugees. He insinuated 
also that Austria evidently intended to avail herself in her interpretation 
of treaties, of the right of the strongest ; and at last succeeded in inducing 
the Count, when defending the conduct of his Government, to say that no 
more serious results were likely to arise from. the question than those 
which had already oceurred. {dined with General de Lamorici¢re the 
same day, when he reported to me what I have now stated to your Lord. 
ship, and [ agreed with him as to the ex vediency of Fuad Effendi’s being 
informed, before his interview with the Ohaneellog of Count Buol's arrival, 
and of General de Lamoriciére's impression that Austria is not disposed 
fo support her pretensions respecting the refugees by other than diplomatic 
means. [did not however think it advisable, as. the General suggested, 
that T should call upon Fuad Efendi again myself in the evening, or that 
the General, who had already left a card updn him in the course of the 
day should do so, as it might not be agreeable to his Excellency, and it 
was perhaps even inexpedient that he should receive second visite from 
either of us until he had seen the Chancellor. 1 therefore proposed that 
the General should send one of his aides-de-camp to the Ottoman Envoy,

No. 56. 


Mr. Buchanan to Viscount Palmerston.— (Received October 19.) 


(No. 339, Confidential.) | 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 9, 1849. 


WHEN I informed General de Lamoriciére on Sunday the 7th instant, . 


of the arrival of Fuad Effendi, he said that as Count Nesselrode had for- 
tunately named an hour to see him on the following day, he would take 
advantage of the SE De ay to have some conversation with his Excel- 
lency on the subject of the demand cf Russia to have the Polish refugees 
delivered up to her by the Turkish Government; and that he would not 
fail to make me acquainted with what might pass between them. 

General de Lamoriciéré. has since told me that he held during this 
interview nearly the same language to his Excellency, which he had 
already done to the Austrian Minister, as reported ‘in my preceding 
despatch; and on his Excellency saying that the I[nd Article of the Treaty 
of Kainardji was clearly in favour of the pretensions of Russia, he 
replied, having previously made himself acquainted with the French 
translation of the Treaty, that it seemed to him incredible that a Mus- 
sulman Government should have ratified a convention acknowledging the 
principle of extradition, Upon this Count Nesselrode produ the 
‘Treaty, and read the Article, of which a-copy is annexed; passing lightly 
over its first clauses, he apparently rested his case entirely upon the last 
one, beginning at “Pareillement.” ‘The General therefore observed, that 
his Excelleney by so doing confirmed him in his original opinions, as if 
the first.and most important clause in the Article did not render obliga- 
tory the extradition of refugees, it was natural to suppose that any 
phrase of a contrary signification in the last clause was incorrectly trans- 
lated from the Turkish, 

His Excellency does not appear to have made any answer to this 
reasoning, but shifting his ground, he endeavoured to maintain that the 
first clause left Russia at all events at liberty to choose between refugees 
being expelled or delivered up; and he said that she considered the case 
sufficiently serious to insist upon the latter alternative. 

It is needless however for me to trouble your Lordship with a detail 
of the arguments used on both sides as to the interpretations of which 
the Article would admit, as all its bearings have doubtless been naturally 
considered by Her Majesty's Government; but I may mention, that Count 
Nesselrode pretended to attach some importance to a portion of the Council, 
or as he said, the Ulemas, or interpreters of the law, having voted in favour 
of the pretensions of Russia, 

The conversation afterwards turned upon the political view of the 
question, The General said that he spoke without any instructions from 
his Goverament; but that he knew enough of his country to feel assured 
that no French Ministry could last for a day, which would permit the 
Porte to be forced into delivering up to punishment the persons who had 
lately sought refuge in their territories; that he could not say that if 
Russia pushed the question to extremities, the present French Govern- 


- ment would support Turkey to the last; but that he could assure his 


Excellency that Russia's using in this case the right of the strongest 
would inevitably force them into measures which they wished to avoid, or 
bring persons into power who would throw the country again into a 
course of which the results could not be forescen (‘dans linconnu"); 
and that the Russian Government would do well ta reflect deeply, for the 
sake of Europe, before they submitted Turkey to a humiliation which 


- might lead to the most deplorable calamities. 


I have, &e. 


(Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN.

Fuad Effendi replied that his presence at St. Petersburgh as the 
bearer of a letter from the Sultan in which His Highness evineed his 
desire to treat the question directly with His Imperial Majesty, as between 
Sovereign and Sovereign, and as one which aflected His Highness’ honour, 
his personal sentiments, and his consideration as a Sovereign in the eyes 
of his own subjects, was a sufficient proof of the conciliatory dispositions 
of the Turkish Government, and of their anxiety not to seck for the inter- 
ference of other Powers, or to take any steps which could offend the 
susceptibilities or dignity of His Imperial Majesty ; and he added that he 
trusted the Emperor would duly appreciate and respond to the sentiments 
which animated the Sultan his master. It appears that M. Séniavine 
became rather less decided in his language towards the close of their con- 
vyersation, and insinuated that the Russian Government had reason to

During our interview I informed his Excellency that the Austrian 
Minister had affected to treat the question lightly in conversation with me 
yesterday, and that he deprecated the idea of Austria ever making it a 
cause for a serious rupture with the Porte; and I alsoinformed his Excel- 
lency of what had passed between General de Lamoriciére and Count 
Nesselrode at the interview referred to inmy despatch No. 339 of yester- 
day's date; and I pointed out to him some other reasons which I had for 
believing that there was a disposition on the part of the Russian Govern- 
ment to accept the explanations of the Sultan in an amicable spirit, 

His Excellency then begged me to inform your Lordship that he did 
not despair that the matter would be arranged without diplomatic dis- 
cussions; but that if he should be unfortunately disappointed in this 
expectation, he would then take his stand upon the rights of the Porte, 
and that in such a case he trusted he should not be left without the support 
of Her Majesty's Government.

J'ai commencé par résumer la substance de notre entretien précé-

«Nous avons constatdé a cette occasion,” lui ai-je dit, “ que jusqu’ici 
l'état de paix entre la Russie et la Porte n'a pas été interrompu, I 
discussion entre les deux Gouvernemens, il y a grief, il y a dillérend, mais 
il n'y a pas de conflit. La suspension te relations diplomatiques a 
Constantinople n’établit pas encore un état de guerre. Méme le rappel 
de la Légation de Russie, s'il avait lieu, ne le constituerait pas non plus, 
Pour qu'il y ait guerre, il faut une déclaration d'abord, un commencement 
d'hostilité ensuite; jusque ld il n'y a ni Iésion, ni attaque. Contre un 
danger qui n’existe point en réalité, la Turquie n'a pas besoin d'assistance. 
Nous avons constaté ces vérités, et nous en avons conclu, que tant que la 
Porte Ottomane reste en paix, le principe de la fermeture des Détroits des 
Dardanelles et du Bosphore, consacré par notre Traité de 1841, demeure 
intact dans toute sa force et valeur,

My Lord oa Warsaw, October 15, 1849. 


T SH it be but natural to suppose that a question of such 
poriscec es that which has arisen between the Porte and the hopes! 
Governments of Austria and Russia, in regard to the extradition of t Pf 
Polish and Hungarian refugees, is not likely to be settled by mere lega 
technicalities or by the weighing of the words of antiquated eaice, 
may not be without some interest to state on undoubted euoryG tha 
the fugitive Bem, who appears to have excited the Emperor o anita 
anger, perhaps more than any other individual at present so nobly protec ed 
by the Turkish Government,—that this bold partisan and determined ene) 
of Russia is not at all a natural-born subject of the King of Poland an 
Emperor of Russia, | s Ntecy tee 

Bem was born in that poon of Poland which until ol late yas 
formed the territory of the free State of Cracow. In 1812 when ol 
district formed a part of the Grand Duch of Warsaw, Bem enterec ae 
military service of that Grand Duchy, and with many of his somansats 
was afterwards ceo i He army which was: organized in 1516 

3 | Kingdom of Poland. 
= Sete years atectwards he was obliged to leave the service of this 
State: and of course with the cessation of his official relations with the 
Crown of the Emperor and King, every tie of alleziance was likewise 


severed. Bem lived in other parts of Poland (Galicia, I believe) until the 


outbreak of the insurrection of 18380 and 1831, when he again appeared 
here to play the well-known part which he bore m some of the most 
remarkable events of that struggle; and although he may have been 
always considered since then as a rebel by the Russian Government, 
that Government most certainly has no right to claim him as a subject 
according to the letter or the spirit of the existing treaties with Turkey, 

It seems doubtful even whether Austria has a well-lefined legal 
right to claim Bem as a subject, because he was a proscribed a a a 
forced exile, not only from the territories of the Emperor of Russia, but 
likewise from the soil of the free State of which he ts a natural-born 
subject, for years before that little territory was incorporated with the 
Austrian dominions, and has therefore never owned any allegiance to the 
Austrian Crown, any more than he has Rerelvee any protection from it.

Viscount Ponsonby to Sir Stratford Canning, 

Sir, Vienna, October 16, 1849. 
I AM happy to tell your Excellency that I feel no doubt of the 
eaceable and satisfactory settlement of the affair between the Sublime 
orte and the Austrian Coveninnnt relating to the refugees, provided 
that nothing be done to create excitement; and (if it meets with your 
approbation) I think it would be well to induce the Admiral Sir W. Parker 
to make the advance of the fleet have as much as possible the air of an 
excursion for the purpose of exercising the crews and so forth, and to 
take any other measure he may please to avoid the appearance of the 
fleet having been sent as amenace. I presume it may be easy for the 
Admiral to remain within call if any necessity should arise for his active. 

interference. 

There are foolish stories in Vienna, sent no doubt by enemies to 
ace, Which state that the Turkish Government is about to give General 


em the command of a corps of troops, and that the Turkish authorities 
place difficulties in the way of the return of the Hungarian soldiers (now 


nad Effendi, reported in his despatch No. 338 of the 9th instant. ° 


ah)

at Widdin) who wish to accept the permission given by fhe Emperor of 
Austria for their return to their own country, under conditions most easy 
to themselves, and communicated to them by a general officer dispatched 
to Widdin by Elis Imperial Majesty for this express purpose. 

I have denied the truth of these stories, being certain that they are 
falae, but I should be glad if your Excellency would empower me to. say 
that they are untrue.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston. —(Recewed October 27.) 


(No, 297. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 4, 1849. 

HER Majesty's steam-frigate “ Odin” arrived here yesterday morn- 
ing with letters from the Commander-in-chief of Her Majesty's squadron 
in the Mediterranean. 

Your Lordship is already acquainted with the tenor of my commune 
cations to Sir William Parker, in consequence of the suspension of diplo- 
matic relations between the Porte on one side, and the Austrian and 
Russian Legations on the other. I have the honour to transmit herewith 
for your Lordship’s further information, & copy of the Admiral’s reply. 

Whatever may be the issue of so gerious a difference as that to which 
our correspondence relates, L cannot feel otherwise than deeply indebted 
by Sir William's prompt compliance with my views, He appears to com: 
prehend the situation thoroughly - and | have no doubt that, in the 
expectation of instructions from home, he will continue to afford me every 
degree of support required by the circumstances, without overstepping the 
limits of prudence and discretion. 

The sudden arrival of the © Odin” has naturally excited curiosity 
in the present critical atate of alfairs, ant | have been careful to account 
for it in a manner calculated to allay that fecling among the public. 
There i less difliculty in 80 doing from the circumstance that Captain 
Pelham, after coming from the Adriatic, had touched at Corfu and Athens 
on his way hither. 


95, 


The “Tartarus ” had returned to this station several days before 
the arrival of the “ Odin,” and | have requested Captain Pelham to place 
the former vessel at my tispoer for two or three matters of public service 
which will not require its a 

which time, or very soon after, a definitive resolution may be ex eted to 
arrive from Petersburgh. it is calculated that Fuad Effendi reached 
that city yesterday, supposing, as ma be reasonably presumed, that he 
has not been stopped on the ussian frontier. 

[ saw the Grand Vizier privately this morning and told him for his 
own personal information and that of the Sultan, that the “Odin” had 
come up to Constantinople in consequence of my application to the 
Admiral; that it would probably stay here long enough to learn the issue 
of the pending dispute; and that the squadron now at Corfu would shortly 
make its appearance in the Archipelago, and keep for a time in communi- 
cation with me, ye so as to avoid attracting any particular attention with 
respect to the affairs of this country. i told his Highness that he was 
not to consider this a proach to a demonstration as immediately indicating 
any opinion of Her Majesty's Government, but as proceeding merely from 
that general knowledge of their solicitude for the welfare of the Porte 
which was necessarily possessed by Her Majesty’s servants on the spot. 
[ again repeated what | had so often urged before as to the expediency of 
the Porte's avoiding the hazard of hostile collision with its neighbours 
and particularly with Russia, so long as it could do so without a sacrifice 
of its honour and inde endence, which are so deeply involved in the ques- 
tion now at issue. ‘The stand to be made by the Porte under present 
circumstances must be one of necessity, created by the paramount duty of 
resisting an unjust and dictatorial requisition. 

The Grand Vizier appeared to enter cordially into this view of the 
subject, He could not conceal his emotion at even so limited an evidence 
of our continued sympathy with the interests of the Ottoman Empire, 
and he expressed his acknowledgments in the warmest terms; but he 
also showed me a due sense of the prudence and caution required in 
presence of adanger, which, however it might be exaggerated for purposes 
of intimidation, was not to be treated with carelessness or to be braved 
without necessity. He told me that unless cou nselled otherwise by friendly 
Powers, the Porte would stand firm to the last; and that even if the 
certainty of war as an immediate consequence of further resistance were 
to shake the Sultan's resolution, he was determined to retire from office. 

It is my firm conviction, notwithstanding some inconsistencies of 
conduct inseparable from the habits of Turkish statesmanship, that Reshid 
Pasha is sincere in this declaration; and I venture to add, that however 
the crisis may terminate, an impression most favourable to our future 
relations with this country has been already made in the minds of all 
those who are attentive to the character and tendency of passin events, 

In the course of our conversation the Grand Viuier inquired whether 
any officers eventually available for the ‘Turkish service had come up in 
the “Odin,” and TI replied in the sense of Sir William Parker's letter to 
me. It appeared to me that his Highness, though he made no remark 
would have been better pleased with the prospect of a larger supply. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

Rie Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received Oclober 27.) 


(No. 298.) 


My Lord, Therapia, October 5, 1849, 

LATE in the evening of the Ist instant a Polish officer named Czayka, 

who has long resided here under French protection, though in fact an 
agent of Prince Adam Czartoryski, called on me to deliver a letter from 

. Kossuth, and to offer some explanation of the incident to which that 
letter referred. The incident in question is the profession of Islamism by 

General Bem and two other Generals, with a number, varying from ten to 
thirty, of less distinguished Polish and Hungarian refugees detained at 
Widdin. It appears to have Series in & message conveyed to them 
from some of the leading Turkish Ministers, by means of an officer sent to 
Widdin with some commission of a military character. It has produced 
mnch excitement and dissatisfaction in the minds of M. Kossuth and those 
who are particularly connected with him, and it has also had the effect of 
betraying M. Kossuth into a very improper and indeed unwarrantable 
use of the answers which General Aupick and myself had severally 
addressed to him in our private capacity from motives of humanity and 
compassion. 

Your Lordship will be able to deriye a clearer idea of what has 
occurred from the several papers which I have now the honour to forward. 

They are, a letter from M. Kossuth to me; a statement which I have 
received confidentially from General Aupick, and which is evidently derived 
from Czayka; a message from Aali Pasha as reported to me by M, Pisani; 
and extracts of a letter from one of those Englishmen at Widdin for whose 
deliverance [ have obtained an order from the Porte. 

Whatever discrepancies are apparent in these accounts, compared with 
each other, it is evident that a message was sent to the Polish refugees 
atleast, and that it has been generally understood as an intimation pre- 
senting the eventual alternative of death by the hand of the executioner, or 
escape by means of conversion to Islamism. 

_ Such an expedient would never under any circumstances have 
obtained my approval - and when the Grand Vizier some weeks ago threw 
out a hint of it in private conversation with me, I did not conceal my 
ep of its untoward character and tendency. Its least bbjectonkble 
shape would have been that of a suggestion reserved for the last moment 
of resistance about to disappear before the certainty of war announced by 
two powerful empires. In the present stage of the affair it is not only dis- 
ereditable to all the parties concerned, but well calculated to produce 
fresh embarrassments and greater irritation against the Porte. Both to 
Aali Pasha and to the Grand Vizier I have declared this conviction in 
pointed terms, and animadverted without reserve on their presumed share 
in the mancuvre. I have further advised the latter to adopt without 
delay such remedial measures as the extreme injudiciousness of the pro- 
ceeding has left within reach, namely, to abstain from giving rank or 
employment at present to the renegades, to send a proper explanation of 
the whole transaction to those immediately concerned, and to carry forth- 
with into effect my previous recommendation as to conveying the principal 
refugees into the interior, under proper security against their escape, 
leaviug the private soldiers under the care of their less noted officers as 
objects of eventual voluntary restitution to their respective countrics, under 
an act of amnesty to be obtained by the Porte's intercession. 

I cannot undertake to say what portion of this advice, if any, will 
be ipisctionly adopted, The Grand Vizier has however declared his 
readiness to follow my counsels generally ; and judging from his langua 
yesterday, I think it probable that the more obnoxious refugees will 
withdrawn from Widdin to Schumla, and that a more elaborate attempt 
will be made in some shape or other to explain away the reprehensible 


character of the message conveyed, as it is asserted by mistake, to the 
unfortunate relugees,

[ AM sorry to Say that a great number of Hungarian officers, at 
least hall of those who have taken refuge here, formally abjured their

however, that though they have made their profession of Islamiasm, they 
will have a sort of noviciate of three months’ duration, at the end of 
which they may, if they please, recant and return to their old faith. It is 
much to be feared this bad example, together with the desperate circum- 
stances in which they are placed, will influence the rest; and few will be 
found to prefer death to dishonour, Amongst these few, however, my 
friend, General Guyon, if not rotected by your Excellency, will embrace

These details, my Lord, were communicated to me the same evening’ 
by the French Minister, upon whom I called, at his own request, at a late 
hour, in consequence of his having received a courier from Paris. General 
de Lamoriciére read to mea series of voluminous despatches, which had 
been received by the French Government from General Au vick, acquaint- 
ing them with the events which had preceded and attended, up to the 
I7th ultimo, the refusal of the Porte to deliver up the refugees. When he 
had finished them, he said that M. de Tocqueville, in forwarding these 
documents to him, had stated, that until the Government of the Republic 
should have ascertained how far that of Her Majesty may be inclined to 
support the Sultan in resisting the pretensions of Russia, he could not 
send him any positive instructions to remonstrate against the pretensions 
of the Impemal Cabinet; but that he had directed him in the meantime, 
in pointing out-to Connt Nesselrode the serious consequences which would 
inevitably result to the peace of Europe, from a determination of the 
Russian Government to push those pretensions to extremities, to hold 
language which the General described as being entirely identic with that 
which he had already used in the interview with his Excellency, reported 
in my despatch No. 339 of the 9th instant, General de Lamoriciére there- 
fore was at first. somewhat doubtful as to whether it would not be expe- 
dient to postpone any further communication with the Chancellor until 
after the arrival of the Queen's messenger to-morrow, who would probably 
bring communications from your Lordship to Her Majesty's Mission, 
stating more clearly the views of our respective Governments as to the 
attitude which they may be disposed to assume in the question. On my 
calling however on him again this morning, | found that he had decided 
upon asking at once for an interview with Count Nesselrode, as he feared 
that his not doing so might lead his Excellency to suppose that the opinions 
of his Government had not eoincided with those which he had expressed 
before the arrival of his messenger. As General’dée*Lamorici¢re invited 
the expression of my opinion upon-the siibjeatl etitirely agreed with him as 
in the expediency of his losing no time in communicating with the Chancel- 
lor; and Lalso suggested that he should express his request for an interview 
so, as to render it difficult for his Excellency to avoid receiving him in the 
course of the day or of the evening, as | considered that it would make 
any representations which might possibly be addressed to the Russian 
Government by Her Majesty’s Government and that of the French 
Republic less difficult to answer, if the Chancellor could be induced before 
receiving them, to express an intention on the part of the Emperor to 


withdraw his demand for the extradition of the refugees, in consideration 


of the feelings and wishes of the Sultan. 

The first answer which General de Lamoriciére received to his letter 
to the Chancellor was a verbal message that his Excellency could not see 
him at all to-day, but that he would write to him to-morrow, His Excel- 
lency however soon after sent him a few lines, expressing his readiness to 
receive him in the evening, 

Qu his return, General de Lamoricitre, who has just left ne, gave me 
a full detail of what passed between them. He described the Chancellor 
as being “trés monté,” and as holding very decided Janguage at the 
beginning of their interview as to the rights of Russia and the dispositions 
of the Emperor; and imaintaining that even if it were admitted that the 
last clause of the IInd Article of the Treaty of Kainardji was badly 
expressed, the history of the past sufficiently explained the intentions of 
the Contracting Parties; and his Excelleney quoted an instance of a troop 
of rebellious cavalry having been disarmed on Russian territory and 
delivered up to the Turkish authorities at their request. 

General de Lamoriciére replied that such an example was enirely 
inapplicable, for if the expression “at least expelled,” had been intro- 


duced into the Treaty to setisfy the scruples of the ‘Turkish Government, 


it was plain that an act of the Russian Government could not do away 
with its validity. . 
Count Nesselrode however depreeated all discussion with other 
Governments on the interpretation of the treaties which regulated the 
relations of Russian with the Porte, saying that the Emperor had given 


103 


sufficient proofs of his determination not to ag randize the Russian 
Empire at the expense of Turkey, to satisfy his allies of his disinterest- 
edness and of his friendly feelings towards the Sultan ; and his Excellency 
concluded by observing that two of the leading refugees had already 
settled the question of their extradition by embracing the Mahometan 
faith; and that if Russia were left alone she would find means of comin 
to an arrangement with the Porte with respect to those who remained, an 
that: no serious consequences need be apprehended as to the means which 
she would employ for this purpose. 

General de Lamoriciére replied that his Excellency’s assurance was 
satisfactory in as far as it evinced a disposition to prevent the » uestion 
assuming a worse aspect than it already bore, but that he should like to 
learn what his Excellenéy meant by arranging the question with the 
Turkish Government, if that Government were left without support to 
discuss it with Russia; as the value of his Excellency’s assurance would 
naturally depend upon whether he intended to say that the Russian 
Government had decided to accept the explanations of the Sultan and to 
withdraw their demand for the extradition of the refugees. 

General de Lamoriciére found it impossible however to obtain a more 
explicit answer from his Excellency, who merely repeated what, he had 
already said ; but it is to be presumed, my Lord, that the courage shown 
by the Ottoman Ministers has already decided the question in favour of 
the Turkish Empire, and that the efforts of this Government will now be 
merely directed, in withdrawing their demands, to save as much as possible 
the Emperor's dignity and the prestige of their name at Constantinople, 
which many persons hate consider to be seriously compromised.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 16, 1849. 


L HAD an interview this morning with Count Nesselrode, and after 
some general conversation, and some a lusions to matters of minor interest, 
eee the subject of the demand of Russia for the extradition of the 

olish refueees who had been lately concerned in the Hungarian war. | 
stated that 1 had not received instructions to enter into any discussions of 
the meritsof the question with the Imperial Government, or the bearings 
of the Treaty upon which the demand of extradition had been based ; but 
that | was desirous to obtain some knowledge of the view which was taken 
of the question by the Imperial Cabinet. | 

The Chancellor was extremely laconic, and he studiously avoided 
saying anything which should leave an opening for a remark ; his reply 
was, that he hoped the affair would be arranged without much trouble, 
but that he could not yet inform me how the difficulties would be 
smoothed, but that he wished this to be effected by negotiations with the 
Porte, 1 endeayoured to obtain some explanation as to the manner in 
which he proposed to get over the articles of the Treaty which bore on 
the demand of extradition, and I regret to say that | was unable to obtain 
any satisfactory answer from his ‘Excellency beyond the assurance that 
‘the matter would probably be arranged by an exchange of notes or decla- 
rations, without reference to the terms of the Treaty. 

At the same time that I have the satisfaction to inform your Lordship 
of the turn which this affnir appears likely to take, 1 am sorry not to be 
able to give any details as to the manner in which the Russian Govern- 
ments propose to remove the irritation which their late demands have 
created at Constantinople, but | hope in a few days that | may be able to 
‘obtain more @xact information,

No. 72. 
Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received October 27.) 


(No: 7. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 16, 1849. 

HAVING heard that Fuad Effendi had had an audience of the 
Emperor this morning, for the purpose of delivering the letter with which 
he fad been charged by the Sultan, | thought it advisable to pay his 
Excellency a visit with a view to learn what had passed at the interview. 
As he had, however, expressed some doubts at the expediency of my 
ealling upon him, on my offering to do so the day after my arrival, I 
requested Mr. Buchanan to see him, and to state that | supposed there 
could now be no objection to my visiting him, but that I would be guided 
by his Excellency’s wishes, and postpone doing so if he preferred it. 
Fuad Eifendi seemed however to have lost all his former apprehensions 
of the Russian Government taking umbrage at the friendly visits of Her 
Majesty's Legation, and expressed a wish to see me. _ ans 

I therefore went to his hotel and was received in the most cordial 
manner, He told me that the Emperor had at first addressed him in a 
somewhat rough and haughty tone, very different he said from the manner 
in which his own Sovereign the Sultan is in the habit of speaking to 
people; but that after a little time His Imperial Majesty became more 
affable, and conversed freely on the subject of his mission. He told me 
that the Emperor, had made use of strong and harsh expressions in 
alluding to the refusal of the Porte to give up the Se according to 
the terms of the Treaty, but he said that His Imperial Majesty had given 
him the assurance of his desire to have the matter settled amicably, 
thoueh he declared that he could not consent to its being done between 
the Sovereigns, but that it must be left to be adjusted by the two Govern- 
ments, and that for this purpose he wished Fuad Effendi to remain at 
St. Petersburgh during the negotiations. The Turkish Envoy told me 
that these were the principal pomts of the conversation, and that he was 
glad when the audience was over, though the Emperor was very kind and 
condescending during the latter part of it, for it lasted upwards of an 
hour. f inquired of Fuad Effendi if he was invested with any powers to 
negotiate with the Russian Government. He replied that he was not, and 
that consequently he should decline putting his name to any papers what- 
ever, without having previously obtained the full authority and sanction 


of his Government, I then endeavoured to impress upon the Turkish 


Envoy the heavy responsibility which was about to rest upon him, stating 
that he would be made answerable for the due maintenance of the dignity 
of the Sultan’s Crown and of the independence of his empire. 

I felt it my duty to use this strong language, because | apprehended 
that the Russian Government might have some sinister object Mh detaining 
Fuad Effendi at St. Petersburgh, and perhaps expect to make him a more 
supple negotiator on the banks of the Neva than on the shores of the 
Bosphorus. His detention here is remarkable, from the fact of Count 
Nesselrode always professing to dislike the presence of Turkish diplo- 
matists at St. Petersburgh; but in justice to Fuad Effendi 1 must not 
omit stating to your Lordship, that he appears at present to be animated 
with the best intentions, and as far as Lam able to judge, to be an honest 
and devoted subject of the Sultan. ay. , } 

Before taking leave of Fuad Effendi, | mentioned to him that 


although Count Nesselrode had given me the assurance, that the Russian 


Government hoped soon to bring the matter to an amicable conclusion, he 
had not mentioned the mode in which he proposed to effect this object, 
and [therefore inquired of him if he could give me any information on 
this point. He replied that he could not, but that he had received an 
impression from his last conversation with Count Nesselrode, that the 
Russian Government would now content themselves with the removal of 
the refugees from Turkey, provided the Porte would consent at the same 


105: 


time to send away certain other Poles, who had been established for some 
time on the banks of the Danube, and whose numbers I understand is 
considerable,

No. 73. 
Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received October 27.) 


(No, 8.) 


My Lord, St Petersburgh, October 19, 1849. 

I HAVE the honour to inclose an article extracted from the St. 
Petersburgh Journal of this morning, announcing that Fuad Effendi 
had been received by the Emperor at a private audience, with all the 
ceremonial usually observed at the Russian Court on the occasion of the 
reception of Ambassadors. : 

Phe object of this article is to remove the impression which has gone 
abroad that the Porte had rejected the demands of Ruasia for the extra- 
dition of certain Poles who had been implicated in.the Hungarian insur- 
rection; and it goes so far as to assert that the mission of Fuad Effendi 
was dictated solely by the desire of the Sultan to come to an understand- 
ing with the Emperor on the bearings of the Treaty of Kainardji 
without the interference of third parties; nevertheless it is satisfactory 
to find that although the Russian Government attempt to place the 
uestion in a new form, they evidently give up the main point—their 
emand of extradition, and express the hope that this affair will be 
promptly arranged to the satisfaction of both Courts. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received October 27.) 
(No. 12.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 19, 1849. 

J HAD an interview this afternoon with Count Nesselrode, and in 
conformity with your Lordship's instructions I read’ to his Excellence 
your despatch marked No. 1 of the 6th-instant, upon the subject of the 
late demand which was addressed by the Russian Government to the 
Porte for the extradition of certain Polish refugees, and I left a copy of 
the despatch with him. 

When I mentioned to the Chancellor the nature of the communication 
| had to make, he said that he wished me to consider whether the reception 
of Fuad Effendi by the Emperor, and the article which had been published 
inthe St, Petersburgh Journal (a copy of which is forwarded in my despatch 
No. 5) were not a sufficient explanation of the matter, adding that he 
trusted the affair was ina fair way of settlement, I replied that I was 
rejoiced to hear such good news, and that if his Excellency would give 
me a copy of the communication he had been making to Fuad Effendi and 
M. de Titoff, I would consider how far it would be possible for me to 
depart from my instructions. 

Count Nesselrode said that he could not assent to my proposal, 
because he could never admit the principle of foreign interference in the 
relations of Russia with Turkey, 

After the despatch had been read, the Chancellor hesitated some 
time before making any observation, and then inquired of me whether the 
Porte really hac requested our assistance and support, for Fuad Effendi 
had assured him of the contrary, 

[ replied that there must be some mistake on this point, for when the 
Porte became seriously alarmed at the peremptory demand for the extra- 
dition of the Polish refugees, which had been addressed to them by M. 
Titoff, they naturally sought the assistance of a friendly Power, and 
applied to us in their difficulty, and that we felt bound to support them, 


because we thought that Russia had puta forced construction upon the 
Treaty of Kainaridji, 
| Pa 


108 


Count Nesselrode then alluded to the violent attacks on Russia in the 
English newspapers, and to the supposition that Russia wanted a pretext 
to make war on Turkey, observing that this wasa great mistake; that she 
was very glad to have got out of one war, and had no wish or inclination 
to enter into another with the Turkish Empire, the existence and stability 
of which she was most anxious to support. He continued that Russia 
wished above all things to live on good terms with her neighbours, but 
that she could not submit to have her frontier kept in a continual state of 
agitation by the numerous adventurers, subjects to the Emperor, who had 
established themselves in the Ottoman dominions. 

His Excellency finished the conversation by saying that he should 
take the despatch into his consideration and would prepare an answer to 
it; but he persisted to the last in expressing an opinion that as the 
Emperor had received the Turkish Ambassador, and the Government had 
forwarded some new proposals to the Porte, which did not insist upon 
more than the expulsion of the dita the communication of the despatch 
which T had read to him was only likely to throw difficulties in the way of 
an early and amicable adjustment of the question which had arisen at 
Constantinople. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.-—(Received October 27.) 


(No. 13. Most Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 19, 1849. 

FUAD EFFENDI. called oa me yesterday and informed me that 
since we last met he had had an interview with Count Nesselrede, and had 
received from him a communication of the proposals of the Russian 
Governement for:the settlement of their differences with the Porte, and 
that he thought these proposals were of a nature to be accepted by his 
Government. He told me that he was about to forward them to Con- 
stantinople; that he saw in them nothing Hcroieaeory to the dignity of his 
Sovereign; and that if they were accepted by his Government, the diplo- 
matic relations of the two countries would be immediately re-established. 
He hesitated for some time before telling me the exact nuture-of these propo- 
sitions, and seemed unwilling tosay more than that Russia would withdraw 
her claim for the extradition of the Poles, and would be contented with 
their expulsion, But on my referring to what had fallen from him ona 
previous occasion (as reported in my despatch No. 7 of the lGth instant, 
marked “ confidential’) as to the probability of a demand being made for the 
expulsion at the same of certain other Poles residing in ‘Turkey, he said 
that such a proposal had indeed been made, and had been accompanied by 
another to the effect that the Porte should endeavour to make arrange- 
ments with other Powers to prevent the subjects of the Emperor from 
establishing themselves in her territory under the protection of foreign 
passports, 

[ at once pointed out to Fuad Effendi the objections to which this 
proposal was open and the inconveniences to which it might lead; but 
though his Excellency was not entirely indifferent to them, he seemed to 
think that the proposal of Russia was at all events important, as affording 
a means of arranging the question without lowering the dignity of his 
Sovereign; and he said that even if it were deemed inadmissible by his 
Government, it would necessitate some negotitnions, ond thus have the 
effect of renewing diplomatic communications between the two Govern- 
ments, which he trusted would eventually lead to an amicable settlement 
of the question. 

I therefore observed that unless his Excellency would communicate to 
me a copy of the note which he had received from Count Nesselrode, | 
could not form any judgment upon the propositions which it contained, 


100 


and I intimated to him my opinion of the expediency of his enabling me to 
give your Lordship the most accurate information upon this important 
subject. 

: He was at first much embarrassed at this proposition, but finally con- 
sented to give me an abstract of the Russian proposals, under an 
injunction of secrecy; and I have the honour to transmit herewith the 


copy of a memorandum containing them, which I received from him this 


morning. 1 believe this document is an abstract of an inclosure in a 
note which was presented to Fuad Effendi by Count Nesselrode two 


0.

of the opinions which have been expressed to him not only by m self but 
by General de Lamoriciére, the French Minister at this Court, these pro-

appears to me, or | may almost indeed say that Fuad iffendi has

the Emperor, but that in order to preven any further delay in his being

No. 85. 
Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—{ Receiwed November 2.) 


(No, 15. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 22, 1849, 

THE French Minister has just called on me, and communicated ta 
mea despatch of the 12th instant, which he received last night from his 
Government, instructing him to inform Count Nesselrode, that in conse- 
quence of the state of affairs at Constantinople, a French squadron had 
been ordered to Tenedos. General de Lamoriciére is directed at the same 
time to make known to the Russian Government, that the Government of 
the Republic entertains the most anxious hope that the differences which 
have arisen between the Russian and the Turkish Governments: will be 
satisfactorily settled; and he is particularly enjoined so to make this 
communication, that the announcement of the movement of the squadron 
shall not have the appearance of a menace. He asked me how I advised 
him to proceed in making this communication; and | told’ him that! 
thought that if it had been known at Paris when the despatch was 
written, that the Russian Goyernment no longer desired to press on the 
Porte their demand for the extradition of the Poles, but would be con- 
tented with their expulsion, that they would not have ordered him to say 
anything about the fleet; and | added that IT had carefully refrained from 
mentioning the orders sent to Sir W. Parker, when | communicated three 
days ago to the Chancellor your Lordship’s despatch No. 1 of the 6th 
instant; and I said further, that after all, he would be only telling the 
Chancellor what he must have already learnt from other sources; and 
that it appeared to me that the direct mention of the departure of the 
fleet would only procuce the undesirable effect of increasing the existing 
irritation; and therefore, if Count Nesselrode did not ask any questions 
on the subject, my opinion was, that the less he said on the ae the 
better, because the mformation this given might he interpreted into a 
threat, which he wished to avoid; and’ that after all, there was no reason 
why our squadrons should not meet in the neighbourhood of the Dar- 
danelles; it was not necessary that their rendezvous should be considered 
as an act of hostility to Russia; for if Russia did not contemplate any 
injury to the Porte, the position of the two squadrons was perfectly harm- 
less; and certainly the Porte would not ask any questions on the subject, 
and she alone had a right to demand an explanation, 

For these reasons [ advised General de Lamoricidre to say nothing, 
unless asked, respecting the fleet; because I thought that at the present. 
moment we dtinald abstain from doing anything of an irritating nature ; 
that we had sufficient proof that Russia was disposed to settle her differ- 
ence with the Porte by negotiation; and that our best course was now to 
leave the matter in the hands of our Governments, and those of our 
Representatives at Constantinople, and trust to them to bring it to a 
satislactory issue, 

Since writing the foregoing I have again seen the French Minister, 
and he has given me the following account of his interview with Count 
Nesselroile, 

He represented himself as haying commenced by stating to the 
Chancellor that the public feeling in France was in a very excited state, 
in consequence of the late peremptory demands addressed to the Porte 
the Russian and Austrian Ministers for the extradition of the political 
refugees, and their assertion that the escape of one of these individuals 
would be considered a declaration of war; and that the intelligence also 
which had reached Paris, of executions of fourteen superior officers having 
lately taken place in Hungary by order of the Austrian Government, had 
preaily added ta the excitement; and that consequently, he had been 
directed to speak to his Excellency on these subjects, and to éndeavour to 
discover what steps the Russian Government were taking to put.an end to 
their differences with Turkey. Count Nesselrode replied that the Ampe- 


114 


rial Government had made a communication to Constantinople, which he 
trusted would be favourably received by the Ottoman Government. That 
he had written to M. Kisséleff, the Russian Chargé d'Affaires at Paris, to 
the effect ‘that the Emperor, out of consideration for the direct appea 
which had been made to him by the Sultan through Fuad Effendi, would 
no longer insist upon the extradition of the Polish refugees, and that the 
question might be considered in a fair way of settlement. , 

In reply to the report of M. Titoff’s having threatened the Porte with 
war if the refugee Poles were allowed to leave Turkey, Count Nesselrode 
asserted that it was unfounded, and declared that he had never said any- 
thing of the sort; and in answer to the allusions which had been made by 
the French Minister to the executions which had taken place in Hangary, 
the Chancellor said that he could inform him, in the strictest confidence 
however, that the Russian Government, far from approving of these 
wholesale butcheries, regretted them deeply; and his ixcellency added, 
that this regret was not only felt by the Government, but that the Russian 
public were indignant on the subject. 

General de Lamorieiére told me that Count Nesselrade held the most 
conciliatory language to him throughout his interview, ant! that he there- 
fore decided on following my advice, and omitted all mention of the 
orders which had been sent to the French fleet. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,
