No. 88. 
Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received November 3.) 


(No. 21. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 24, 1849. 

WITH reference to my preceding number, I have the honour to 
inform your Lordship, that after Count Nesselrode had communicated to 
me his despatch to Baron Brunnow, af this date, we had a conversation 
of some importance, which I hasten to report to your Lordship. 

His Excellency began by saying that he hoped nothing would happen 
to prevent the affair under discussion at Constantinople from being satis- 
factorily arranged. 

He then observed that a rnmour had reached him of orders having 
been sent to our squadron in the Mediterranean to proceed towards the 
Dardanelles; and he said that he trusted this ramour would prove to be 
untrue, because such a step would infallibly embroil the whole affair, which 
was now in a fair way of settlement. ‘The Chancellor next alluded 
to a report which he understood had reached Her Majesty’s Government, 
of M. ‘Titoff having declared, previously to the interruption of his diplo- 
matie intercourse with the Porte, that the oe of one of the Poles, the 
surrender of whom had been demanded by the Russian Government, would 
be considered a declaration of war; and said to me (as he had already 
done on a former occasion to the French Minister, as reported in my 
despatch No. 15) that this statement was unfounded. 

I replied to Count Nesselrode that this report had certainly reached 
Her Majeaty Government; that it had been learnt with dee ig ad and 
that possibly it may have had some influence in inducing Her Majesty's 
Government to take the affair of the demand for the extradition of the 
Poles into more serious consideration than they would otherwise have done. 
That as to the destination of the British squadron I had no commu- 
nication to make to his Excellency; [ thought it, however, not impossible 
that Sir William Parker might move the force under his command east- 
wards: but were this to take place Russia need have no alarm for the 
consequences, for we had no aggressive intentions against Turkey, and 
the Mediterranean was a long distance from any portion of the Russian 
Fimpire. 

"Count Nesselrode then said that he very much feared some such move- 
ment as he had mentioned had been contemplated by Her Majesty's 
Government, for he had learnt from M. Kisséleff, the Russian Chareé 
d'Affaires at Paris, that Her Majesty's Ambassador had been actively 
engaged in urging (avait beaucoup travaillé) the French Government to fit 
out a squadron for the waters’ of the Levant; and he could assure me, if 


this were true, that the apparition of our fleet would be the signal for, 


greater complications than had yet taken place. 

Count Nesselrode seemed to attach so much Hy) keg to hp eee 
that I have considered it my duty to dispatch the messenger right 
without a moment’s delay, in order to submit to the consideration of Fer 
Majesty's Government the expediency of sending such fresh instructions 
to Sir William Parker as they may deem advisable under present cir. 
cumstances. 

Ihave, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

The Marquis of Normanby to Viscount Palmerston.—{Received Noveniber 6.) 
(No, 524.) 
My Lord, Paris, November 5, 1849. 


GENERAL HAUTPOUL, charged ad interim with the Foreign 
Department, called on me this morning, and amongst other subjects men- 
tioned that M. Kisséleff, the Russian Chargé d’Affaires, had seen him 
yesterday, and the purport of his communication had been that the diffi- 
culties at Constantinople were now over, as the Emperor had confined his 
demands as to the refugees to that which the Sultan had from the firat 
offered, The General said, under these cireumstances, he thought we 
should probably consider that the possible eventualities to guard against 
which our combined fleets had been sent into that neig bourhood, no 
longer existed. He wished me to consult your Lordship on the subject, as 
he felt it was of the utmost importance that no separate orders should be 
sent on this subject. It was extremely desirable, in his view, that the 

erfect accord which happily existed on this question between France and 
ngland should be made apparent to all the world. The General then 
reciprocated most cordially with me the expression of his conviction that 
upon that alliance depended the best mterests of the two countries, and 
probably the peace of the world.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston—(Received November 10.) 


(No. 308.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 20, 1849. 

1 HAVE communicated privately this morning, by means of Mr. 
Alison, with Aali Pasha and the Grand Vizier, It appears from the lan- 

uage held by those Ministers, that no ostensible change has taken place 
in the state of the pending question since | had last the honour of address- 
ing your Lordship. Appearances are generally much more favourable toa 
pacific solution of the dillerence in so far as Austria is concerned; but 
with respect to Russia, nothing further is known except the passage of 
Fuad Effendi through Warsaw on the 30th ultimo, and the expectation of 
hia reaching St. Petersburgh in less than a week from that time. 

i am also distinctly assured that the Porte is ola ea the mea- 
sures previously adopted with respect to the refugees at Widdin and the 
Turkish troops in Wallachia. 

The former, with the exception of the three English gentlemen who 
have been given up to me, of the Italians who are going to embark at 
Gallipoli, and of ihe Hungarian privates and non-commissioned officers, 


‘whoremain at Widdin, are by this time on their way to Schumla, if not 


actually arrived there. 

The Hungarians remaining at Widdin will be allowed to go home 
under an amnesty to be settled, if pdssible, with an Austrian officer already 
sent thither from Vienna. Omer Pasha and the Pasha of Widdin are 
instructed to see that none of the Hungarians return under Austrian 
authority without their own free consent, 

The Sultan has sent a present of 150,000 piastres to the leading 
refugees, and orders are sent to supply the others with military clothing. 

The troops withdrawn from Wallachia, to the number of 10,000, are 
to be stationed at Schumla and other points in Bulgaria. ‘The Turkish 
Ministers persist in rating the military force in this neighbourhood at 


-G0,000 men, and three-fourths of them being militia, whose terms of 


service would naturally expire in afew days, t ieir dismissal to the pro- 
vinces will be suspended for a month, Throughout Roumelia, as Reshid 
Pasha aflirms, there are not less than 110,000 or 120,000 men in actual 
military service, 

In Bosnia a contest is still going on between the Pasha of that pro- 
vince and a body, more or less numerous, of insurgents ; but the Porte 
seems to have no apprehension of the result, and nothing has occurred 
‘n Servia, as far as 1 am informed, to compromise the public tranquillity. 

It may be added that the position of the Russian armics, and the 
measures adopted for recruiting and provisioning them on & large scale, 
are far from tranquilizing, and among those who regret the termination 
of the Hungarian war, there are some who would willingly increase the 
causes of suspicion and alarm. Against this Gan eoros excitement, and 

myself strenuously to 


warn the Turkish Ministers, and | have now reason to believe that their 
present state of mind is one whieh promises a steady adherence to the 
ine prescribed by honour and humanity, without any tendency to rush 
unreasonably or unnecessarily into the hazards of war. 
I have, &c.

Sir, Warsaw, October 1, 1849. 


LONG before this letter can reach Constantinople your Exeelleney 
will have heard that the Emperor of Russia left Warsaw a few hours 
after the death of his brother the Grand Duke Michael. which occurred 
here in the evening of the 9th ultimo. Fuad Effendi, upon reaching this 
place yesterday, therefore determined to follow His Majesty as, quickly 
as possible to St. Petersburgh, and as the Emperors amicstnick even 
was not here, every motive for delaying the execution of that resolution 
was wanting, and the Sultan’s Commissioner in fact did not remain here 
more than two or three hours. . 

| was however fortunate enough to obtain a pretty long imterview 
with Fuad Effendi before his departure, and was thus enabled to discuss 
with him the contents of your xcellency’s letter relative to the object of 
his mission, and in some taice I hope to second your views for the satis- 
factory solution of that mission, by putting Fuad Effendi in possession of 
every information within my own power as to the chance of such a solu- 
tion; the difficulties of the undertaking, and the military means that 
Russia at this moment possesses of enforcing her demands, so far as 
those means can be estimated by the mere numerical force and the actual 
distribution of her different armies, and by the real means of maintaining 
them beyond the frontiers of their own country. ae 

As i deemed that your letter was addressed to me principally under 
the impression of the Emperor of Russia's being still at Warsaw, and as 
I thought that its confidential communication would be equally appli- 
cable to any one of Her Majesty's Political Agents in a ition to give 
the Sultan’s Commissioner that information and that moral support in his 
trials which I feel proud to think you relied on his receiving from my 
sympathy and at my hands, I thou ‘ht Leould not better respond to yo 

renerous intentions, or more foreib M advocate the cause with which | am 
nappy to identify myself, than by sending your own letter to: Mr. 
Buchanan, Her Majesty's Chargé d’ Affaires at St. Petersburgh, well con-

from me will be given with equal zeal, and probably greater efficacy, by 
my more favourably situated colleague, if so I may be permitted to 
designate Mr. Buchanan. nO

arrival of a British squadron in the neighbourhood of the Dardanelles. 

To your Lordship and to Her Majesty's Government it will be highly 
gratifying to know that the Porte has been apprized of the intentions so 
well calculated to encourage and support her in the unflinching main- 
tenance of her honour and independence; while the decision which has 

robably been taken by this time at St. Peteraburgh is still unknown at 

onstantinople, Appearances favourable to a peaceful solution of the 
pending difference continue on the whole to prevail, but nothing in that 
respect is known with certainty, except that Fuad Effendi had reached the 
Russian capital; that he had been received officially by Count Nesselrode,

by the Porte; that he was to have an audience of His Imperial Majesty in

to his Government immediately afterwards,

even if it were to be a generous relinquishment of the Emperor's present 
demand, without the substitution of any other more or less embarrassing 
to the Porte, your Lordship may rest assured that an impression not easy 
to be effaced has been made on the Sultan and on his Ministers by the 

enerous alacrity with which the Governments of England and of France 
ave come forward in their support; and that whether we look to the 
character of the Sovereign himself, having from his youth a long reign in 
prospect, to the relations of this country with those European Powers 
which have its future interests most at heart, or to those more enlarged 
considerations which affect the balance of power throughout Europe, a 
degree of lasting advantage, which no one can better appreciate than your 
Lordship, is already secured. 
see no reason at present to apprehend any deviation from a prudent

respect he only represents the character-and policy of the Sultan. The

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—( Received November 10.) 
(No. 27.) | 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 30, 1849. 

SEVERAL persons having lately mentioned to me that stories were 
industriously circulated at St. Petersburgh, to the effect that Her Majesty's 
Government had made threatening representations to this Court on the 
eubiect of the differences which had arisen between Turkey and Russia ; 
sat it having been asgerted that the honour of Russia would consequently 
require her to depart from her last determination on the subject of these 
differences, in ater not to appear to yield to a menace from England; | 
alluded to these reports in the course of my last conversation with Count 
Nesselrode. His Kxcellency replied that he at all events was able to 
declare that 1 had never used an expression in my conversations with him 
which could bear a meaning of the kind, and that further, there was 
nothing in your Lordships despatch of the 9th instant which looked like 
a menace. 1 then said to the Chancellor that | fay ae pets to hear 
from him a.refutation of these malevolent rumours; but I added, that if 
ever there were a question of menacing, the accusation would more fairly be 
brought against the Imperial Government, for the language and conduct 
oftheir Minister at Constantinople had certainly been of a most threatening 
character. 

The Chancellor then remarked that he wished he could say the same 
of the French Government as of the English, but that it was not 60; and? 
he regretted also to add that, according to the reports which had reached 
him from Paris, he had good reason to believe that the French Government 
would never have taken up the line they had done in this question, but 
for the influence which had been exercised in the councils of the Govern- 
ment of the Republic by that of Her Majesty, for at the outset of this 
affair M. Kissélelf's reports were by no means 80 unfavourable to Russia 
as-they had afterwards become; but his Excellency said, in spite of all 
these ‘difficulties, he trusted everything would yet be settled without 
serious complications. Piast oe i

replied that he had not; that he had communicated to the Austrian 
Government the decisions which had been taken here, and that he had

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received November 10.) 
(No, 28.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 30, 1649. 


FUAD EFFENDI has been confined to his bed for some days past 
by a severe attack of rheumatic gout, but is now better, and I saw him 

is afternoon. 

He said that he had nothing new to communicate to me on the subject 
of the differences between his Court and that of Russia; but that Count 
Nesselrode had been to see him, and had left with him a translation of 
As Lordship’s despatch of the 6th instant, and a copy of his answer to 

aron Brunnow. 

He told me that the Chancellor taxed him with not havin mentioned 
the fact of the Porte having applied to England for-advice and assistance, 
but that he did not dwell much on the subject ; and Fuad Effendi described 
himself as having evaded a direct answer to this accusation, by saying 
that the alarm had been caused to the Porte by Austria, whose represen- 
tation had been most violent and menacing. 

The Turkish Ambassador told me further, that since we had last met 
he had been onsideelog with Bars care the proposals which he had sent 
to Constantinople, and that he felt every day more satislied that they 
would be favourably received b his Government; that the difficulty of 
removing Russian subjects residing in Turkey, who were placed under the 
protection of foreign passports, would not, he thought, be an insuperable 
objection to the acceptance of these proposals, because he said the Porte 
could certainly enter upon negotiations with foreign Powers, without 
binding herself to succeed in them, and after all, if she failed, the question 
might be undertaken in some other form and perhaps become a subject 
of negotiation between the Powers themselves, which would exonerate the 
Porte from her responsibility to Russia. 

Fuad Effendi mentioned that he had seen the Grand Duke Constan- 
tine, who told him that the Emperor had learnt with much dissatisfaction 
the movement of an allied English and French squadron towards the 
Dardanelles, and His Imperial Highness appears to have spoken in a 
manner which caused the Turkish Ambassador to apprehend that unlooked 
for obstacles would probably be raised by the Russian Plenipotentiary at 
Constautinople if the squadrons were to remain so near the scene of the 
negotiations. 

On the whole, however, | may say that the Turkish Ambassador 
seems full of hope; and he said as | was leaving him, that happen what 
might, he trusted he should be able to show that Turkey had at all events 
done averyshing: in her power to conciliate matters and to prevent the 
calamity of an European war. 

I have, &c, 


(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

My Lord, Foreign Office, November 10, 1849. 


ITH reference to your conversation with General Lamoriciére, 
ee in your despatch No. 29, of the 30th of October, I have Ee 
to your Lordship that there are very few persons indeed in pane in me 
enjoyment of British protection, who are not actually British subjects by 
birth or naturalization, or else citizens of the fonian Islands who are 
placed by treaty under British protection. The instructions given to Her 
Majesty's servants in the Levant on this head are very precise, and in the 


few instances in which British protection is allowed to be given to parties. 


who are not strictly entitled to it, the individuals so favoured are either 
subjects of the Porte who are in some way or other connected with British 
subjects, or who have claims on the British authorities for past services, 
or else subjects of some European Power which has no national Represen- 
tatives on the spot. ‘To these classes, however, have latterly been added 
some Russian Jews in Palestine, who by an arrangement between the British 
and Russian Governments have been placed under British protection. 

It ia possible that there may be some few persons under British pro- 
tection in ‘Turkey who would not be included in the above enumeration, 
but their number must be very small.

Inclosure 2 in No. 110. 


Consul Calvert to Vice-Admiral Sir W, Parker. 
( Private.) 


Sir, Dardanelles, October 26, 1849. 

HER Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople having requested me 
to communicate to your Excellency without loss of time the existing 
regulations regarding the entrance of the Straits of the Dardanelles by 
ships of war, | have the honour to inform you that “vessels of war of 
all nations arriving in these straits without the necessary permission for 
their passage onwards having been received from Constantinople, are 
allowed to make choice of any anchorage between the outer castles and 
Point Nagara, which their respective commanders may consider the most 
convenient or safe, and where they will be required to remain until the 
arrival of the firman for them to pass on to Constantinople.” 

Should therefore your Excellency consider it desirable for the squadron 
under your command to take up an anchorage within these straits, which 
will be in all respects more protected than Besika Bay, I take leave to 
inform you that Lam perfectly understood on this subject with the Pasha 
commanding these forts, who has sent the requisite urders for the com- 
manders of the outer castles to allow the squadron under your command 
to enter these straits without let or hindrance, by day or by night, and to 
proceed to any anchorage between the said castles and Point Nagara. | 
venture to suggest the anchorage situated between Barber'a Point and 
the Inner Asiatic Castle of Sultanieh Kalessi, as being the most conve- 


i 


nient in all: respects, for it is safe in all weathers; ani! there is an excellent 
watering-place with an abundant supply of good ‘fresh water on the 
European shore about a mile below the battery of Namasia. 

Che anchorage of Nagara Bay would in many respects have been 
presente had not the supply of water, which once supplied the so-called 
Captain Pasha’s fountain in great abundance, now totally failed. 

The present communication is made in duplicate and given in charg 
of two persons in whom all confidence may be placed, and who will 
deliver it to you either at Besika Bay or off Tenedos. 

As soon as | hear of the arrival of the squadron anywhere on the 
coast, I shall have the honour of waiting upon your Excellency, when I 
shall take an opportunity to communicate the substance of a private and 
confidential letter received to-day from Her Majesty’s Ambassador, who 
has authorized me to show it to your Excellency. 

. I have, &e. 
(Signed) F. W. CALVERT.

Consul Calverf to Vice-ddmiral Sir W. Parker. 

(Private and Confidential.) 
Sir, Dardanelles, October 31, 1849, 2 p.m. 

AFTER writing my private and confidential despatch of this date at 
2v.m., the Pasha commanding the forts called to inform me that the 
French Consul had just had an interview with him for the purpose, and, 
as he said, by order of the French Minister at Constantinople, of ascer- 
taining what anchorage within these straits would be assigned to the 
Brench squadron, in case they arrived here, as he shortly expected. He 
further wished the Pasha to promise that the anchorage between Barber's 
Point and these castles would be reserved for the French squadron; but 
the Pasha declined making any promise whatever until the French squad 
ron should arrive in this neighbourhood; and he lost not a moment after

My Lord, Therapia, October 27, 1849. 

THE observations ascribed to M. Blondel, His Belgian Majesty's 
ig d'Affaires at this Court, ina despatch addressed to your Lordship 
by Mr. Waller, and communicated to me in copy with your Lordship’s 
instruction No, 246 of this year, refer to points of argument which did 
not escape notice when the discussions that immediately preceded and 
accompanied Prince Radazivil's mission to Constantinople were going on. 
Aali Pasha made special and emphatic use of the examples afforded by 
Austria and Russia, when the Porte at former periods demanded of those 
Powers the extradition of fugitive malcontents owing allegiance to the 
Sultan; and the position of Russia in the present instance as entitled to 
demand the extradition of ber refugee subjects in the sole character of an 
auxiliary to Austria, far from being lost sight of, was only not put for- 
ward prominently in the discussion, because the Treaty Article appealed 
to hy Honaia admitted of an easy refutation, when cited in support of the 
Russian requisition, and offered by itself a solid argument for refusal. 

Your Lordship may be assured that every proper exertion was made 
at the time to place the question at issue on just and strong grounds; in 
testimony of which I venture even at this late hour to submit to your 
Lordship a paper comprising the principal considerations in favour of the 
Porte's view, and prepared by me for eventual communication to the 
Sultan's Ministers. ‘Their firmness, however, sup norted by similar argu- 
ments, repeatedly pressed on them in detail, did nut call for any more 
elaborate reasoning to keep them steady. ‘The memorandum I refer to 
is inclosed herewith. Had I thought proper to give it in, I should have 
endeavoured to make it more cogent and complete. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

lowed by a similar proceeding on the part of the French Admiral, should 
cause any unfavourable excitement, as you appear to apprehend at Vienna, 
your Lordship I am sure will find no difficulty in placing it in its true 
point of view, with reference to the very unusual and threatening circum- 
stances which attended the peremptory demand addressed to the Porte 
by Austria and Russia at the time of Prince Radzivil's mission to Con-

misapprehended; but the fault, so far from lying at our door, is exclusively 
owing either to the Imperial Cabinets themselves, which appear to have 
acted in strict concert together, or to the Agents who respectively repre- 
sented them here. 

Though menace and unnecessary excitement are as remote as possible 
from the views of Her Majesty's Government in this instance, it would be 
hard to require that in order to avoid the mere appearance of either a 
British squadron should run about disguising the fair object of its presence 
in this neighbourhood, and remove, while suegaNt ey still hangs over the 
decisions of the two Emperors, to a distance which at this season and 
in these latitudes, as your Lordship must know, might eventually 
paralyze its means of interfering with effect. 

: resolution of some kind has in all probability been taken by this 
time at St. Petersburgh; and should it so far realize your Lordship's 
anticipations as to tranquillize every just apprehension of danger to this 
empire, the position of the squadron will be naturally subject to 
reconsideration, . 

The foolish stories respecting General Bem, which your Lordship 
wishes me to authorize you to contradict, have I really believe no foun- 
dation in fact, and are probably excrescences from the reports, unhappily 
better founded, of his profession of Islamism, On hearing them some time 
ago, IT expressed my opinion to Reshid Pasha, and received from his 
Highness an assurance that neither rank nor employment had been given 
to any of the refugees who had declared their readiness to turn Turks. 

8 to any obstacles alleged to have been opposed by the Porte's 
officers to the return home of any Hungarian soldiers now at Widdin, I 
can state on the same authority that a promise of amnesty from Austria, 
and the free consent of the individuals are the only conditions required; 
and these I conceive to be quite indispensable.

: Jassy, October 25, 1849. 
| HAV® the honour té acquaint your Excellency that the Turkish 
regiment cantoned in Jassy for the winter has been recalled by orders, 
and ‘left this capital on the 2ist instant for the frontiers of ‘Turkey. Mr. 
Cunningham has had the honour to communicate to your Excellency the 
cortesponding ‘movement of the Turkish troops of the Imperial Guard at 


. Galatz and [braila. 


‘On speaking with the Hospodar on the motives of the departure of 
the Turkish troops, his Highness replied that he regarded it as an execu- 
tion of the Treaty of Balta Liman between Russia and Turkey for the 
reduction of the auxiliary corps in the two Principalities, and thought ‘it 

robable that it would be immediately followed by the departure of the 
Russian troops, leaving only an effective force of 20,000 men of the two 
armies to occupy both Principalities. That he had not received any posi- 
tive news of the result of the mission of Fuad Effendi, but did not enter- 
tain a doubt that it would be followed by an adjustment of the difference 
between the respective Governments. Sineya Bey, on the contrary, con- 
ceived that the measure was one of precaution, and that the Ottoman 
troops had been recalled from Jassy, as they were too far removed from 
any support in the unfortunate event of any rupture. 
There has been a considerable outlay and expense for the quarters 
and subsistence of these troops, who were to form a part of the garrison 
of the town. Those quarters remain now unoccupied, and there are con- 


siderable amounts of commissariat stores and provisions collected in them, 


applicable to military purposes.

Excellency’s despatch announcing his arrival with the squadron under 
his command in the immediate neighbourhood of the Dardanelles, is here- 
with inclosed, together with a copy of my reply.

tion of this intelligence with lively expressions of satisfaction. 
Some doubts have arisen, though not with them, as to the expediency 
of the squadron's anchoring within the mouth of the Dardanelles, Toe 
language of the Treaty is not so ex ‘licit on that point as it is with reapect

Sir, ** Queen," Besika Bay, October 28, 1849. 


I HAVE just had the honour to receive by Mr. Calvert junior, your. 


Excellency’s despatch of the 26th instant.* 
' 1 have not seen the “'Tartarus,” and conclude that Sir Godfrey 
Webster has proceeded in compliance with your wishes to Athens. 
It had not entered into my contemplation to pass the inner castles of 


the Dardanelles without previous communication with your Excelleney, , 


although Mr. Calvert's letter, a duplicate of which I inclose,t inform me 
that lam perfectly at liberty to do so. 

On the question of our having permission to obtain a secure anchorage 
between the outer and inner castles, there appears to be no doubt; and as 
[ have in my despatch of the 27th instant noticed to your Excellency that 
this bay cannot be considered secure at the present season of the year, | 
may probably proceed to the position recommended by Mr. Calvert, should 
the wind become favourable for such a movement, although it is not 
unlikely, from the appearance of the weather, that 1 shall maintain our 
anchorage here until the return of the “ Odin” or * Dragon,” 

[I was not, until the receipt of your Excellency’s letter, aware that the 
“'Tartarus” had proceeded to Athens. 

If you think a steamer indispensably necessary at this moment at 
Constantinople, the ‘‘ Dragon” will be at liberty to remain until the return 
of the “ ‘Tartarus.” 

I am led to this arrangement in consequence of an unfortunate acci- 
dent by which Her Majesty's ship “ Vengeance” came in contact this 
afternoon with the “Dragon” and “ Caledonia,” whereby considerable 
damage has been caused to the steam-vessel, which may perhaps be 
adjusted in the Bosphorus, 

The presence of both steamers will however be very useful until we 
reach our proposed anchorage, when one of them can be sent back to 
Constantinople if the “'Tartarus” does not in the meantime make her 
appearance.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viee- Admiral Sir W. Parker. 


Sir, Therapia, October 31, 1849, 
FROM the hands of Captain Hall, who arrived here this morning 

with Her Majesty's ship “ Dragon,” [ have had the honour to receive your 

Excellency’s despatches of the 27th and 28th instant informing me that 


* Bee Inclosure in No, 98, + Bee Inclovure 2 in No. 110, 


M45 


ou had brought the squadron under your command to anchor in Besika 
Bay, and that you entertained the intention of taking up a more protected 
station either at some greater distance from the Dardanelles, Mosconissi 
being the nearest, or in the mouth of those straits within the outer 
castles, 

Your Excellency’s prompt appearance in this neighbourhood ia @ 
subject of just congratulation, and the Turkish Government has received 
the intelligence of it with feelings of cordial satisfaction and gratitude. 
Appearances continue to warrant a hope that the difference still pending 
between the Porte and the two Imperial Courts of Russia and Austria, 
will be finally settled by a peaceable accommodation. But nothing is yet 
known here of the decision, if any, taken by the Russian Cabinet on 
learning the Sultan’s ereron to the required extradition of the refugees 
from Hungary, and all diplomatic intercourse continues to be suspended 
between the Ministers of the two Allied Courts and the Turkish 
Government. 

In this state of things, which may at any moment change to better or 
to worse—the former contingency appearing the more probable of the 
two—l can only suggest the expediency of your waiting for such farther 
communication as fay have to make you whenever the present uncer- 
tainty shall be removed. It is evidently desirable meanwhile not only to 
provide for the convenience and safety of Her Majesty's squadron at this 
advanced period of the year, but also to secure those objects without 
removing the ships to any considerable distance from the scene of their 
prospective services, should they be eventually required. 

ou are already informed by Her Majesty's Consul at the Dardanelles, 
that orders have been given by the Pasha of those straits, in conformity 
with the existing general regulations, to admit the ships under your com- 
mand within the outer castles. Although some cavil might probably be 
raised or jealousy excited by your reception there, I conceive that no such 
ground ol objection can be expected to outweigh the advantages, essential — 
as they are, of a sheltered anchorage, and an easy appreach to Constan- 
tinople. The Turkish Government itself recommends the anchorage of 
Havouzlar, situated I understand on the Asiatic coast, somewhere between 
the outer and the inner castles. | 

With respect to the “Odin” and “ Dragon,” there is no longer any 
immediate call for the presence of the former here; and Captain Pelham, 
with whom I have had the advantage of holding a confidential and most 
satisfactory intercourse, has apprized me of his intention to return to your 
squadron to-morrow. 

The “Tartarus” being absent, | avail myself of the latitude you have 
obligingly left me, to detain the * Dragon” for the present, with a view to 
communication in case of emergency. As her repairs will be gon on for 
some days without preventing her from going to sea, if wanted, I hope the 
arrangement will meet with your Excellency’s approval, 

Captain Slade remains at my request with the “ Dragon.” 

Orders will be forthwith sent down by the Porte to afford every due 
attention to the wants and comfort of Her Majesty’s squadron, together 
with permission for the immediate passage through the straits of any 
single vessel charged with communications for the Embassy. 


I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston. —(Recewwed November 19.) 


(No. 327.) 
My Lord, Therapia, November 4, 1849. 
BY the messenger Vyner | forwarded copies of a correspondence 
showing in what terms the decision of the Austrian Cabinet concerning the 
uestion of the refugees from Hungary, had been announced to the Porte 
rom Vienna. Yesterday at a fate hour of the evening, no official 
¢ mmunication on that subject had been received by Aali Pasha from the 
Internuncio. 
Thave now the honour to inclose for your Lordship’s information a 
similar set of papers received from St. Petersburgh, with respect to that 
part of the question which relates emphatically to Russia, M. de Titolf 


149 


‘ealied on Aali Pasha this morning, and talked over the terms of the 


Russian propositions with that Minster. His visit was carefully charac- 
terized as private, or rather personal, and [| regret to learn that the re- 
sumption of diplomatic intercourse between hia Le ation and the Porte is 
still made to depend upon the final adjustment of the question. 

In the course of yesterday I endeavoured to ascertain the impression 
made upon the principal Ministers of the Porte by these important com- 
munications from the two Imperial Cabinets. It may be deseribed in a 
ginele sentence,—They are naturally much gratified by the relinquishment 
of the principal demand, but are not yet prepared to accept the proposals 
now addressed to them, without the removal or modification of some 
objectionable points. 

{ may be allowed to add that they feel the honour of the Sultan and 
the independence of his Government to be sufficiently vindicated. The 
lives of the unfortunate fugitives thrown upon their hospitalit by the 
issue of the Hungarian contest are no longer endangered. The language 
and attitude of dictation, so justly and wisely resisted by them, are 
replaced by the more commendable forms of negotiation. It may even be 
hoped that the reserve of complete diplomatic intercourse is a mere 
formality, intended rather to guard the dignity of the proposing parties, 
than indicating the continuance of an imperious or unfriendly spirit on 
their part. 

Something however of no inconsiderable importance, and which may 
prove more or less difficult in the arrangement, remains to be done. It 
would be a just ground of regret if the Porte, while relieved from the 
dangers involved in the late demand, were to be entangled in fresh embar- 
rassments, or obliged to accept unreasonable terms of accommodation. 
Some apprehension may fairly be entertained on this score when the pro- 

sals now made by Austria and Russia are carefully examined. . 

With respect to Austria, it is evident that if the Porte’s engagement 
be carried to the extent of guarding the refugees in the interior of her 
dominions during the pleasure of that Power, she will place herself in a 
very invidious and responsible position during a period of indefinite dura- 
tion, and entitle the Austrian Agents to claim a most inconvenient and 
disparaging right of superintendence over such measures of restraint as 
she may be called upon to adopt. It is greatly to be wished that the 
Turkish Government may find itself at liberty to substitute the expulsion 
of the refugees from ‘larkey for their detention in the interior of the 
country, But of this latitude the Porte would appear to have deprived 
herself, if not by the notes which her Representatives at Vienna and 
Petar ure presented without any special authority to Prince Schwarzen- 
bere and Count Nesselrode, at least by the terms of the Sultan's letter to 


- each of the two Emperors, 


Concerning the Russian proposals, it may be observed that the first 


‘transcends the limits of the original demand of extradition; that the 


second requires of the Porte to contract an engagement of which the 


- execution would not depend upon herself; and that the third may find 


an obstacle to its acceptance in the religious convictions of the country. 
Notwithstanding these palpable objections Tam inclined to hope that 


- the desire, known or presumable, of all parties to terminate the present 


difference, will eventually, perhaps almost immediately, prevail to effect a 
satisfactory accommodation. 

Your Lordship may depend upon my earnest endeavours to con- 
tribute towards this desirable result with the least possible delay. I for- 
ward this despatch to your Lordship through Her Majesty's Ambassador 
at Paris, It will be conveyed ‘to Toulon or Marseilles by a French 
steamer of war, whose intended departure this evening has been obligingly 
announced to me by General Aupick, 

The messenger Robbins is gone to Alexinitza in order to clear his 
quarantine and to be ready for the despatches which | propose to trans- 
mit to him by a confidential tartar in the course of two or three days. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

(Extract.) Dardanelles, November 2, 1849. 

1 HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Excellency’s 
letter of the 31st of October by the “Odin,” and beg to inform you that 
as the wind set in very strong from the southward yesterday, making 
Besika Bay a doubtful anchorage in such weather, | availed myself of the 
permission which had been intimated to me By Her Majesty's Consul, to 
pass the outer castles of the Dardanelles with Her Majesty’s squadron 
under my command® between the inner castles and Barber's Point. 

Since 1 last addressed your Excellency I have been joined by the 
“Thetis” frigate, bringing a large supply of provisions, which is now bein 
distributed amongst the ships, and | hope to get them completed wit 
water from our present anchorage.

to acknowledge the receipt of your two despatches dated the 19th and

Whatever difficulties may retard that final arrangement, which |

between the Russian Legation and the Porte, [ am unwilling to believe

eas they are of a nature to prevent an early settlement of the whol 
affair, 

My persuasion in this respect is greatly strengthened by.a confidential 
conversation which | have had this morning with M. de Titoff, whom I 
was happy to receive at his request with that good will and frankness 
which have always characterized our personal communications. 

It may be desirable for you to know that he spoke to me on the sub- 
ject of Her Majesty’s Mediterranean re aaa now anchored at the Dar- 
danelles, giving me to understand that he questioned the propriety of its 
having entered the mouth of the straits, and intimating the embarrass-

occupying a position to which the publie voice would hardly fail to attac 
the idea of a menace, 

I endeavoured to remove any unfavourable impression from his mind 
by reading to him Sir William Parker's statement of his motive for shifting 
the squadron’s anchorage from the outside to the inside of the entrance to 
the straits. 

You will see by the extract inclosed herewith, that the Admiral’s 
motive was one of weather alone, and that there is no idea whatever of 
either violating the Treaty or assuming an attitude of menace. I assured 
my Russian colleague, moreover, that he might rely upon my spontaneous 
sentiments for raising no unnecessary obstacle to the conclusion of a 
satisfactory arrangement between him and the Porte, supposing even that 
the improved state of the weather had not of itself already induced the 
Admiral to take up his former or some more distant station beyond the 
outer castles.

I WENT toexplain to the President this morning that some unforeseen 
difficulty inust have prevented the arrival of the despatches accepting his 
proposition of referring to the Ambassadors at Constant'nople the question 
of the recall of the Aeets, or their continuance in the neighbourhood of the 
Dardanelles. I was aware that from embarrassments with members of his 
Government and others he was very anxious that there should no longer 
be any delay in sending out instructions to this effect ; and I had therefore 
communicated to him Senay yesterday, what I had reason to 
expect from your Lordship’s private letter | should receive such despatches 
this morning. 
_ | then adverted to the intelligence 1 had just received from Sir 
Stratford Canning, and stated that I could not conceive this could make any 
difference as to the mere fact of sending out discretionary orders, as it only 

roved, from its contradiction with what we had been led to expect, that 
t was ay upon the spot that the question as to the flects could be satis- 
factorily decided; but with respect to the effect such intimations would 
have upon the movements of the fleets, 1 thought it destroyed the motive 
for the extraordinary precipitation which had Ges urged upon him; for 
when we heard that the renewal of diplomatic relations was made by 
Russia contingent upon the settlement of the many novel demands she had 
made, if one placed oneself in the situation of the Ambassadors, one 
cond not suppose they could choose such a moment to send away the 
eebe. 

Qur good offices had first been required on account of the threatening 
attitude assumed in the interruption of diplomatic relations. It seemed to 
me obvious whilst the menace was still maintained, the support could not 
with safety or with honour be withdrawn,

we all hoped would soon be pacifically obtained.

No, 125. 
Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston — (Received November 19.) 


(No, 31. Con fidential.) 
My Lord, Si. Petersburgh, November 6, 1849. 


1 HAD some conversation two ste ago with Count Orloff respecting 
the extradition of the Poles, and was glad to find that he did not altogether 
approve of the proceedings of M. Titoff, who he said had gone too far it 


the matter, adding that the Emperor was dissatisfied with his conduct. 

I was somewhat surprised to hear this admission from Count Orloff; 
because I had been informed by Count Nesselrode that the conduct of the 
Russian Minister at Constantinople had received the formal approval of 
his Government ; and on my 84 fing so to Count Orloff, he attempted to 
explain that the system of the Russian Government was never to ¢ isavow 
their Ministers, as such a course would be attended with too many incon- 
veniences, but that | might rest assured that M. Titofl had been severely 
censured ; for that although the Emperor had.a full right to demand the 
exact fulfilment of the Treaty of Kainardji, M. Titoff had been over 
vealous, and that nothing was further from the Emperor's jntentions than 
to raise such a cry on the subject as had been got, up at Constantinople, at 
London, and at Paris. 

Count Orloff made some inquiries of me as to the position of our 
squadron in the Mediterranean, and said that the movement towards the 
Dardanelles would he feared complicate matters. 1 endeavoured to make 
him feel that the attitude of the Russian Minister at Constantinople was in 
itself sufficient to warrant this movement; but he said that there were 50 
many precedents for the cessation of diplomatic intercourse between a 
foreign Minister and the Porte, that he must confess his opinion to me that 
that there was no sufficient necessity for our having given the affair so 
serious a turn, 

He next made some observations on the conduct of France in the 
question, and wished me to understand that according to the reports which 
had reached the Russian Government, they were persuaded that France 
followed us most unwillingly, and. that but for the influence of the 
President, the French squadron would not even at the present moment 
have sailed for the Levant. 

I replied to Count Orloff that | knew nothing and had nothing to do 
with the individual opinions of the members of the French Cabinet, or the 
question which had been lately discussed by them, and that all | had to 


consider wus the decision at which they had arrived, and the zeal and: 


activity with which that decision appeared to have been carried out by the 
execulive power. 
1 have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Inclosure 5 in No, 125. 


The Hon. Captain Pelham to Sir Godfrey Webster. 


HIS Excellency Sir Stratford Canning having informed me that he 
was obliged to send one of the gentlemen of the Embassy to Rodosto on 
public service, and that the presence of a vessel of war off that de during 
the time would tend to bring the case to a satisfactory result, it is my 
direction that you proceed in Her Majesty's vessel “'Tartarus,” under 
your command, to that port, taking with you Mr. Alison, of the British 
Embassy; and you will be back at this anchorage by 4 p.m. of the 13th, 
or earlier, should Sir Stratford Canning’s mission be finished. 

In execution of this service you will remember that you are not 
authorized to take part in any transaction at Rodosto, beyond affording 
the support which the presence of a British vessel of war must always 
give to a British Agent in a foreign port. 

Given under ny hand this 10th day of October, 1849. 


(Signed) F. T. PELHAM.

Inclusure’3 in No, 137. 
Consul Calvert to Sir Stratford: Canning. 


(Extract.) Dardanelles, October 30, 1849. 

AS to the propriety of the squadron entering the Dardanelles and 
taking up a more sheltered anchorage than that of Besika Bay, I feel now 
convineed that doubts can only have arisen in consequence of the true 
meaning of the word détroits, as contained in the original Treaty 
signed in French on the 10th July, 1841, having evidently been erroneously 
rendered in the English text by the word straits. The Straits of the 
Dardanelles are always designated in French as Le Canal des Dardanelles, 
and the real sense of the word déireils, in the present instance, would 
evidently have been more appropriately rendered by calling it the 
narrowest passages, thus implying that of the inner castles, 

Considering furthermore, that the instructions of the Turkish Govern- 
ment to the various olficers in command of the forts of the Dardanelles, 
since the signature of the Treaty, have invariably admitted the right of all 
foreign vessels of war to enter within the outer castles of the Dardanelles ; 
and also the fact that Russian, Austrian, and American vessels of war 
have at all times availed themselves without hesitation of the faculty thus 
granted indiscriminately to ships of all nations.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received November 25.)

My Lord, 


Therapia, November 7, 1849. 
IN my ostensible despateh of this date, I have stated for your 


Lordship's information the course which I had thought it my duty to 
pursue with respect to the position of Her Majesty’s Mediterranean 
3 ratalie in consequence of the relinquishment by Austria and Russia 
of that demand and dictatorial mode of enforcing it, which had compelled 
the Turkish Government to solicit Her Majesty’s sympathy and active 
support. It remains for me to acquaint your Lordship in this confidential 
form with certain circumstances and considerations bearing on the subject 
of that despatch, and also to avail myself of the opportunity thus afforded 


for drawing your Lordship's attention to the terms of the Treaty con- 


91 


166 


eluded in 1841 between the Porte and the five principal Powers of 
Europe. 
1 shall probably be borne out by the reports of our officers, in statin 
that neither the land defences of the Bosphorus, nor the available Turkist 
Navy, would be found sufficient to secure Constantinople against a suc- 
cessiul attack by sea, were Russia determined to risk the enterprize by 
means of her squadron at Sebastopol. The same reasons, which had 
peeveiles with Her Majesty’s Government to order the ships under Sir 
Villiam Parker’s command to the Dardanelles, continued necessarily to 
have their effect so long as we remained in ignorance of the decision taken 
at St, Petersburgh on learning the issue of Prince Radazivil’s mission to 
Constantinople. Appearances had indeed become gradually favourable to 
a peaceful solution © the pending difference, but a credulous reliance on 
appearances at such a juncture was fraught with hazard, and might 
eventually have proved fatal to the abject of Her Majesty's intervention. 

Such being the case, it was evidently desirable that the British 
auxiliary squadron should at once approach the possible scene of action 
so nearly as to insure its arrival there in time, if the danger, which is 
still problematical, should become on a sudden not only real but urgent, 
To its passage through the straits in time of peace, the First Acticle of 
the Treaty of 184] presented, as your Lordship knows, a distinet and 
unquestionable barrier; but the distance from Constantinople might be 
materially shortened by the atlvance of the squadron to an anchors 

below the inner castles which constitute the effective defences of the 
straits, and occupy those points where the channel assumes its most 
decided character The standing regulations, and consequent local 
practice, corroborate a distinction which public convenience had already 
suggested. Kven the terms of the Treaty may be so taken as to warrant 
that exercise of discretion which the Porte has for some time at least 
practically assumed with rezard to the admission of foreign ships of war 
outside the ‘above-mentioned castles and their adjacent batteries. I am 
aware that the word détroit applies generally to the whole length of a 
channel, but surely its more emphatic application belongs to that part of 
the channel where the shores approach most ea to each other, and 
where the right of eontroul is officially exercised by the constituted 
authorities. 

Notwithstanding these various considerations in favour of a liberal 
interpretation of the Treaty, and my conviction, not lightly entertained, 
that the Porte had no objection whatever to the squadron’s reception at 
the inner anchorage, | was unwilling to add my official sanction without 
the further inducement of hazard to the ships from remaining longer in 
an exposed situation. Of this important point the Admiral was neces- 
sarily the proper judge; and your Lordship will have learnt from the 
correspondence between Sir William Parker and myself that the pressure 
of a strong south wind was the immediate cause of his advance to the 
second’ place of anchorage, in the propriety of which-movement at the 
time I still most cordially concur. 

An important change has since however occurred in the diplomatic 
bearings of the question. Not only has the Russian and Austrian demand 
of extradition been given Up, but together with the removal of any imme- 
diate cause of apprehension as to the views of those powers with respect 
to Turkey, a more distinet knowledge has been acquired of the umbrage 
occasioned at St. Petersburgh by the movements of the British and Freneh 
squadrons in’ this direction, and of the unfavourable effect which. its 
inerease may have upon the proceedings essential to a complete and 
satisfactory accommot ation. In consequence of the former andin con- 
templation of the latter cireumstance, L did not hesitate to addreas my 
letter of the 4th instant to Sir William Parker. 

M. de Titoff called upon me the next day, and, after referring vo a

sources of the deciston taken at St. Petersburgh, which he handsomely 
attributed to the expression of public opinion i England as well as to 
regard for the Sultan’s desire expressed through Fuad Effendi, asked my

The expulsion of the Polish refugees who took part in the Hungarian

Consul Calvert to Vice-Admiral Sir W. Parker. 


Sir, Derdanelles, October 30, 1849. 

AFTER seriously considering the substance of the private communt- 

cation made to me yesterday by your Excellency whilst I was on board of 
the “Queen,” and after maturely weighing the nature of the doubts 
entertained by Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople as to fae 
ropriety of the squadron under your command entering the Straits of the 
Dardane les, and taking up a more sheltered anchorage than that of 
Besika Bay, I have the honour to state that [ feel now convinced that such 
doubts can only have arisen in consequence of the true meaning of the word 
détroits as contained in the original ‘Treaty signed in French on the 10th 
July, 1841, having evidently been erroneous! rendered in the English 
text by the word straits. ‘The Sératts of the Dardanelles are always 
designated in French as Le Canal des Dardanelles, and the real sense of 
the word détroit in the present instance would evidently have been more 
appropriately pene by calling it the narrowest passages, thus implying 
of the inner castle. 
et This assertion will be further corroborated by the substance of the 
inclosed copy of a despatch received at this Consulate from Her Majesty's 
Embassy at Constantinople on the 27th March, 1645, together with the 
copy of a memorandum from the Sublime Porte which accompanied it. 

" Considering furthermore that the instructions of the Turkish Govern- 
ment to the various officers in command of the forts of the Dardanelles 
since the signature of the Treaty have invariably admitted the right of all 
foreign vessels of war to enter within the outer castles of the Dardanelles, 
and also the fact that Russian, Austrian and American vessels of war have 
at all times availed without hesitation of the facility thus granted 
indiscriminately to ships of all nations; | am the more confirmed in the 


opinion expressed by me to your Excellency as to the undoubted pro-. 


priety that the squadron under your command should anchor for shelter 
within these straits, 
1 have, &e. 


(Signed) F. W. CALVERT,

(Extract.) Constantinople, March 22, 1845. 
IN directing your attention to the importance of conforming strictly 
to the regulations adopted by the Ottoman Government, I have the satis- 
faction to state that any British vessel, whether it be a merchant-vessel or 
a vessel of war, is allowed to come within the outer castle of the Dar- 
danelles at once, as far as the anchorage of Kepez Bournou or Point 
Barbieri, by night as well as by day. a am assured by the Ottoman 
Minister that a permission to this effect, including the vessels of other 
friendly Powers, will form a part of the instructions addressed to the 
commanders of the castles and other Turkish authorities of the Dardanelles. _ 


P.S.—March 26, 1845.—I am assured by the chief interpreter of the 
Embassy, upon the authority of Chekib Effendi, that the above-mentioned 
instructions have already been dispatched.

Your Lordship will not fail to observe the marked difference of tone 
which distinguishes the Russian from the Austrian note. The latter 
declares that Russia is to be satisfied as well as Austria before the Inter- 
nuncio will consent to resume his usual diplomatic intercourse with the 
Porte. The Russian note on the contrary makes no mention of Austria, 
The Austrian note requires the confirmation and execution of the measures 
apparently agreed upon at Vienna, The Russian note may be construed 
as leaving open a door for modification and the mutual adjustment of 
terms. I have a strong misgiving that the Sultan and his principal 
Ministers will make little more than a flourish of opposition to what is 
most objectionable in the Austrian proposes:

My Lord, Therapia, November 8, 1849. 
NO positive intelligence of the arrival of the French squadron in the 
Archipelago has yet reached Constantinople. 

fhe French Minister has dispatched one of the gentlemen of his 
Embassy in a war steamer to find Admiral Parceval. understand that 
there is no present intention of inviting the French squadron to the 
Dardanelles, and that if it has reached Vourla, it will stay there for the 
present. 

| have seen a despatch addressed by General Lamorici¢re to my 
French colleague, who put it into my hands to read. Its author takes 
much credit to himself for having, as he imagines, succeeded in softening 
Count Nesselrode’s feelings towards this country before the Emperor of 
Russia was prepared tolisten to Fuad Effendi, and before Lord Bloomfield’s 
return with your Lordship’s instructions of the Gth ultimo in his pos- 
session. From the tone and tenour of this despatch it might be supposed 
that England was playing only a secondary part in the vindication of 
Turkish independence. 

General Lamoriciére’s despateh has been communicated to Reshid 
Pasha, who told me that his feelings had been deeply wounded by 
observing that the Ambassador had Tistened without remark to Count 
Neaselrode’s assertion that the Turkish Empire had for some time existed 
only by the sufferance of Russia. 

While stating these facts for your Lordship’s information, I am 
willing to believe that, in case of any active operations by sea for the pro- 
tection of Turkey, the French Admiral would not be slow to act in concert 
with Her Majesty's squadron.

Inclogure in No. 144, 

‘The Marquis of Normanby to Sir Stratford Canning. 

Sir, Paris, November 23, 1849. 
THE French Government are about to send conditional instructions 
to General Aupick as to the recall of the fleet, leaving it to the discretion 
of the General, after consulting with your Excellency, to decide when 
affairs are so surely in a train of satisfactory arrangement at Constanti- 
nople as that the two fleets may, without abandoning the objects for 
which they were both sent to those parts, return to their winter quarters. 

I ele avail myself of the opportunity kindly offered by General de 
la Hitte to enter thus into communication with your Excellency on this 
subject, because J am afraid that otherwise you would not be aware, at 
the time of the arrival of the French Government steamer, that this step 
has been taken in cordial concert with Her Majesty's Government, and 
that despatches of a similar character addressed to your Excellency will 
either follow by the next Marseilles steamer, or be sent within a day or 
two by an overland messenger. I think it of the more importance that 
your Excellency should have it in your power to correct any erroneous 
impressions which might arise at Constantinople from the circumstance 
of General Aupick alone receiving instructions on this subject, because | 
am aware that it has been wrongfully asserted, and industriously cireu- 
lated here, that with respect to the future movements of the fleets there 
had been established a separation between the policy of the two countries ; 
and [ cannot but foresee that should such an idea be current at Constanti- 
nople it might exercise an injurious influence on the result of pending 
negotiations, 

The facts of the case are shortly these. Upon the communication 
of a despatch from St, Petersburgh, stating that the differences with the 
Porte were upon the point of adjustment, accompanied by an expression 
of a desire that the French fleets should not therefore longer remain in 
that quarter, I was requested to consult Her Majesty's Government as to 
the time of the withdrawal of the two fleets. I received an answer from 
Lord Palmerston (a copy of which may probably eee time have been 
forwarded to your Excellency) stating that Her Majesty's Government 


were eanally desirous for the return of the fleet, but suggesting that it 
ve well to wait at least for the next intelligence 


would rom Constanti-

176 


nople. This was in the first instance assented to by the French Goyern- 
ment; but two or three days later another proposition was made to me 
by the President, that instructions should without delay be sent to the two 
Ambassadors, but only to the effect that they must themselves judge 
upon the spot according to cireumstances, what was the approximate 
moment for the withdrawal of the fleets. I received an answer from Lord 
Palmerston assenting to this new mode of action, and promising 
despatches to pass throu h Paris to that effect. | 

‘A week has since elapsed, during which time I have induced the 
French Government to keep their yease] waiting at Toulon for these

vet heard any explanation; but I can easily imagine that it ma have

novel in their nature, had been arran d. This in my mind would natu- 
rally have induced Her Majesty’s Government to think there was no 
extraordinary haste necessary in sending out conditional orders to your 
Excellency. 

‘As, however, I have heard that M. Drouyn de Lhuys had an inter-

the facts within my own knowledge will sulfice.

Sir, Ss ae Foreign Office, November 30, 1849. 

i to observe to your Excellency that no doubt there 1 
foree in the arguments which in your despatch No, 330 of she Veh Soobant 
you state as reasons why the anchorage immediately within the outer 
castles of the Dardanelles might be considered as not included in the 
prohibition contained in the First Article of the Treaty of July 1841; but 
nevertheless the natural and most obvious construction of the Treat 
would make the other way. ‘The Straits or the Détroit of the Dardanelits 
must, geographically considered, be deemed to be the narrow passag 
between the Mediterranean and the Sea of Marmora; and it is difficult 
to draw any such substantial distinction between different portions of 
that passage with reference to their relative breadth, as to be able satis- 
factorily to affirm that any portion of that passage can justly be excluded 
from the ae of the expression “the Straits, or the Détroit of the Dar- 
danelles.”" In any matter which bears on the construction of a treaty it 
is best to be, if possible, on the safe side, and not to run matters so shar 
as to be obliged to contend for a disputable interpretation. But in the 
pee case there is a strong motive of interest which ought to induce 
ee Britain to observe very scrupulously the engagements of this 
freaty, for the example of Great Britain in disregarding the Treaty 
paca readily be followed by Russia; and from the relative positions of 
the cruizing grounds of their respective fleets, a Russian squadron would 
have oceasion to enter the Bosphorus far oftener than a British squadron 
would have to enter the Dardanelles, and while the British squadron 
entering the Dardanelles would still not be in a position to produce an 
serious moral effect at Constantinople, the Russian squadron enterin the 
Bosphorus would aicect and imminently threaten the Turkish ‘capital | 

Chis last-mentionec consideration scems to answer the reasonin 
which led your Excellency to think that the presence of the British 
squadron within the outer castles would render it much more efficacious 
than if it had remained at Besika Bay, For from that inner anchor r 
as well as from Besika Bay, it could probably not have reached fein: 
tinople as soon as a Russian squadron would have run down into the 
Bosphorus, and have placed itself abreast of Constantino le; but the 
knowledge that a British squadron was close to the Dar anelles, and 
could in a short time make its appearance in the Bosphorus, would ‘natu. 
rally act-as an effectual restraint to prevent the Russian squadron from 
making any such attack; and this restraining eflect would be produced

Government might either engage to enter into the communications therein 
mentioned with foreign Governments, explaining to Russia that it must 
rest-with such foreign Governments to give or to withhold their consent 
to the specified arrangement, or the Porte might suggest that the Russian 
Government should itself make application to the foreign Powers con- 
cerned, 

With regard to the third demand, it is to be observed that it is not 
founded on the stipulations of the treaties between Russia and the Porte, 
and that on the contrary it is at variance with those treaties; for the 
Treaty of Kainardji, which entitles each of the two Governments to 
demand the expulsion or surrentler of such of their rebellious subjects as 
may take refuge in the territory of the other, distinctly exempts from the 
scope of such demands Turkish subjects who in Russia may become 
Christians, and Russian subjects who in Turkey may become Mahometans. 

Moreover Christians who in Turkey embrace the Mahometan faith 
become thereby subjects of the Sultan, and Her Majesty’s Government do 
not know whether the Sultan could deem himself justibed in imprisoning 
any of his subjects at the mere request of a foreign Power, and without 
those subjects having committed any offence within the Turkish dominions, 
or against the Turkish laws, ‘The duties of good neighbourhood would 
indeed require that the Sultan should take care that these newly acquired 
subjects should not, any more than any of his natural-born subjects, make 
any attempts to disturb the tranquillity of neighbouring and. friendly 
States; and he would no doubt be able to make such arrangements as to 
the places of their residence as would prevent there being any just ground 
for apHrenen sien on this score on the part.of the Government of Russia. 

There seems therefore in these last made Russian demands little if 
anything that is not nuRrOnSIIAS of easy arrangement by friendly commu- 

nication between the two Governments. 

The last Austrian demand is more simple, but at the same time more 
difficult of arrangement. The Austrian Government requires that all the 
refugees of whom it has already given in a list, amounting to about forty, 
and that all those of whom it may hereafter give euler ete should be 
sent, to some suitable place in the interior of the Turkish dominions to be 
there placed under “surveillance,” so that it should be impossible for 
them henceforward to undertake anything against legal order in the 
Austrian States; and that this arrangement should not cease without the 
jointconsent of the two Governments. 

Upon this it is to be observed that such a demand is not borne out by 
the treaties between Austria and the Porte, and that the engagement 
which it requires the Turkish Government to take would place the Sultan 
in some respects in a position unbecoming an independent ake) 

The Austrian Government engiiehes indeed its demand that the 
Sultan should by the surrender of the Hungarian refugees become acces- 
sory to consigning to the fate that would have awaited them, men who 
have committed no offence against his authority or against the laws of his 
country, and who before entering his territory were assured by his officers 
that they would enjoy therein the protection which the laws of hospitality 
prescribe. But the Austrian Government now requires that the Sultan 
should constitute himself the keeper of state offenders against the Austrian 
Government; that he should make himself responsible to Austria for the 
exact and vigilant performance of his tusk in that eupacity, and that he 
should not be at liberty to cease to perform these functions without the 
consent of the Austrian Government. 

_ It is for the Turkish Government to judge how far it would have any 
effectual means of carrying into effect such an arrangement, and they best 
know how far the promises made in their behalf to the Hungarian refugees, 
before those refugees entered the Turkish territory, would be broken b 
such an engagement towards the Austrian Government, But it ja mani- 
fest that such an engagement wonld impose upon the Sultan unbeeomin 
obligations, which neither the stipulations of treaties nor internation 
amity require him to undertake, 

That which the spirit_of his treaty engagements and the general 
principles of international amity bind the Sultan to do, 1s to prevent any 
part of his territory from being ay by any persons, whether his own

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.— (Received December 3.)

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, Nocember 21, 1849. 

THE newspapers having lately mentioned that the Turkish troops 
had left Bucharest. 1 inquired yesterday of Count Nesselrode if this report 
was true, and if so, whether we might not expect to hear of a similar 
movement of the Russian forces from the Danubian Principalities. 

The Chancellor replied that the retreat of the ‘Turkish troops had, he 
believed, taken place as a matter of precaution on the part of Omer Pasha, 
and was dictated by the apprehension of a possible collision with the 
Russians in the event of the arrangement of the differences which had 
arisen respecting the Polish refugees having been seriously retarded ; 
and that it had not been done with any previous concert between the two 
Powers, 

His Excellency added that as I had put this question to him, he 
would inform me that he nevertheless hoped a reduction in the Russian 
occupying force would soon take place, for that he had already directed 
M. 'Titoff, as soon as his diplomatic intercourse with the Porte was re-es- 
tablished, to discuss the subject with the Ottoman Government, in order 
to carry out the arrangements which had been stipulated by the Act 
ae to the Principalities, signed at Balta Liman on the Ist of May 
ast, 

Lam not able to discover the exact amount of the Russian forces at 
present in the Danubian Principalities; but my French colleague, with 
whom L have lately had some conversation on the subject, lias informed 
me that he believes it to amount to 36,000 men, whereas he calculates the 
force uncer Omer Pasha to be only 16,000 men, —

Memorandum from the Porte to the Internuncio. 


(Traduzione,) Safer, 1261. (23 Febbrajo, 1845.) 
COME ¢ pur noto all’ Eccellenza vostra fi proibito, gia lungo tempo 
fA, ai bastimenti di guerra di qualunque Corte straniera di entrare ne’ 
Dardanelli ossia nel Se tor. e questo vecchio divieto fi confermato di 
nuovo nel Trattato conchiuto fra la Sublima Porta e le Cinque Grandi 
Potenze ai di 19 Regeb dell’ anno 1257. Benché sia noto dunque a tutto 
il mondo che se nulladimeno un tal bastimento, grande o piccolo, apparte- 
nente a qualsiasi Corte, mostrasse voglia di entrare in uno degli stretti 
summentovati, verebbe primo avvisato del divieto; se non ascultasse, 
verrebbero tirati uno a due colpi di canoni senza palle, e se anche questo 
non producesse verrun effetto, si prenderebbero, avendo il hastimento 
agito contro il regolamento ed 1 trattati, le misure necessarie ad impedire 
Ventrata per mezzo di colpi di canoni carricati a palle; benché poi sia 
noto che ¢ proibito anche ai bastimenti mercantili delle amiche Corti ed a 
quei della Siblima Porta stessa di passar il Bosforo ed i Dardanelli di 
notte: ci venne pure notificato dagli impiegati di quelle parti: “Cercar 
di tempo in tempo qualche bastimento mercantile, senza riguardo al 
suddetto regolamento, di entrar negli stretti, e per quanti colpi di canoni 
che essi mostrino di valer impedire Ventrata di esso, non riuscirv: punto, 
oiché si sa che sono colpi poco nonvoli. GQuestyu veechio divieto contro i 
bastimenti mereantili non essendo necessario che perché di notte non si 
pud distinguere se sia un bastimento mercantile oppure uno di guerra, e 
non essendosi finora traltato di realmente danneggiar i hastimenti mer- 
cantili che entrano il tal guisa, la maggiore parti de hastimenti mercantili 
attribuendo il non tirar a palla ad una specie di tacito permesso, cercare 
d'infrangere il regolamento in discorso,” 
In consezuenza di cid ¢ stato fermamente deciso di mantener in vigore 
il divieto assoluto pit volte citato, il quale ¢un’ antica massima governiale 
della Porta confermato ultimamente nel Trattato conchiuso colle Cinque 
Potenze unite, Tal divicto sara seriamente eseguito contra qualunque 
bastimento che intraprendesse di passar il Bosforo oppure il bardanelli 
dopo il tramontar del sole, in modo che a comminciar dal mese di Marzo 
di quest’ anno 1261 (1845), sara ancora fissato un termine d 3 mesi; 
spirato il quale gli impiegati di quelle parti receveranno l'ordine di avvisare 
del divieto i bastimenti che persistessero nel yolere entrare nei summento- 
yati stretti, se non ascoltassero di tirar uno o due colpi di canoni senza 
alle, ¢ se auche a questo non badassero, di prendere le misure necessarie 
perché venga impedita Ventrata per mezzo di colpi di canoni caricati a 
palle. Abbiamo quindi diretto questa memoria ufficiale all’ Eceellenza 
vostra per pregarla di compiaccersi siu da ora far significare quanto sopra 
ai capitani de’ bastimenti Austriaci, dar loro £ ordini necessari ed infor- 
marli parimente che qualora dall’ esecuzione della piuddetta misura emer- 


gesse qualche danno a qualcuno, egli non potra lagnarsi ne domandanre

Baron Brunnow to Viscount Palmerston. 


Londres, le Sh223e", 1849, 

LE Soussigne, &c., par une note en date du 48 Novembre, a cu lhonneur 
d'inyiter M. le Vicomte Palmerston, &c., 4 vouloir bien lui faire connaitre si 
ordre de retirer lescadre de l'Amiral Parker du Détroit des Dardanelles, a déa 
été expédié, afin que la Cour Impériale de Russie puisse se convaincre que les 
engagemens mutuels résultant de la Convention du fy Juillet, 1841, continuent 
4 recevoir leur pleine et entitre exécution. 

En réitérant aujourd'hui cette demande, le Soussigné se fait un devoir d'y 
ajouter les considérations suivantes, qu'il se permet de signaler 4 Pattention 

séreuse du Gouvernement de Sa Majesté Britannique. 

Il commencera d’abord par Ini rappeler les motifs de haute prévoyance qui 
ont dicté la Convention du 7/5 Juillet, 1841. Ils ont eu deux objets en vue. 
premier a été d'offrir 4 l'Europe une garantie de la conservation de la paix géné- 
rale, en constatant l'union et l'accord des Cing Grandes Puissanees; le second 
a été de donner a l'indépendance et au repos del’Empire Ottoman un gage 
nouveau, én placant sous la sauvegarde d'une transaction Européenne le respect 
di 4 Vaneienne régle de cet empire, en vertu de laquelle les Détroits du Bosphore 
et des Dardanelles sont fermés aux batimens de guerre étrangers, tant que la 
Porte se trouve en paix. 


Sur la base de ces principes l'Article I de la Convention de 1841 a fondé les 
déclarations solennelles ci-apreés : 

Dune part, Sa Hautesse le Sultan a déclaré sa ferme résolution de main- 
tenir 4 Vavenir le principe invariablement établi comme ancienne régle de son 
empire, en vertu duquel il a été de tous tems défendu aux batimens de guerre 
des Puissances étrangéres d'entrer dans les Détroits des Dardanelles et du Bos- 
phore, et que, tant que Ja Porte se trouve en paix, Sa Hautesse n'admettra aucun 
batiment de guerre étranger dans les dits détroits. 

“De autre, les Cing Grandes Puissances se sont engagees A respecter cette 
détermination du Sultan et 4 se conformer au principe ci-dessus énoneé.” 

“Par l’Article 1], le Sultan s'est réservé, comme par le passé, de délivrer des 
firmans de passage aux batimens légers sous pavillon de guerre, lesquels scront 
employés, comme il est d’usage, au service des Légations des Puissances amies,"' 

Hi suffit de citer les stipulations ci-dessus pour se persuader que les Hautes 
Parties Contractantes n’ont certainement pas prévu qu'un jour le commandant 
d'une escadre, pour se mettre & couvert du mauvais tems, allat chercher un 
sees dans le Détroit des Dardanelles, que la Convention de 1841 déclarait 

ermeé. 

Un eas de détresse maritime meérite assurément de justes égards, Cependant 
dans la circonstance actuelle l'Archipel n’avait-il pas d'autres rades pour lieu 
d'abri? La réputation de l'Amiral Sir W. Parker n’est-elle pas trop bien établie 
pour qu'on puisse douter de l'habileté avec laquelle il aurait pu choisir un autre 
ancrige tout aussi silr que celui qu'il a cherché sous le chiteau des Dardanelles. 

Mais, dira-t-on, en choisissant ce mouillage, le commandant de lescadre 
Anglaise n’a fait que se prévaloir d'un réglement du Gouvernement Ture, qui 
autorise les navires marchands A attendre dans la Baie des Barbiers, entre le pre- 
mier et le second chiteau des Dardanelles, 'expédition des firmans de passage 
qui leur permettent de traverser le canal, 

Ict le Soussigné se félicite de rendre 4 M. le Vicomte Palmerston la justice 
dle dire que c'est ce Ministre qui a été le premier & réfuter Fargument qui vient 
Wétre allégué, En effet, il n'a point hésité & reconnaitre que le réglement Ture, 
ci-dessus mentionné, ne s'applique qu'aux navires marchands et aux batimens 
legers sous pavillon de guerre, qui peuvent obtenir la permission de traverser 
le canal, mais qu'il ne suurait s’étendre aux vaissenux de guerre de haut bord, 
huxquels le passage du détroit reste expressément interdit, 

Cette distinction, que M. le Vicomte Palmerston a ¢tablie spontanément 
dans son entrevue a Broadlands avee le Ministre de Russie, est d'une justesse 
trop évidente pour qu'elle ait besoin de Somat :

refugees to be detained under surveillance in the interior of the Sultan's
