Having secured these important points on behalf of the Porte's honour 
and interest, no less than on that of the refu~ees themselves, and having 
subsequently received the dralts of Aali’s Pasha’s notes with a view to the 
sugeestion of any amendments which might still be found desirable, I 
soueht an interview with General Aupick, and, proposing to him such 
further alterations as had occurred to me, caneetied with him the course of 
proceeding best adapted to the accomplishment of our common purpose. 

In execution of this agreement we sent our respective interpreters to 
Aali Pasha, who after receiving M, Pisani and settling with him the points 
recommended for adoption, communicated the result to M, Cor, the French 
dragoman, who arrived shortly afterwards. The only expressions retained 
by Aali Pasha, notwithstanding our opinion to the contrary, were few and 
of minor importance. Your Lordship, if it be worth while, can appreciate 
the whole a this arrangement by referring to the drafts which are here- 
with inelosed, with the original version entered on the margin opposite the 
amended passages. 

I learnt from M. Pisani with regret, that the drafts thus amended 
were to be shown privately to Count Stirmer and M, de Titoff before 
their final delivery, a step which seems to invite objections, and which is 
not in keeping with the suspension of diplomatic intercourse so invidi- 
ously continued by those Representatives. It. appears from Aali Pasha’s 
explanation that a promise to that effect had been given without my 
knowledge, and consequently that the joint exhortations of General 
Aupick and myself could only avail to obtain an assurance that no essential 
change would be admitted. r 

RL cicther object of our joint remarks, bhowgh the Porte agrees with us 
in opinion, is still left uncertain, and that is the transfer of some Polish 
names, among others, those of General Dembinski and Count Zamoyski, 
from the Russian demand of extradition to the Austrian list of refugees to 
be detained in the interior. The march thus stolen on the Porte is any 
thing but fair to the individuals concerned, and it raises more than one 

uestion which may embarrass this Goyernment in its relations with other 

owers. Count Zamoyski was born at Paris, and on former occasions 
has been protected by the French Embassy here. General Dembinski, 
besides having a French passport under the name of Dubois, is a native 
of Cracow, transferred to Austria by an irregular exercise of power repu- 
diated by Her Majesty's Government. These distinguished men were 
claimed by Russia, when there was a prospect of obtaining their extra- 
dition, that is, their consignment to the executioner; and now they are 
claimed by Austria, that instead of being sent away in liberty, they may 
be subjected to an irksome detention of indefinite duration, in some remote 
and barbarous province of Turkey. 

In bringing these details to your Lordship’s notice, J am influenced 
not. only by sentiments of humanity such as they naturally involve, but 
also by a sense of the deep interest which attaches to this whole question 
by reason of its bearings on the eharacter and external relations of the 
Turkish Government, BES part of it requires to be treated with deli- 
cacy and firmness; nor should I feel that the spirit of your Lordship's 
instructions were properly carried out unless I exerted the influence of 
this Embassy to dissuade the Porte as well from making any unworthy 
concession or holding any unworthy language, as from pursuing an intem- 
perate course or maintaining pretensions not founded on her just rights 
and substantial interests.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston. —(Received December 8.) 


(No, 342.) 
My Lord, Therapia, November 18, 1849. 

AT a late hour last night I received information from M. Pisani that 
Aali Pasha had apprized him of his intention to cancel the notes which he 
had communicated privately to the Austrian and Russian Envoys prepa- 
ratory to their official delivery. ‘The sole reason alleged by his Excellency 
for this unexpected change oF proceeding, was the information obtained 
from those Ministers, that even if Aali Pasha were to admit the Russian 
amendments, M. de Titoff would not be at liberty to renew his diplomatic 
intercourse with the Porte until he had obtained the express permission of 
his Government. | 

Persuaded that so marked a proof of uncertainty and weakness could 
only discredit the Turkish Government, and put to hazard the best results 
of our frrendty interference, I lost ne time in going down to Constanti- 
nople and declaring my sentiments in person to the Ottoman Secretary of 
State. ‘The performance of this duty was the more incumbent upon me, 
because there had been previous indications of an unsteady and compro- 
mising line of conduct on his Excellency’s part, which, from whatever 
cause it proceeded, could not be left unchecked without placing both the 
Porte and Her Majesty's Government in a false position towards each 
other, and endangering the success of their common exertions at the 
presentim portant juncture, 

[any happy to state that my friendly though unreserved expostula- 
tions with Aali Pasha produced their desired effect ; and before the close 


of our interview I had the satisfaction of receiving his positive assurance 


198 


he notes prepared for Count Stirmer and M. de Titoff would b 
ieeiclly delivered eR them as amended by the joint advice of the British 
and French Representatives. | had the further satisfaction of finding, in 
so far as Janguage could express it, a complete agreement of his opinions 
with mine in all that respects the nature of the present negotiations, its 
bearing on the prospects of the Turkish Empire, and the disastrous con- 
sequences which would result from disappointing the generous and 
reasonable expectations of SoRie ad See 

lave, Sc.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palnerston.—(Recewed December 11.) 


(No. 51.) | | 
My Lord, St, Petersburgh, November 29, 1849. 

LETTERS from Constantinople of the 16th instant have arrived 
here, and Fuad Effendi has communicated to me copies of some of the 
papers which have been sent to him by his Government on the subject of 
the differences which have arisen between Russia and Turkey. 

I have taken copies of them and have the honour to transmit them 
herewith :— ; | 

ist. Letter addressed by M. Titoff to Aali Pasha on the Sth ol 
November.* 


® Seo Inclowure 2 in No. 14). 


199 


2nd. Draft of a note which the Porte proposes to address to the 
Russian Mission, and which has been submitted to the consideration of 
M. Titoff. 

4rd. Some additions*® which M. Titoff desires to have inserted in the 
Turkish note. 

Kuad Effendi is still confined to his room, and Count Nesselrode 
having been likewise indisposd for some days past, they have not met 
since the receipt of the last Turkish mail, and [am therefore unable to 
inform your Lordship whether the Russian Government will insist on the 
additions to the note as proposed by M. Titoff, or will consent to a 
modification of them. 

I had an interview with Count Nesselrode this afternoon, and asked 
his Excellency whether the negotiations at Constantinople upon the 
subject of the refugees would soon be closed. He replied that some addi- 
tions to the draft of the Turkish note had been suggested by M. Titoff, 
but that he had not yet had time to consider their full weight anid import- 
ance: that as soon as he was well enough to go out, he should call on the 
Turkish Ambassador for the purpose of concerting with him as to the 
answers to be sent to Constantinople, and in the meantime he could 
assure me that he was most desirous to avoid throwing any difficulties in 
the way of bringing this affair to a speedy termination, 

From Count Nesselrode | went to see Fuad Effendi. His Excellency 
told me that M. Seniavine of the Russian Foreign Office, had paid him a 
long visit last evening, and that he had evidently heen sent to find out 
whether he thought his Government would be disposed to consent to the 
Mens ane note to be delivered by the Porte, which had been suggested 

1. Titoff. 

Z Fuad Effendi said further, that M. Seniavine had made no new sug- 
gestions, and that although they discussed the matter for a long time, 
their conversation ended without arriving at-any result. 

In a few days I shall probably learn from Fuad Effendi the nature of 
the instructions which are sent to M, Titoff, and in the meantime I shall 
endeavour to impress upon the Turkish Ambassador the advantage of 
taking his stand on the terms proposed ‘in ‘the draft of note submitted by 
Aali Pasha to the Russian Minister, and conceding as little as possible, 
because the abject of Russia in these additions appears to me to be 
dictated by a desire to increase the responsibility of the Porte as to the 
refugees, and to lessen her freedom and independence of action. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

one made by the Ambassador to your Lordship for the information of Her 
Majesty's Government, and for no other end; that it came to me in the 
ordinary course of communications sent from the Foreign Office to this 
Embassy, for my information, without any direction accompanying it that 
it should serve any other purpose; that when it was written, and also 
when it wag sent from London it could not be known at Constantinople 
or in London, that the entrance of the squadron had given umbrage here 
in Vienna; and therefore that the statement of our A baneader at Con- 
stantinople and of the Admiral could have no other object than to 
acquaint Her Majesty's Government with the fact itself, not to dis- 
euise its motives. That the fact, namely, the entrance of the fleet within 
the castles being proved to be completely innocent of design, and an effect 
of the pressure of bad weather, and the squadron being shown to have 

so immediately quitted the station when enabled to do so by the return 

of good weather, rer could imagine that there was any design to 

violate the Treaty. I added, that the position occupied by the squadron 

within the old castles at the mouth of the Strait of the Dardanelles, is a 

position always occupied by vessels of all sorts and of all nations, when 

the weather makes the anchorage outside dangerous or inconvenient. 

The Prince was informed by the best authority, namely, by Mr. 
Musurus, the Ottoman Minister, that the position occupied by the British 
squadron is not within the limits of the Dardanelles, as the denomination, 
Dardanelles, is applied by the Sublime Porte to the spot beyond which no 
vessels of war shall pass, and which is used for the designation of that 
spot in the Treaty of 1841; that spot being many miles higher up the 
Strait, that is, where the two castles denominated the inner castles of the 
Dardanelles are situated, and where the firmans are given by the autho- 
rities of the Sublime Porte to vessels passing up the Straits to proceed to 
Constantinople, = 

1 think it proper to give this long detail that there may be no doubt 
respecting the matter. |

add that in the whole of the late affairs with Turkey, he has acted with 
BBESCILY, with prudence, with moderation, and with firmness, speaking 
unblemished truth in the most conciliatory language, and maintaining the 
dignity of his own Government without touching the sensibilities of any 
other,

My Lord, Theramia, November 24, 1849. 


INCLOSED herewith is a statement which pretends to great accu- 
racy, of the number of Russian troops constituting the army 0 occupation 
in Wallachia. | 

I have not obtained it from any responsible agent, nor do I possess 
the means of immediately testing its correctness. It comes from an 
intelligent though not disinterested source, and appears to be considered 
ie of credit by the officers of the French Legation. | 

onr Lordship will observe that the Russian army is still kept up to 
nearly the number allowed under the highest supposition by the Porte's 
agreement with Russia. 

The Porte havin withdrawn so large a proportion of its own army 
as to leave in Wallachia a number unequal to that which was fixed on 
the lower supposition, and there being to all appearance no danger what- 
ever of freah disturbances on the frontier of Transylvania, it might 
fairly be expected that the Court of St. Petersburgh would also dimi- 
nish in a similar roportion the burthen which has so long and painfully 
weighed on the in abitants of the two Principalities. aie 

If any re resentations conveyed under your Lordship’s authority to 
the Russian overnment were to have the effect of hastening that measure 
of justice and eM | am convinced that so important an addition to the 
services rendered by Great Britain to this empire would be gratefully 
acknowledged by the Sultan and his Ministers. 

_ Lhave, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston,— (Received December 14.) 


(No. 354.) | 
My Lord, Therapia, November 24, 1849. 

i AM indebted to the courtesy of my French colleague for the 
accompanying report drawn Up by an agent sent towards the close of 
October to Widdin by the French Consul at Bucharest, with the view of 
inquiring into the truth of certain alleged occurrences which had shed 
considerable discredit on the Turkish authorities. 1 cannot answer for 
the impartiality of M. Hory’s inquiries or the correctness of his impres- 
sions; but his statement ‘s by no means destitute of interest; and those 
details, which more immediately concern the number and destination of the 
geveral classes of refugees, may be considered as varying but little, if at 
all, from the real state of the case. 


+s 


209 


It is by no means satisfactory to add that conversions to Islamism 
continue even here among the Italian, Polish and Hungarian refugees. 

This disreputable practice appears to be encouraged by the prospect 

of obtaining employment in the arkish service, a prospect which natu- 

rally offers strong temptation to exiles shut out from any other resource, 

and reduced in many cases to extreme indigence. 

T have, ae 


(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Inclosure in No. 171. 
Report addressed to the French Consul-General at Bucharest. 


M., l'Agent, Quarantaine de Calafat, 41 Octobre, 1849, 

J'AI déja eu Vhonneur de vous annoncer que jétais arrivé a Calafat le 
24 de ce mois, aprés trois jours de voyage: 

Le lendemain matin, le Directeur de la Quarantaine mit a ma dispo- 
sition une barque et une garde de santé pour me conduire a Widdin. 
Arrivé chez Zia Pacha, Gouverneur de la forteresse, j'ai dd renoncer A la 
faculté de rester en libre pratique, car elle eit non seulement entravé la 
mission délicate qui faisait l'objet de mon voyage, mais elle était incom- 
patible avec les investigations minuticuses auxquelles je devais me livrer. 

Zia Pacha aprés avoir pris connaissance de la dépéche qui lui annon- 
eait le but de ma mission, eut Voblireance de mettre 4 ma disposition tous 
les moyens pour faciliter les recherches tendant 4 constater dans tous les 
détails la yéritable situation des réfugiés, qui avaient cherché un asile sur 
ie territoire Ottoman, Le Commandant Militaire, Colonel Ismail Bey, ne 
mit pas moins d’empressement A satisfaire la demande que je lui fis de 
voir les réfugiés. 

La forteresse de Widdin compte environ 12,000 habitans, moitié Tures 
et moitié Bulewres de la religion Grecque; sa garnison de 4,500 hommes, 
dont 1500 artilleurs. 

Par les investigations auxquelles je me suis livre pendant six jours, 
tant auprés des chefs qu’auprés des soldats émigrés, jfacquis les convic- 
tions survantes, 

“Bien avant la fin de Vinsurrection Hongroise,” m’a dit M. Kossuth, 
“et dans l'appréhension d'une issue défavorable, nous ayons acquis la cer- 
titude que le Gouvernement Ottoman accorderait le droit d'asile & tous 
ceux qui se réfugieraient sur son territoire.” C'est done sur la foi de cette 

romesse sacrée que M. Kossuth et les Généraux Mezzaros, Perezel, et 
beibinaki se sont rendus & Widdin vers le 18 Ao(t, en passant par la 
Valachie. 

Le 22 Aofit 2000 hommes sous les ordres du Général Stein y arrivé- 
rent de Torno-Severin, et environ autant de la Tour Rouge, & travers la 
Valachie, 

Le 25 du méme mois la Légion Polonaise, forte de 1100 hommes, 
et la Légion Italienne de 500, entrérent sur le territoire de Viddin, ayant 
traversé la Servie; total environ 5,600 hommes. 

Tout ce monde, 4 l'exception de quelques chefs qui logérent en ville, 
campa sous des tentes en-lehors de la forteresse, Dilla du camp ‘Ture. 

Les premiers jours de leur arriyée les soldats manquérent en effet 
des objets de premitre nécessité, les vivres étaient insullisans, et les Hon-

Sir, Queen,” Besika Bay, November 13, 1849, 


1 DO myself the honour of informing your Excellency with reference 
to my letter of the 9th instant, that the strong gales which had prevailed 
for many days at the anchorage we occupied within the outer castles of 
the Dardanelles became ‘sufficiently moderate for the departure of the 
squadron from thence this morning, when Her Majesty’s ships resumed 
their position in Besika Bay, where I propose to continue, weather per- 
mitting, until I am apprized by your Excellency that our presence in this 
vicinity is no longer desirable. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) W. PARKER.

intention to remain at this anchorage with the squadron, weather per- 
mitting, until | receive decisive information from ous Excellency of the

to a more secure anchorage, pending a fresh reference to the Courts of

No. 174. 
Viscount Ponsonby to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received December 14.) 


(No. 278.) 
My Lord, Vienna, December 9, 1849. 


I VERY fully stated to Prince Schwarzenberg your Lordship’s views 
and opinions, as_ they are stated and enforced im your instructions No. 
307% to Sir Stratford Canning, and in other communications with which 
you have honoured me, respecting the question of the treatment of the 

ungarian refugees in Turkey. 

Srinee Schwarzenberg refused most peremptorily to consent to the 
removal of those persons from Turkey at present, alleging that the 
‘nterest of Austria required their detention. 

He said that the Imperial Government would hold the Ministers of 
the Sublime Porte to the terms they had themselves made: to wit, that 
the cessation of the confinement and surveillance of the refugees should 
not be terminated, except with the consent of Austria. 

That he had propor to limit to two months the term within 
which the Austrians § ould be at liberty to give the names of the addi- 
tional persons, to be subjected to restraint in Turkey. 

He said that the relations between the Austrian Legation, and the 
Ministers of the Sublime Porte, should not be renewed until the Ottoman 
Ministers had performed their en agement. In reply to some observation 
of mine, he said “ that state of things will be detrimental to Austria, but 
it will be much more so to Turkey.” 

I think it useless to trouble your Lordship with details of what was 
gaid in the conversation between his Highness and myself; the subject in 
all its bearings is familiar to your Lordship. The result of our con- 
versation is a refusal to. admit the force of your Lordship's arguments, or 
to act in conformity with your recommendation. 

I have, &c, 
(Signed) PONSONBY.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received December 17.) 
No. 59.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 5, 1849. 


1 HAVE just seen Fuad Effendi, who informs me that Count Nessel- 
rode called on fia yesterday afternoon for the purpose of communicating 
with him respecting the instructions which he was about to address to 
M, Titow, and which he assured me were sent last night to Constan- 
tinople, 

Mruad Effendi told me that the Count began by finding great fault 
with the manner in which the Turkish Government had eommunicated all 
the documents sent from St. Petersburgh to Sir Stratford Canning and to 
General Aupick, stating that this was a breach of confidence on their 


art. 
i To this Fuad Effendi appears to have replied that England and 
France had a right to be made fully ac vainted with everything con- 
nected with this question in consequence of the generous manner in which 
they had come forward to the assistance of Turkey at a moment of such 
serjous difficulty, After these words Count Nesselrode read to the Turkish 
‘Ambassador a few notes containing what he described to be the substance 
of the instructions to be forwarded to M. Titoff, but would not leave any 
copy with his Excellency; but from the assurances which have been given 
to me by Fuad Effendi, and which have been fully confirmed by General 
de Lamoriciére, who has just called upon me after an interview with 
Count Nesselrode, | have the satisfaction to inform your Lordship that 
the Russian Government have consented to separate the question of the 
expulsion of the refugees from that concerning the negotiation with 
foreign Powers as to the protection to be given to those subjects of the 
Emperor of Russia who have been naturalised in other countries, 

Fuad Effendi told me further, that the Porte had _in fact carried her 

oint, and that the draft of the official note to the Russian Mission at 

Benatnatiaonla which had been submitted to M. ‘litoff, and a copy of 
which was sent in my despatch No, 51, was accep ted withsome very slight 
alterations: and that he had no doubt whatever but that the differences 
would be arranged after M. Titoff received the communication which was 
sent to him last night. 

| beg your Lordship’s indulgence for the manner in which I have 
written this despatch, but I have been obliged to do so in great haste in 
order not to lose the safe opportunity offered to-day by the departure of 
Sir Edward Baynes. 

I have, &

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston —(Received December 20.) 
(No. 362.) 
My Lord, Therapia, November 28, 1849. 


ON the 26th instant I received the following information’ from Aali 
Pasha through M, Pisani. 

The Ottoman Secretary of State haying declined the exchange of a 
signed list of the detained Hungarian refugees, as proposed by the Inter- 
nuncio, the latter requested that at least the Porte’s official note should 
be made to contain the list. This proposal was also declined, on the 
ground of its being necessary for the Porte to rectify the list in concert 
with the Internuncio, some persons comprised in it being claimed by 
France as protected subjects of that Power, and others of them being 
liable to be claimed by some other Power. With the consent of the 
French Minister, Aali Pasha communicated subsequently to Count 
Stiirmer an official note presented to him by General Aupick, and claimin 
General Dembinski and Count Zamoyski as persons entitled to French 
protection, 

Count Stirmer called on Aali Pasha this morning and assured him 
in friendly terms that he was satisfied with the above-mentioned explana- 
tions, acd had written in consequence to his Court.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston—(Received December 20.) 
(No. 370.) 


My Lord, Therama, December 4, 1849. 

THE accompanying copy of a despatch addressed to me by Her 
Majesty's Consul at Varna will serve to put your Lordship in possession 
of my latest intelligence respecting the refugees transferred from Widdin 
to Schumla, 

In answer to my inquiries respecting the Austrian and Russian agents 
stated to have arrived at the latter place, the Grand Vizier has sent me 
word that he knows nothing of any Russian agent there, and that the 
Austrian Consul from Rustehuk, who was lately at Widdin, had gone on 
to Schumla for the purpose of persuading others of the Hungarian refugees 
te return into the Austrian dominions, It appears that the Porte is not 
disposed to prevent the return of those who are willing of their own 
accord and at their own risk to accept the Consul’s proposal. 

In the meantime it appears that others of the reli ces, besides Colonel 

Neale’s informant, have contrived to get away from Schurila: and of those 
who have reached Constantinople, several, in addition to some of the 
Italians previously there, have embraced Islamism, and made themselves 
candidates, not always without success, for employment in the Turkish 
service. 
__ The case which has excited most attention is that of a Count 
Rivadrowsky, an officer in the Austrian service, who arrived with a regu- 
lar passport and was received with courtesy by the Internuncio. This 
gentleman subsequently declared his intention of turning Turk; and not- 
withstanding Count Sttirmer’s dissuasions to the contrary, obtained the 
assistance of an Austrian interpreter, and carried his intention with due 
regularity into effect. His wife, a Venetian, I am told, by birth, and a 
lady of good connections, has since followed his example, 

I am informed that the number of Hungarian and Polish officers who 
have here professed their faith in Mahomet amounts to about twenty ; that 
they are all below the rank of colonel, and have obtained corresponding 
positions in the Turkish army, 1 learn from Mr. Wood's correspondence, 
that a Colonel Kollman, who escaped with an English passport given to 
him at Belgrade, has obtained military service in the Turkish army at 
Damascus under the name of Mehemet Faiz Bey. : 

Of the converted Italians two have been sent to the Dardanelles, 
one to the castles of the Black Sea, and two are retained at Tophana, 

It is not a little remarkable that the Sultan, having received a petition 
from Count Rivadrowsky, directed Aali Pasha to see him and to use his 
best endeavours to dissuade him from abandoning the creed in which he 
had been born, The convert’s new lights and edi ying perseverance have 


however procured him an appointment in the Ordnance. 

The scandal of these reli ious prostitutions Can hardly be viewed in pS 
ways by any one—be he Christian or Mahometan—of tolerable education 
and common hahits of reflection. To me I confess they are completely 
disgusting; and I must be allowed to doubt whether any decree of 


224 


advantage in point of military knowledge, equal to the discredit and other 
eventual drawbacks, can be reasonably expected to result therefrom to the 
Sultan’s service. 

I have, & 


Lb 
(Signed) STRATFORD, CANNING. 


Inclosure in No. 185. 
Lieutenant-Colonel Neale to Sir Stratford Canning. 


Sir, Varna, Noveniber 27, 1849. 

I HAVE the honour to inform your Excellency that M.Goroyé, an ex- 
Hungarian Deputy, arrived yesterday in Varna from Widdin by way of 
Schumla; and this gentleman having called upon me, I have been enabled 
through him to obtain positive information respecting the refugees in 
Schumla, and which | hasten to communicate to your Excellency, as cor- 
recting the imperfect intelligence I had previously received. The refugees 
now in Schumla are Generals Bem, Percezel, Dembinski, and Messaros. 
Kossuth and Count Casimir Batthyany were also arrived there. 

About 1000 Poles, under General Vishotzki and Colonel Zamoyski, 
were also in Schumla, with 300 Hungarians, civil and military; the latter 
chiefly officers of the subordinate ranks. 

The Poles, as M. Gorové informs me, arrived in Schumla about. the 
16th instant, and Kossuth with the H ungarians on the 22nd. 

General Bem and Perezel were living in the barracks; the. other 
refugee chiefs were residing in the houses of the inhabitants; but they 
were all guarded by Turkish soldiers. M. Gorové states that General 
Messaros had received a passport from the French Ambassador at Con- 
stantinople, of which he had endeavoured to avail himself, but the 
Governor of Schumla had refused to acknowledge its validity. A ver 
strict surveillance it would appear was exercised by the Turkish authori- 
ties in Schumla with respect to the refugees generally ; and the departure 
from Schumla, for Constantinople or elsewhere, of even individuals 
amongst them, was rendered extremely difficult. | 

T'vwo Polish officers with French passporta had left Schumla for 
Varna, but as | am informed to-day, they were arrested six hours’ dis- 
tance from hence; and the acting French Vice-Consul of Varna, who is 
also the Austrian Vice-Consul, having claimed the release of these officers, 
they were permitted to come on to Varna, though not without much 
opposition on the part of the Pasha. 

The Austrian Viee-Consul of Rustchuk T understand has arrived in 
Schumla, as also a Russian agent. 

M. Gorové states that a great gloom and feeling of disappointment 
wevails in the minds of the refugee chiefs and others, at a rumour which 
ad been conveyed to them at Schumla, to the effect that they would be 

removed to the interior of Asin Minor, and there be placed under restraint; 
and in the opinion of M. Gorové they would not leave Schumla for that 
destination voluntarily, and had remonstrated against the adoption of 
that measure. 

Fearful lest his departure for Constantinople might be prevented by 
the Turkish authorities of Varna, should his arrival here be known to 
them, or lest he might be arrested and detained at Constantinople, M. 

iorové earnestly requested that [ would provide him with a passport; but 
| have not felt myself warranted in complying with hia request in the 
absence of instructions from your Excellency. In the relative situations 
af Varna and Schumla, the former being the nearest port of embarkation 
for Constantinople, it is not improbable that such applications to me may 
be renewed, and | have the honour to solicit your fevealiensy’a instruc- 
tions for my guidance in such an eusergeney, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) KE. ST. JOHN NEALE.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received December 26.) 
(No. 60.) 
My Lord, | St. Petersburgh, December 9, 1849. 


COUNT NESSELRODE gave a memorandum some days ago to 
General de Lantoriciére upon the subject of a certain Pole of the name-of 
Czaykowsky or Czaika, who has been residing for several we at 
Constantinople under the protection of the French Legation. M.-Czay- 
kowsky is one of the individuals whose expulsion from Turkey the Russian 
Government is desirous of obtaining. He is supposed by the Imperial 
Government to be the mainspring of many of the intrigues which are 
practised against Russia in that part of the world; and though frequent 
attempts have been made by M. Titow to effect his removal from 
Constantinople, they have hitherto proved fruitless, in consequence of the 
foreign protection under which he has resided in the Turkish dominions. 
ek informed that Count Nesselrode is endeavouring to prove to the 
French Government that M. Czaykowsky has never obtained letters of 
naturalization from France, and therefore has no right to seek refuge at 
the Legation; that the protection given to him by General Aupick is 
unjustifiable, and that it ought to be withdrawn.

No, 192. 


Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—( Received December 26.) 
(No. 64. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 13, 1849. 

SINCE writing my despatch No. 59 of the 5th instant, [ have had 
some further conversation with Fuad Effendi respecting his last interview 
with Count Nesselrode, He said that the Chancellor did not conceal from 
him the disappointment which was felt by the Russian Government at the 
late proceed nes at Constantinople, and that he made strong allusions to 
the necessity of abiding by the stipulations of Treaties, mentioning: espe- 
cially those which were agreed upon by Russia and the Porte at Kainardji. 
Fuad Effendi assured me that he replied to Count Nesselrode that the 
Porte would always endeavour to abide by her treaty engagements, and 
that of course those contracted at Kainardit must be adhered to; but his 
Excellency observed to the Chancellor that if terms such as those con- 
tained in the Treaty of Kainardji were proposed to the Turkish Ministers 
of the present day, they would not be entertained for a moment; that the 
men at the head of affairs in Turkey were of too enlightened a stamp to 
accept such propositions; and that in addition to the natural opposition 
which would be raised to any proposals of this kind, the stipulations of 
the Treaty of Kainardji were in reality a contradiction to the spirit of the 
capitulations of the Porte with foreign Powers; and that as far as he him- 
self was concerned he would never consent to put his name to a treaty 
which he must consider humiliating to the Turkish people. 

Count Nesselrode appears to have made some remarks also on the 
question connected with the advance of the squadron under the command 
of Sir W. Parker to the outer castles of the Dardanelles, and te have 
stated that the Treaty of July 13, 1841, had been violated, and that the. 
Turkish authorities were in fault for not having given the necessary orders. 
to prevent the advance of our ships of war. His Excellency appears to 
have added likewise, that it was a precedent which might be turned to 
advantage by Russia, if she were ever disposed to do so, because she had 
as good a right to bring her ships from the Black Sea to the Bosphorus, 
and to advance as far as the castles near Buyukdéré, where the usual 

2G2 


228 


frmans are delivered, as ships of war of other countries had to advance 
from the Mediterranean to the outer castles of the Dardanelles; and there- 
fore the Ottoman Government must not be surprised if communications 
are made on the subject, and the proceedings of the British squadron 
commented upon. . 
Fuad Effendi said that Count Nesselrode appeared seriously dissatis- 
fied with the late proceedings of his Government, and to be much vexed 
at the ill success that has attended his last negotiations at Constantinople. 
The Turkish Ambassador then observed to me with satisfaction that in 
his opinion a most important effect would be produced on public opinion 
in his country by the sudden apparition of our squadron at the Darda- 
nelles; for that the rapidity with which England had come to the assist- 
ance of ‘Turkey at this critical moment, has proved that, with proper fore- 
sicht, aid will be at hand in the hour of need, and that it can always be 
obtained in ample time to meet the advance of a Russian naval force on 
Constantinople. This fact, he said, will shake the conviction of many of 
his countrymen who haye hitherto looked upon the power of Russia as 
irresistible, and consequently the cause of their independence as almost 
hopeless; but that their cour will now return, and they will be the 
better disposed to support the Government in their efforts to carry out the 
systems of reform, which are already working most successfully. He 
added, that the favour shown by the Porte to the Christian population 
was also domg much good, for they began not only to feel greater security 
than formerly, but were now better off when simply confiding to the laws 
of the ‘Turkish Empire than under the protection of Russia. 

Fuad Effendi said further, that frequent remarks have been made to 
him on this point by the Russians who had visited him since his arrival at 
St. Petersburgh; and that at Constantinople the Russian Leration are 
extremely opposed to the new system adopted by the Porte with respect 
tothe Christians, and, strange to say, are exerting their utmost endeavours 
to thwart them in the development of their plans for the improvement of 
the condition of the Christian population in the Turkish Empire. 


I have, &e. 

(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston,—(Received December 26.) 


(No, 66.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 14, | 840, 

| HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that General Duhamel, 
who has been lately employed as Russian Commissioner at Bucharest, 
arrived at St. Petersburgh a few days ago. He has called on Fuad 
Effendi, who mentioned to me in the course of my last conversation with 
his Excellency, that the General had assured him that a considerable 
reduction in the number of Russian troops in the Principalities had 
already taken place; that his Government regretted that it was impossible 
for them, on account of the lateness of the season, to withdraw a greater 
number: but that all the necessary arrangements were making to reduce 
the force to 10,000 men, which he believed would be effected by the month 
of March, 

General Duhamel is to return shortly to Bucharest to resume his 
duties, Uhearon the other hand, that Fuad Effendi, after he has closed his 
Embassy at St. Petersburgh, which he hopes to do in five or six weeks, is 
to proceed to Constantinople, where I believe he expects some new 
appointment. It is his intention, however, to pass through Bucharest, for 
the purpose of terminating some yet unfinished business. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

Viscount Palmerston to Lord Bloomfield. 
(Private,) | 
(Extract.) Broadlands, November 25, 1849. 

SIR STRATFORD CANNING has sent me a copy of his letter to 
you about the anchoring of our squadron within the outer castles of the 
Dardanelles, to obtain temporary shelter from bad weather, and you will 
have been able to explain the circumstance to Count Nesselrode; but | 
wish you to say to him that I do not Eyal ugree in the interpretation 
given at Constantinople of the port regulations about the Dardanelles,— 
that it was regular and allowable for the § uadron to anchor there, 

The words of the regulation certainly admit of, it, but I think the 
spirit of the regulation, counted with the stipulations. of the ‘Treaty al 
July, 1841. are against it, The regulation says, that all ships of war of 
all nations coming to the Dardanelles are to stop and wait at the 
anchorage between the outer and inner castles till they know from Con- 
stantinople whether a firman will or will not be granted to allow them to 
proceed further on. But this regulation can, I think, in fairness he con- 
atrued only as applicable to those ships of war to which, under the Treaty 
of 1841, the Porte reserved to itself the right to grant in time of peace 


*i 


231 

rmission to pass up the Straits, that is to say, to light vessels destined 
or the use of the Embassies and Missions at Constantinople; but I do 
not think that this regulation can properly be understood as applying to 
heavy ships of war, which are by the Treaty of 1841 precluded from 
entering the Straits; and therefore I think that our squadron ought to 
have sourht shelter elsewhere, and not to have anchored within the 
Straits. [ have explained this to Sir Stratford Canning, and the same 
thing will not happen again after he gets my letter. But you may assure 
Count Nesselrode that there was no design on the part of our Ambassador 
or Admiral to infringe the Treaty, and that what has been done was the 
consequence of stress of weather, and of a too literal interpretation of the 
port regulations affecting the Dardanelles.

Viscount Palmerston to Viscount Ponsonby. 
(No. 1.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 1, 1850. 


| HEREWITEL transmit to your Excellency for your information, 
copies of a note* which has been addressed to me by the Austrian Chargé 
d'Affaires at this Court, and of an instruction from Prince Schwarzen- 
berg to Baron Koller, which Baron Koller has communicated to me; both of 
these communications being on the subject of the entrance of the British 
squadron into the anchorage between the outer and,inner castles of the 
Dardanelles; and I have to instruct your Excellency to say to the 
Austrian Government in reply, that the circumstance that Sir William 
Parker's squadron resorted for a few days for shelter to Barbers’ Bay, 
during stormy weather, which rendered its previous anchorage in Besika 
Bay insecure, does not appear to Her Majesty's Government to carry with 
it that degree of importance which the Austrian Government seems to 
have attached to it. 

But if Her Majesty’s Government were to consider it necessary to 
argue the matter upon the grounds on which the Austrian Government 
has placed it, they might have much to say in answer to what is 
contained in Baron Kkoller's note and in Prince Schwarzenberg's 
despatch. For by the Treaty of July 1841, the Five Powers bound 
themselves to respect and conform themselves to the regulations of the 
Turkish Government in regard to the Straits of the Dardanelles and 
Bosphorus; and it appears that by the port regulations established by 
the Turkish Government in 1845 for the Dardanelles, ships of war of 
all nations are allowed to anchor in the broad bay between the outer, 
and the inner castles; and that the Straita of the Dardanelles, properly, 
so called, are considered by the Turkish Government as beginning only 
at the town-of the Dardanelles where the narrow passage commences ; 
and it might thence be contended that this anchoring of the British 
squadron in Barbers’ Bay, a place which, according to the standing, 
regulations of the port, is open at all times to ships of war of all nations, 
was no infringement of the Treaty of July 1841. 

It might further be contended, and with much show of reason, that 
even if the anchoring of the.British squadron in Barbers’ Bay were an 
infringement of the Treaty of 184], yet as that ‘Treaty not only forbids the 
entrance of foreign ships of war into the Dardanelles while the Porte is at 
peace, but also records the declared determination of the Five Powers to 
reapect and to uphold the independence of the Porte, the appearance of the 
British squadron.in Barbers’ Bay, even if it was an infringement, was at 
all events not the first infringement of that Treaty. But it might well be 
argued that this appearance of the British squadron was in fact, under the 
peculiar circumstances of the moment, not altogether irreconcileable with 
the spirit and:true meaning of that Treaty; lor the independence of the 
Sultan having been placed in jeopardy by demands' which were made on 
him in a threatening manner, and which were not warranted by the 
stipulations of treaties, the presence of Her Majesty's squadron within

My Lord, Foreign Office, January 1, 1850. 

YOUR Lordship will perceive in Prince Schwarzenberg’s despatch 
to M. Koller, of the 27th of November, of which a copy is inclosed in my 
despatch No. 4 of this day, that considerable stress is laid upon the 
memorandum communicated by the Porte to the foreign Missions at Con- 
stantinople in the month of February, 1845, which professes to lay down 
the rule for the admission of foreign vessels, whether vessels of war or 
merchantmen, into the Straits of the Dardanelles and Bosphorus; and 
which the Austrian Minister contends, notwithstanding that they were 
subsequently modified as regards mercharit-vessels, are still in force as 
regards ships of war in their original extent. 

I think it therefore right to furnish your Lordship with copies of the 
inclosed despatches from Sir Stratford Canning to this office, written 
about the time when the regulations were promulgated. Your Lordship 
will perceive from the first of these papers, No. 67, of the 20th of March, ° 
1845, that on the regulations being communicated to the British’ Embassy, 
Sir Stratford Canning at once applied for and obtained a modification of 
them in regard to the Dardanelles; and the precise nature of that modi- 
fication is more fully explained in his Excellency’s despatch to Her 
Majesty’s Consul at the Dardanelles, of the 22nd of March, 1845, of which 
an extract is herewith transmitted to you; and which states that any 
British vessel, whether it be a merchant vessel or vessel of war, is allowed 
to come within the outer castles of the Dardanelles at once, as far as the 
anchorage of the Kefez Bournou, or Point Barbieri, by night as well as 


by day. 

, But not satisfied with having obtained this modification of the 
original regulations as regarded the Dardanelles, Sir Stratford Canning, 
as you will see from his deapatches, No, 206, of the 3rd of September, No 
217, of the 16th of September, and No, 237, of the 16th of October, all of 
the year 1845, induced the Porte to consent toa similar modification in 
regard to vessels arriving in the Bosphorus from the Black Sea. The 
assent of the Porte was contained in a note of the 13th of October, 1845, 
of which a copy is inclosed-in Sir Stratford Canning’s despateh No. 237 ; 
and it appears from the same despatch that the dragoman of the British 
Embassy having about the same time made some inquiry as to the pas- 
sage of the Dardanelles, Ali Effendi assured him that the concession 
previously made in that respect continued in force, 

The last papers which I have to transmit to your Lordship on this 
matter are copies of two lettera from Her Majesty's Consul at the Dar- 
danelles to Vice-Admiral Sir William Parker, dated the 26th and 30th of 
October last, in the first of which your Lordship will find in inverted 
‘commas the regulation now in force Feeding the entrance of ships of

Dane eg Kowaver to state to your Lordship that although I have

Sir Stratford Canning to the Earl of Aberdeen. 


My Lord, Constantinople, September 3, 1845, 


WITH my despatch No. 67 of this year, I transmitted to your 
Lordship a memorandum from the Porte, notifying certain regulations 
respecting the passage of the Bosphorus and Dardanelles by vessels, 
whether native or foreign, arriving at the entrance of either strait after 
sunset. The concession which | succeeded in obtainin from the Porte, 
as stated in that despatch, was found to be sufficient only with respect to 
the Dardanelles. The erie assigned to vessels arriving in the 
Bosphorus after-dark from the Black Sea, has been sincé ascertained, on 
the testimony of experienced seamen, to be unsafe, and it was therefore 
necessary to request that they might be allowed to anchor at some conve- 
nient place more completely within the batteries. 

The accompanying copy of a memorandum which | addressed to the 
Turkish Minister for oreign Affairs, will explain more com letely to 
your Lordship the grounds of my demand, which was supported by similar 
representations from other foreign Missions, whose national vessels hac 
been fired at by the Turkish batteries; and I have now the satisfaction to 
state that after the usual proportion of delay and difficulty, the point has 
been conceded, as your Coniitip will perceive by the reports inclosed 
herewith from M. Frederick Pisani.

Inclosure 9 in No. 198. 
Memorandum. 


Pera of Constantinaple, September 11, 1845. 


CONSIDERING the regulations notified by the Sublime Porte with 
reapect to the navigation of the Straits of the Bosphorus and Dardanelles, 
whether by native or foreign vessels, after sunset, and bearing more parti- 
cularly in mind the principles established by treaty with respect to the 
passage of foreign armed vessels through the straits, the Undersigned has 
received with much satisfaction the Ottoman Minister's message in reply 
to his representations of the dangers experienced by vessels when obliged 
to anchor at night in the exposed situation of Bu uk Liman. He under- 
stands that, while in the Straits of the Dardanelles British vessels may 
anchor at any hour within the outer castles as high up as Cape Barbieri, 
the former practice is re-established with respect to merchant-vessels 
entering those of the Bosphorus from the Black Sea after dark; and con- 
sequently that such vessels, instead of being obliged to cast anchor in the 
waters of Buyuk Liman, are now at liberty to seek a safer anchorage 
further within the straits. ‘This isthe substance of what the Undersigned 
has notified to the British authorities, for the information of those con- 
cerned; and he has performed this duty in the conviction that corre- 
sponding orders have been given by the Sublime Porte to the commanders 
of the forts in each strait.

Inclosure 14 in No, 198. 
Consul Calvert to Vice-Admiral Sir W. Parker. 


Sir, Dardanelles, October 30, 1849. 

AFTER seriously considering the substance of the private commu- 
nication made to me yesterday by your Excellency, whilst I was on 
board of the “Queen,” and after maturely weighing the nature of the 
doubts entertained by Her ip fe Ambassador at Constantinople, as 
to the propriety of the squadron under your command entering the 
Straits of the Dardanelles, and fang up a more sheltered anchorage 
than that of Besika Bay, I have the honour to state that I feel now 
convinced that such doubts can only have arisen in consequence of the 
true meaning of the word Détroits, as contained in the original treaty 
signed in French on the 13th July, 1841, having been erroneously 
rendered in the English text by the word Straits, The Sérails of the 
Dardanelles ave always designated in French as Le Canal des Dar- 
danelles, and the real sense of the word “détroit” in the present instance, 
would evidently have been more appropriately rendered by calling it 
the “ narrowest passages,” thus implying that of the inner castles, 

This assertion will be further corroborated by the substance of the 
inclosed copy of a despatch received at this Consulate from Her Majesty's 
Embassy at Constan suena on the 27th March, i845, together with the 
copy of a memorandum from the Sublime Porte which accompanied it. 

“Considering furthermore that the instructions of the Turkish Go- 
vernment to the various officers in command of the forts of the Darda- 
ne les since the signature of the Treaty, have invariably admitted the 
right of all foreign vessels of war to enter within the onter castles of 
the Dardanelles; and also the fact that Russian, Austrian, and American 
vessels of war have at all times availed without hesitation of the facility 


24] 


thus granted indiscriminately to ships of all nations; | am the more -con- 
firmed in the opinion expressed by me to your Excellency as to the 
undoubted propriety that the squadron under your command should anchor 
for shelter within these straits, 


I have, &c. 
(Signed ) F. W. CALVERT. 
No, 199, 
Viscount Palmerston to Lord Bloomfield. 
(No. 6.) 3 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 1, 1850. 


| HAVE received your Lordship's confidential despatch of the 14th 
ultimo, reporting your communications with Count Nesselrode respecting 
the entrance of the British squadron under Vice-Admiral Sir Williats 
Parker within the outer castles of the Dardanelles, and stating the 
reasons which induced you to furnish the Russian Minister with an 
exert of my private letter to vou of the 25th of November on that 
subject. 

i have to state to your Lordship in reply, that I entirely approve 
of your having communicated to Count Nesselrode the extract of my 
ada letter; and | have to instruct your Lordship to say that Her 
Majesty’s Government concur with the Russian Government in thinking 
that, according to the true intent and meaning of the Treaty of July 
1841, the Straits of the Dardanelles and Bosphorus ought to be under- 
stood as being the whole extent of the passages between the Archipelago 
and the Sea of Marmora, and between the Sea of Marmora and the Black 
Sea. This opinion has been communicated to Her Majesty's Ambassador 
at se emOp les and will be acted upon by Her Majesty's ships of war 
in future, 

At the same time your Lordship should assure Count Nesselrode 
that if Her Majesty's squadron took refuge during a few days of, bad 
weather in Barbers’ Bay, neither Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constan- 
tinople, nor Mer Majesty’s Consul at the Dardanelles, conceived that in 
informing Sir William Parker that in case of stress of weather he was 
at liberty to anchor in that bay, they were infringing upon the Treaty of 
1841; and the Russian Government will long since have learned that 
the squadron did not remain in Barbers’ Bay longer than the bad weathe 
which had driven it thither continued, But if any similar bad weather 
shall have come on during the rest of the time that the squdronr 
remained in those parts, it will have sought shelter elsewhere, and will 
not again have passed within the outer castles of the Dardanelles. 


T am, &c, 
(Signed) PALMERSTON.

He declared to me, that after having done this he did not expect so

understand by this expression, he replied that if he wished Turkey to fall 
into a state of complete anarchy and confusion, nothing would be required 
of him but to withdraw his influence from Bulgaria, Servia, Wallachia, 
and Moldavia, and these provinces would soon be Joined by others as 
well as the Christian population in Turkey; and once freed from the 
restraint which he exercised on them, and by which alone their allegiance 
to the Porte was maintained, they would make short work of the Turkish 
Empire, and we should soon see it crumble to pieces. 

From this subject he turned to the anchoring of our squadron in the 
Dardanelles, and related some anecdotes connected with the blockade of 
the Dardanelles, durin 


the last war with Turkey, by the Russian fleet 
under the command of Admiral Ricord, which he said was effectually 


maintained during a whole winter without a serious accident happening 
to any of the ships employed on this service, and therefore he said that he 
could not understand how a British squadron under an Admiral of such 
great experience, and which was doubtless better commanded, better 
manned and equipped, than any fleet he could send to sea, should be 
forced by stress of weather to pass the entrance of the Dardanelles, and 
thereby to violate the Treaty of 1841. 

I took advantage of a moment of silence to say that I had hoped the

WITH reference to my despatch marked ‘ confidential,” of the l4th

which | had with Count Nesselrode on Sunday last, his Excellency told 
me that the communications which [ had sent him containitig the opinions 
of ‘Her Majesty’s Government on the subject of the anchormg inside the 
Dardanelles of the squadron under Sir William Parker, had done away 
with the necessity in which the Imperial Government would otherwise have 
been placed, of addressing to Her Majesty’s Government a formal protest 
on the matter such as had been sent from Vienna, and which they could 
not have avoided doing, if | had not placed them in possession of some 
written document; and he added that.as soon as he was sufficiently reco- 
vered from the attack of illness, under» which he had been suffering for 
some days past, to leave the house, he should submit to the Emperor the 
draft of a despatch to Baron Brunnow, the object of which would be to 
terminate this affair, 

I now hasten to report that [ have this instant had an interview with 
the Chancellor, at which his Excellency stated that since we last “met, he 
had seen His Imperial Majesty, and that he proposed sending a messenger 
to London to-morrow, who would be the bearer of a communication to 
Baron Brunnow, which he had‘no doubt° would be satisfactory to your 
Lordship, and which he trusted would put an end to all further diseussion 
between the two Governments of the affair of the Dardanelles.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Recetved January 3, 1850.) 
(No. 77.) 


My Lord, St, Petersburgh, December 19, 1849. 

! HAVE just seen Count Nesselrode, who mentioned to me that he 
had no doubt but that the relations between the Russian Legation at 
Constantinople and the Porte were re-established by this time, and that 
he hoped to have his expectations confirmed by the first Turkish post, 
which would be due at ‘the end of the week. 

- In reply to an inquiry which | made as to the instructions which had 
been sent to M, Titow, which enabled his Excellency to look forward with 
so much certainty to this desirable result, he replied that he had directed 
that Minister to accept the assurances which were given by the Porte of 
their readiness to expel from Turkey the refugees now there, and not to 
press the question affecting those who might hereafter seek an asylum in 
the Ottoman dominions, saying that was a matter which could be settled 
by negotiation at some future time.

THE paper inclosed herewith has been communicated to me in 
confidence is a private. hand, as. illustrating the kind of interference 
which Russia is allowed to exercise in all that relates to the administra 

tion of the Danubian Principalities. It appears either to have originated 
with the Russian Legation, or to have passed through that channel to the 
Porte, That those who exercise the influence of Russia here should take 
an interest in obtaining for the Hospodars, whether regularly or irregu- 
larly, the means of defraying the expenses of their late visit to Constan- 
tinople is natural enough, for there ts strong reason to believe that no 
inconsiderable part of those expenses may be fairly set down to the 
account of their own avidity. 

I have, &e. |

No, 207, 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received January 4, 1850.) 


(No. 380.) 
My Lord, Therapia, December 18, 1849. 

THE Porte has not yet succeeded in terminating ils vexatious 
differences with Austria and Russia, and the suspension of diplomatic 
relations between the Representatives of those Powers and the Turkish 
Government continues to this hour. No inconsiderable progress his 
however been made towards a final accommodation, and there 1g reason 
to hope that the obstacles to a complete adjustment may soon be so far 
removed as to leave but little danger of any move serious complication, 
It is no unfavourable symptom that each of the Porte’s antagonists 
while urging his own pretension, inclines to take credit for recommending 
moderation to the other, 

On the side of Russia there is really no further ground of dispute 
Fuad Effendi has informed his Government that its modifications of the 
Russian demands in their second stage are accepted; and a communien- 
tion made to Aali Pasha by M. de ‘litoll!’ two days ago confirms that 
intelligence. Your Lordship will perceive, on reference to the accom- 
panying memorandum, which forms the communication in question, thit 
the terms in which the Russian acceptanee is expressed, are even more 
favourable to the Porte’s view than those employed in the ‘Turkish 
official note. ! ; 

lt is however to be observed at the same time, and to he regretted 
that the additional coucessions thus announced by Russia should be 
vlogged, if not by absolute conditions, by demands embarrassine Lo the 
Porte, and attaching an appearance of constraint to the act of Teconei- 
liation, M. de 'Titoff has explained the last paragraph but one of his 


254 


memorandum, by requiring that a formal protocol, comprising the points 
of agreement, should be drawn up between him and the Turkish Ministers, 
and that the instrament thus prepared should be signec by the Grand 
Vizier himself, It is also pretended that the Porte shall proceed to the 
execution of the measures adopted by mutual consent, before the 
suspension of its diplomatic relations with Russia shall be removed. ree 
At an interview which took place yesterday, on the proposition of 
M. de Titoff, at the Grand Vizier’s house, the Russian Envoy told that 
Minister and Aali Pasha, who was also present, that an rSraiatag Ae by 
protocol would be particularly acceptable to the Emperor } icholas, and 
that Count Nesselrode was extremely desirous on that account to obtain 
its adoption by'the Porte. The language and manner of the Russian 
Representative appear to have been free from that dictatorial character 
which they had formerly exhibited, and I should infer from the terms 
of his memorandum that he is not prepared to insist peremptorily on the 
signature of a protocol. The Turkish Ministers, on their side, would be 
lai to éscape from so inconvenient and superfluous a demand. Aali 
Bash: indeed, observed to the Russian interpreter with much, propriety, 
when it was first proposed, that Count Nesselrode himself would probably 
abandon his idea, when he received the original of the Turkish note 
which had reached his hands only in draft, when he suggested the 
aloption of a protocol. But they shrink, nevertheless, from the conse- 
quences of creating another disappointment at St, Petersburgh, and 
apply for my opinion, rather for the sake of consistency, and to satisfy 
the Sultan's mind, than to obtain support for the purpose of eae a 
misplaced pretension, Your Lordship is aware that under any difficulty 
“of the kind, no Turkish Minister, however‘ superior he may be in talent 
and character, is entirely exempt from. that infirmity which ever sets 
‘expediency above principle, and looks rather to personal considerations 
‘than to political results. This general tendency among the individuals 
who compose the Ottoman Cabinet is a constant source of embarrassment 
to mein advising them, and occasionally a great disparagement to my 
position as acting under instructions which are directed with no less 


solicitude to the preservation of peace than to the maintenance of the . 


Porte's essential interests and honourable independence. It is not 
unfrequently incumbent upon me to urge resistance to unreasonable 
demands, and to forego the eredit of suggesting conciliatory expedients, 
because my counsels are generall y more needed to discourage a dangerous 
subserviency than to restrain a miscalculating: rashness, 

In answering the present appeal to my opinion, | have endeavoured tt 
provide for the twofold object of accommodation and consistency, Greatly 
as | wish to contribute, as Her Majesty's Representative, to the speed 
removal of all that retards an adjustment of the still unsettled differences, 
I cannot shut my eyes against the objectionable tendencies and probable 
intention of the act by which the Court of St. Petersburgh has unex pect- 
edly proposed to complete it. 1 am persuaded that the Porte will increase 
its entanglements with Russia and lose a portion of its present advantages, 
by acceding to the Russian proposal. Lam algo convinced that Russia 
would not be warranted in making a condition of that proposal, because 
the formality of a protocol is not required for any useful or customary 
purpose, and heeause the Porte has already granted more than Russia 
hada right todemand. It is no doubt desirable on the other hand to 


close the breach in as speedy and good humoured a manner as the real, 
interests at stake will allow. Consequently, while advising the Porte to . 


endeavour, by urging every reasonable argument to avoid the signature of 
any kindof protocol, | have suggested a form of transaction which, leaving 
to Russia the name, would neutralize any improper effect of an instrument 
ealeulated, like the Sened of last May, to have the air and force of ah 
convention, 
In explanation of this idea | beg to refer your Lordship to the accom- 
panving copy of an instruction which T have just now addressed to M, 
isani, after consulting fully with the French Minister, and ascertaining 
that he was prepared to take a similar course in com municating with the 
Turkish Ministers. 


205 


With respect to the Austrian part of these affairs, it was only at a late 
hour to-night that I received a hurried ren rt of what had passed at an 
interview held this morning at the Grand Vizier's house between his High- 
ness, assisted by Aali Pasha, and the Internuncio, Inclosed herewith is a 
memorandum of the several points on which Count Stiirmer continues to 
insist. ‘They are open, as your Lordship will perceive with sorrow, to 
stave, and in one regpect at least to insuperable objections, I allude more 
particularly to the second demand, which requires that the eventual libe- 
ration of the refugees to be detained in the interior should be preceded 
by an agreement previously concerted between the twa Courts. The other 
objectionable points appear to be more susceptible of adjustment. But if 
Count Stiirmer's instructions admit no latitude with respect to the point 
of mutual consent, I can only foresee an unworthy compliance on the part 
of the Ottoman Government, or a fresh and vexatious postponement of the 
renewal of diplomatic relations between the Austrian epresentative and 
the Porte. Tam assured by Aali Pasha that no reply has been given to 
Count Stiirmer except that his terms of arrangement will be submitted to 
the Council. But I have reason to suppose that on this subject as well 
as that of the Russian protocol, the Turkish Ministers are not much dis. 
posed to stand out, although they reserve their final decision until they 
are made acquainted with my opinion and the opinion of my French 
collearue, which perfectly agrees with mine. 

In the course of to-morrow they will probably be put in possession of 
both opinions, and your Lordship need not be assured that while the 
sanction of.my approval will be given to no arrangement prejudicial to 
the honourand independence of the Porte, our joint exertions will be used 
to assist the Grand Vizier in trying to effect an immediate and satisfactory 
solution of the whole digpute. 

T have, &. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

AUSSITOT que jai regu ce matin la dépéche que votre Excellence 
m’a fait l'honneur de m'éerire en date du 21 Novenitie, jé Me suis rendu 
chez M, le Prince de Schwarzenberg pour conférer avec lui sur son con- 
tenu. Il m’a exprimé ses regrets de ce que la Sublime Porte, en méme 
tems que, dans ses communications yerbales, elle déclarait tenir a la 
décision arrétée & Vienne entre sa Légation et le Cabinet Impérial, et 
reconnaitre que la constatation du rétablissement de la tranquillité en 
Hongrie était du ressort du Gouvernement <Autrichien, elle évitait de 
sexpliquer sur ce point, et d'une maniére précise, dans sa note officielle, I 
a ajouté que plus la Sublime Porte persévérait dans une omission qui, selon 
lui, Glait en opposition avec les assurances contenues dans la lettre de Sa 
Majesté Impériale le Sultan {Sa Majesté l’Empereur d’Autriche, plus la Cour 
de Vienne avait raison de douter des intentions ultérieures du Cabinet Otto- 


man, et plus elle était résolue d'insister sur ce point. Enfin, il m’a dit que 


la question des réfugiés ne serait définitivement terminée que quand yotre 
Excellence se serait servyie dans sa note, soit de l'expression “ commun 
accord,” soit de l'expression “ entente préalable.” Toutes les observations 
que j'ai di lui faire pour le convaincre de Ja suffisance de la rédaction'de 
votre Excellence, n’ont produit aucun effet sur le Prince, qui a terminé la

de Stiirmer des instructions précises et positives. Quoiqu’ilen soit, j'espare

toute prétention du Cabinet de Vienne, qui ne serait pas fondée sur lanéces-

A cette oceasion je dois faire connaitre 4 votre Excellence que Lord

délai fit fixé A cet effet, cette affaire, d'aprés ce que le Prince m'a dit,

No, 210. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received January 4, 1850.) 


(Private and Confidential.) 


My dear Lord, Therapia, December 18, 1849. 

INCLOSED herewith is the copy of a letter marked “private and 
confidential,” which I addressed to Sir William Parker in more complete 
execution of your Lordship's despatch respecting the entrance of Her 
Majesty's squadron within the outer castles of the Dardanelles. I trust 
your Lordship will approve my having used all practicable delicacy in 
making the Vice-Admiral sensible of the objections to that proceeding, in 
consideration of the Treaty as interpreted in its stricter sense. Your 
Lordship is too just not to make every fair allowance for the pressure of 
circumstances; and with respect to the Treaty, whatever responsibility 
may have been incurred, devolyes—I must in fairness admit it—rather upon 
me than upon the Admiral. 

Tam, &e. 


, ee : 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING. 


Inclosure in No. 210. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Vice-Admiral Str W. Parker. 


(Private and Confidential.) . 
My dear Sir, Therapia, December 15, 1849, 
REFERRING to the last paragraph of my ostensible despatch of 
this date, | wish to explain to you that J introduced the final clause of it 
in consequence of a despatch from Lord Palmerston intimating that, to 
avoid cavil with respect to the Treaty, it would have been better if you 
had sought a more sheltered anchorage in the neighbourhood of the Dar- 
danelles, at Enos or at Saros for instance, he says, than give occasion 
for raising ailoubt as to our respect for the precise terms of the Treaty, by 
entering within the outer castles. 
His Lordship had not, when he wrote, received a confidential despatch 
which [I addressed to him in explanation of the circumstances. | am 
however of opinion that without some positive instruction from England, 
modifying the view which has been taken of the squadron's former 
entrance, it will be advisable for you to make no distinction between the 
outer and the inner eastles of the Dardanelles, which latter there never 
was any question of passing by the squadron without a distinct requisition 
from the Porte, transmitted through Her Majesty's Embassy ; or pouitive 
instructions from home. 


263 


In further explanation of this matter 1 send you in this confidential 
form for your own personal information, such passages of Lord Palmerston’s 
instructions as it may be satisfactory for you to see. 

Believe me, &c. | 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received January 10, 1850.) 


(No, 384.) 
My Lord, Therapia, December 24, 1849. 


I KNOW not whether it be owing to the nature of the questions 
themselves, to the overbearing temper of one party, to the vacillating 
character of another, or, what is most probable, to a mixture of these 
causes, but the difficulty, be it how it may, of bringing the Porte’s difler- 
ences with Russia and Austria to a rneeseae settlement appears to be 
nearly interminable. ‘Their approach towards a conclusion might be 
imagined to proceed on the principle of those mathematical lines which, 
though continually approximating, never meet, | 

t is alrendy well nown to your Lordship that the Cabinets of Vienna 
and St. Petersburgh, after relinquishing the demand of extradition, put 
forward propogals hot warranted by treaty, unbecoming and discreditable 
for the Porte to attept, and, if accepted, threatening to produce: much 
future altercation seal burresament The firm but temperate objections 
which the Sultan's’ Ministers, with my concurrence and that of General 
Aupick, opp to such overweening pretensions, were fairly appreciated 
by the Russiiti Government, and repelled for the most part by that of 
Austria, Yet Russian was not satisfied without requiring a new and unne- 
cessary concession, in appearance a formality, but even in that character 
showing a mistrust of the Porte, and lying open to the suspicion of ulterior 
views. 

This state of things is the more perplexing, because it inverts the rule 
of Turkish policy, making Austria an object of estrangement, and Russia, 
for a time at least, the more complying neighbour of the two. 

My advice to the Porte has uniformly been of that tenour which your 
Lordship’s instruction of the 30th ultimo so pointedly inculeates. | have 
never ceased to recommend a faithful execution of treaties, a willing: fulfil- 
ment of the duties of good neighbourhood, and a steady unobtrusive 
maintenance of the Sultan's honour, dignity, and independence, ‘These 

rinciples would justify the Porte, if it were worth while, in declining the 
Rinsian demand of a protocol. They engage the Porte to persist in repel- 
line those Austrian conditions which would interfere with the free exercise 
of her sovereignty. But although the right and the duty are alike acknow. 
ledged by the Sultan's principal Ministers, various motives of a less rigid 
character incline them to give way after a decent show of resistance, and 
would in all likelihood hurry them to an inconsiderate and unworthy con- 
clusion, if they had not also to consult the publie opinion of Europe, and 
to preserve the goodwill of England and France. 

OF these important considerations they seemed, however, a few days 
ago, to have so much lost sight, that I was obliged to enter imto a warm 
expostulation with the Grand Vizier, who finally expressed his readiness 
to abide by my counsels, directed as they were to the permanent welfare 
of this empire, and agreeing as they do in the present instance with those 
of my French colleague. 

The advice which | tendered, in consequence, to Aali Pasha, who does 
not always perceive where firmness ts safer than concession, was any tping 
but abla at or exaggerated, In substance, with respect to Russia, 
recommended that the protocol should be signed with M. de Titoff, if the 
measure could not be avoided without a fresh period of delay, but in that 
simplest possible form, which would give it rather the character of a procés 
verbal than that of a sened or convention; taking care to have it understood 
that the renewal of diplomatic relations should follow at once. With 
respect to Austria, | approved the Porte’s intention, as well to preclude 
any Austrian inspection over the refugees, when detained in Asia Minor, 
as to accept the fatersuacio’s amended proposal of keeping open the list 


for two months, As to the main requisition of making the eventual libe-, 


ration of the refugees dependent on Austria’s consent, | suggested terms 


265 


of agreement which bordered so closely on Prince Schwarzenberg’s 
demand as barely to reserve the Sultan's right. 

To make this more clear, | beg to refer your Lordship to the 
accompanying memorandum, which exhibits the very terms of my sug- 
gestion, and to the copies inclosed herewith, of two instructions 
addressed by me to the first interpreter of Her Majesty's Embassy. 
An extract of M. Pisani’s intermediate report, and a project submitted 
to Aali Pasha by Count Stirmer, are also inclosed for your Lordship’s 
additional information. ; 

The actual state of the whole affair, as resulting from these commu- 
nications, may be thus described. A meeting is to take place to-morrow, 
at the Grand Vizier’s house, between that Minister, Aali Pasha, and M. 
de Titoff. A protocol will no doubt be signed, and probably in the 
form inclosed herewith, which is baserl on my suggestion, and contains 
no addition which I think it worth while to resist; but it is by no means 
impossible that the Russian Mnvoy may thls and carry amendments 
less admissible, and withhold the renewal of his diplomatic relations with 
the Porte until Count Stirmer is also satisfied. 

As to the Austrian part of the difficulty, a: the statement of 
M: Musurus to be correct, and the language of Count Stiirmer sincere, 
there is little prospect of an immediate accommodation, with the 
consequent renewal of diplomatic relations, except by means of an 
unqualified submission to the most objectionable of Prince Schwarzenberg’s 
demands, ; 

However regrettable the continuance of this disagreement may be, 
1 confess that, whether | look to your Loridship’s instructions, or to'm 
own personal convictions, I hold that inconvenience to be a less evil 
than the surrender of the Porte’s independence and dignity to a requi+ 
sition grounded on no treaty right, and likely to be raduetines areata 
of ek vexatious intermeddling and unnecessary suflering. 

It is manifest at the same time that I should travel out of my 
province, if I ventured on this occasion to control the free judgment 
af the Porte. The two leading Ministers are fully ceaaited with my 
opinions and with those of the French Representative, I despair of 
striking out any fresh expedient for reconciling the pretensions of 
Austria with the fair and rightful objections of the Porte. The only 
sort of menace | could by possibility employ, would be the immediate 
withdrawal of Her Majesty’s squadron from the neighbourhood of 
Turkey, and the application of such a lever would be almost equally 
ébjectionable, whether it succeeded, or whether it failed, 

So much daring the protracted struggle has been accomplished in favour 
of Turkish independence, and, consequently of that pacific system which 
in the Fast is so intimately connected with its progressive catablishment, 
that it is impossible not to watch with a deep and anxious interest over 
the terms of final accommodation. But, deeply as the Porte would 
compromise its essential interests by any unnecessary weakness or incon- 
sistency in the closing act of these negotiations, and much as the Powers 
friendly to this empire would have to deplore such an ill-timed com- 
hlianee, the most useful and best-intentioned interference hag its. limits. 

ur's, | conceive, has reached them under the present circumstances.
