Sir, Therapia, December 23, 1849. 

WITH reference to your report dated yesterday, | understand that 
the pending negotiations fete the Porte, on one side, and the Austrian 
and Russian Representatives on the other, respectively, are in the follow- 
ing state; namely, that Count Stirmer has not accepted the Porte’s 
modification of his proposition concerning the ‘ entente préalable ;” that 
the clause touching the list of Hungarian refugee chiefs to be detamed 1s 
mutually arranged, with the addition communicated to you by Aali Pasha; 
that the two proposals giving a right of inspection over them to Austria 
are rejected by the Porte; and with regard to Russia, that M. de Titoff, 
while insisting positively on the adoption of a protocol, does not object 
to that form of protocol which the Porte has finally delivered to him 
through his interpreter, with my concurrence. , 7 

ow, my opinion in answer to Aali Pasha's message is, that his 

Excellency will do well to sign the intended protocol, in concert with M. 
de Titoff, as soon as he obtains the Sultan's permission, which ought not 
to be delayed: that the difficulties with Count Stiirmer, submitted mean- 
while to the Council, and therefore necessarily kept in suspense for two 
or three days, should then, and not till then, if possible, be brou ht to a 
final result, by his Excellency’s informing Count Stirmer that the Porte 
has gone to the utmost extent of concession, in accepting his proposal 
touching the “entente préalable” in the limited form of expression last 
communicated to him; and that if he is unable to accept it with the 
renewal of diplomatic relations, nothing will remain for the Porte but to 
execute fairly and conscientiously what she has offered; unless the 
Austrian Government should be disposed to exchange the intended dleten- 
tion of the refugee chiefs for their expulsion from Turkey, in the manner 
agreed upon with Russia as to the Emperor's Polish subjects at Shumla. 

Understanding that the Sultan is pecees to the “internement,” bat 
not to the “entente,” I perceive no other mode of proceeding, consistent 
with His Majesty's honour and the rights of the Porte as an independent 
Government, oe s 

In submitting to the Grand Vizier and Aali Pasha the paragraph 
accepted by them and objected to by Count Sturmer, I exhausted what 
little ingenuity and diplomatic experience I possess, in trying to satisfy 
Austria without humiliating the Porte. In’so far as my counsels are con- 
cerned, nothing further remains for me to suggest, unless | determine to 
set aside my instructions as well as my own personal convictions. No 
one can possibly be more anxious than I am to witness and to promote 
the settlement of these vexatious differences; but the settlement, to be at 
all satisfactory, or consistent with preceding circumstances, must be not 
only conciliatory but honourable too. ‘To anything short of that I can 

a party, 

dace will and the whole of this to Aali Pasha before the Council 
meets, and if time allows of it you will also read it to General Aupick, 
who I have no doubt will be ready to express a similar view of the ques- 
tion to his Excellency. 3 

You are at liberty, should it Mp ear advisable, to make this commu- 
nication to the Grand Vizier himself, and notes, if wanted, may be taken 
for the consideration of the Council.

No. 216. 
Sir Straiford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received January 18, 1850, 


(No. 387, Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, December 26, 1849, 

_ EP is now more than a fortnight since one of my colleagues, the 
Representative of an [talian Government, came on purpose from town to 
inform me that a plan had been formed to assassinate Count Batthyani, 
Kossuth, and two others of the principal Hungarian refugees, Intelligence 
to this effect, he said, had been secretly given to him by & man named 
Bardi, who had served in the Sardinian army against Austria, in the rank 
of a corporal or sergeant, and had emigrated to Turkey after its discom-

Inclosure | in No. 216, 


Colonel Neale to Sir Stratford Canning. 
Air, Varna, December 15, 1849. 

I HASTEN to bring to the knowledge of your Excellency the following 
secret and confidential communication which has been made to me by Rodolf 
Pardy, late an Hungarian officer, who arrived here from Constantinople last 
night by the Austrian steamer. Having at once come to me, he stated that he 
had been dispatched in all speed from Constantinople for the purpose of pro- 
eeeding to Shumla and of warning Kossuth, Count Batthyani, Generals Dem- 
binski and Messaros, that a plan had been combined at Constantinople for their 
as#assination by some hired Croats, and that it was his object to depart imme- 
diately for Shumla with that intention. 

far in confirmation of the above statement, seven armed Croats in fact 
arrived in Varna by the same steamer last evening. 

The following are the particulars of the plan for the assassination of 
Kossuth and the other chiefs named, and the manner in which it had been 
discovered, as detailed to me by M. Pardy. 

M. Turazi, of the Austrian Embassy at Constantinople, being, it appears, 
extremely intimate with the Baron Michael Orban, and being pressed by the 
latter on all occasions to communicate to him what measures had been adopted 
PeeperHn the refugees at Shumla, secretly betrayed to the Baron that two plans 
had just been combined by the Austrian authorities (that is to say, by the 
Austrian Consul-General, who is-himself a Croat, as M. Pardy especially stated), 
for the assassination of Kossuth and his companions ; and that those plans were 
as follows, 

Ast. That fifteen armed Croats should be dispatched to Shumla, who were 
to avail themselves of whatever opportunity should present itself to accomplish 
their purpose when at Shumla; and with a view of lessening suspicion, that half 
of the above-mentioned Croats should be landed at Bourgas, and proceed from 
thence to Shumla, 2nd, That two individuals, who lately arrived in Constan- 
tinople from Trieste, and who had formerly been in the Hungarian police, but now 
in the service of Austria, and personally known to Kossuth, and supposed by 
him to be friendly to him, should proceed to Shumla with the Croats, provided 
with passports and Turkish teskérés, and offer their services by means of these 
passports to effect the escape of Kossuth, Count Batthyani, Dembinsky, and 
Messaros, This plan, it was deemed, was the most easy of accomplishment, and 
if accomplished, these agents were charged with the assassination of Kossuth and 
his companions during their flight from Shumila, 

Such is the statement solemnly made to me by M. Bardy. He added 
that he believed that your Excellency had been made acquainted with the pur- 
port of his statement upon the moment of his departure from Constantinople ; 
but Dk this point he was not certain. . 

have deemed it to be my duty to facilitate the departure of M, Bardy for 
Shumla, as he found some difheulty in obtaining horses; and in so serious a 
conjuncture I have also deemed it to be my bounden duty to apprize his Excel- 
lency the Pasha of Varna, contidentially and in guarded terms, that I had 
obtained information from a private source, that some armed Croats, accom- 
panied by two superior agents of police, had arrived in Varna, in the intention 
of proceeding to Shumla with the evil designs which | have above related to 
your Excellency, but without any detailed particulars ; and I added from myzelt, 
in making this communication to the Pasha, that in doing so J had discharged 
myself of what both my conscience and duty dictated, and that his Excellency 
would be the best judge of the eredit which could be attached to information of 
gnch an astounding nature, and the measures to be adopted in consequence. 
The Pasha, in reply, conveyed to me his thanks for this communication; and | 
have reason to believe that his Excellency will communicate upon the purport of 
it, with the Governor of Shumla. 

The statement of M, Bardy, which I have the honour in this despatch to 
bring to the knowledge of your Excellency, is of so serious and delicate a 
nature, that had it not been made to me by M, Bardy, in all its minute details, 
and accompanied by the most solemn: pene of its veracity, | woul have 


274 


hardly ventured to have communicated the same to your Excellency in an 
official form. 7 

It remains for me only to add with reference to this subject, that from my 
own positive information and knowledge, seven armed Croats, as | have already 
had the honour to state, did arrive here by the Austrian steamer yesterday, as 
also an Austrian agent of superior rank to themselves, which latter has taken 
up his residence at the Austrian Vice-Consulate, and is the person pointed out 
by M. Bardy as the police agent referred to in his statement. Eight Croats, 
accompanied by another individual, were likewise positively landed at Bourgas, 
The -Austrian Vice-Consul at Bourgas also came on to Varna by the same 
steamer. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) EDWARD 5S. JNO. NEALE. 


P.S.— December 16—I have not deemed it to be prudent to forward this 
despatch to your Excellency by the Austrian steamer which returned last night 
to Constantinople, and I regret that no speedier conveyance presenis itself than 
the Turkish land-post which leaves this day. 

M. Bardy left for Shumla at daylight this morning, and six hours after, 
the Croats who had arrived by the steamer accompanied by the traveller, said 
to be a police agent, left likewise for the same destination.

Report from a Confidential Agent. 


Pera, December 18, 1849. 


IN regard to the person named Bardi about whom your Excellency desired 
information, | beg to say that after having lost all hopes of learning anything 
tbout him, 1 think | have just succeeded through the accidental call of two 
Hungarians at the office, named Francois Gara and Andrea Lehotsky. 

They say that they knew a man of that name very well. That he came 
here several months ago from Italy ; that he is of a rich family in that country ; 
that he had served about eight years in the Austrian service, in a Hungarian 
regiment ; that he was here as a Hungarian refugee ; that his rank was that of 
a lieutenant. He remained here only a few days and left, with a ‘Sardinian 
passport, with the hopes of reaching Hungary again; but on arriving at Widdin 
found it too diffieult, and returned here. That he left again a short time since 
for Shumla, and is expected hack in a few days. They spoke very favourably 
of him, but said he had been reduced to great distress whilst here. 

I have made inquiry respecting the Lieutenant-Colonel mentioned in your 
Exeellency's last note ; but cannot learn anything, although it should have been 
easily learnt if he had been at the Austrian Palace as stated. Don Agostino 
says he does not know him from my description. 

I] have seen M. di Civinis. I had not made the acquaintance of Neshet 
Bey, present director of the Passport Office, and this was an excellent motive for 
calling. He was absent, and I was received by M. Civinis, who, after the usual 
compliments, began to speak of the present position of the Austro-Russian 
question; and taking our side of it, launched out against the Internuncio, and 
tol me explicitly what | had before heard and mentioned to your Excellency 
about the Croats. 

He spoke openly as to Count being the mover of the scheme; and 
stated that one day last week an Austrian dragoman came to their office late in 
the day, when he knew that he (Civinis) would be gone, and finding the good 
man (Neshet Bey) alone, ordered twelve teskérés for so many Austiau subjects 
(Croats), and came for them early the next morning before Civinis could be 
there. He (Civinis) sail the plan laid was for an agent to represent to Kossuth, 
Bem, &e., that they were going to be given up to the Russians, and to recom- 
mend them to escape from the place as quickly as possible; and if they should 
do so, they were then to be made away with on the road, Civinis added that 
the Porte had taken precautions against the success of the plan; but he 
mentioned 1t ax showing the turpitude of the parties, 

la regara co tae chiefs in the affair, I could only learn from him that there

are two or more Austrians, lately arrived from Vienna, in the confidence of 
Count ———, and, as he insinuated, are here for any such kind of service. 


These are very bold things to state so freely, but I think it my duty to tell your 
Excellency exactly whathe said. . . . . 


Pera, December 25, 1849. 

This morning | have obtained some information that may be relied: on, 
and which I should have got yesterday had the person I sought not been absent 
from home. 

I was not aware of the Baron’s name until your Excellency gave it: me, 
although, if my informant is correct, it is not Michael by Giovanni Urban, 

I have not learnt yet all your Excellency wishes to know, but 1 think it 
may be relied on that i have obtained his exact name. He is, Iam told, a 
Transylvanian, He is a military man. He lives in a disreputable part of Pera 
called Tarlabashi, and he-is visited by an Austrian employé; but who he is, or 
af what grade, have not yet learnt. This person is however stated to be 
constant in his visits, indeed every morning, as I am told; and Urban goes 
frequently to the Internuncio. 

I have not heard from this source anything about the females of the family; 

but I had previously heard that there are a daughter and a wife; also that 
Urban has been here for perhaps two years past, looking after the inheritance of 
his wife’s mother who died here about two years ago. 
_ . » . | have been down to see M. Civinis. He confirmed to me the report of 
his having been waylaid on Friday night, nearly in the terms in which I have 
since seen it reported in the jourual of tc-day. He had been passing the even- 
ing with M. Sommaripa, the correspondent of the “* Impartial.” The conversa- 
tion passed very easily to what I wanted to learn, and he confirmed to-meall | 
had previously learnt about Baron Urban or Orban, whose Christian name he 
however did not know, so that whether it was Michael or Giovanni I could not 
learn. All the circumstances he mentioned prove him to be the same person ; 
and he gave me the name of the Austrian who visits the family as Turagsi, not 
an attaché of the Embassy, but an inferior employ¢ in the Cancelleria. 

Civinis says that he himself met the Baron once at the house of Count 
Andrassy, and then told the Count that he thought it very simple of him to 
receive such a person, who was‘a known spy of the other party.

Confidential Report addressed to Str Stratford Canning. 


(Extract.) Pera, December 28, 1849. 
M. DE CIVINIS called upon me this morning to say that he thought it 
his duty to state, in relerence to the Baron Urban, that he (the Baron) having 
heard of the plot in reference to the refugees, made a communication of it to the 
Turkish authorities. 

Civinis added that he did not know what may have been his real object 
in doing this, whether from remorse at having done them and others an il! 
turn in other ways, and ‘rot liking to see them exposed to 60 serious @ danger, 
or from ‘any ‘private interested motive in taking credit to himself in com- 
municating what he might have been aware had been already communicated 
from other ‘quarters. He merely thought it his duty not to conceal this cir- 
cumstance, and apologised for not having thought of it in our conversation at 
the time,

No. 217. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston —(Received January 18, 1850.) 
(No. 388.) : 
My Lord; - Therapia, December 28, 1849. 

J CANNOT yet have the satisfaction of announcing the conclusion of the 
Porte’s differences with Austria and Russia. The Internuncio continues to 
stand out for the entente préalable, and M. de Titoff hesitates to. resume his 
oflicial relations with the Porte before the remaining demand of Count Stiirmer 
is accepted. The consequences in prospect are a fresh reference to Vienna, 
and a prolonged term of coldness between the Sultan and the two Emperors. 

To clear up the uncertainty which still prevailed, notwithstanding the 
agreement concluded between M. de Titoff and the ‘Turkish Minister, I 
directed M. Pisani to make some inquiries of Aali Pasha, The accompanying 
paper contains his Excellency’s replies, together with the questions which drew 
them out. ‘They were reported on the 26th instant at a late hour of the 
evening, and M. Pisani transmitted to me at the same tine & special message 
from the Grand Vizier, describing the state of the negotiation, and inviting me 
to declare whether the British and French squadrons would go or stay, if the 
Russian and Austrian Representatives persisted in pursuing their present 
course, <A copy of M. Pisani's report communicating this message is inclosed 
herewith. sil 

Perceiving in the councils of the ‘Purkish Ministers a degree of embar- 
rassment which it was most désirable td remove, | determined to see the Grand 
Vizier myself, and accordingly went on the following day to Constantinople, 
where Thad an interview with his Highness and the Secretary for Hore 
Affairs, I declared to them frankly my persuasion that the time was come for 
taking a final resolution, and that the present equivocal situation could not be 
prolonged without much inconvenience and disparagement, I reminded them 
that your Lordship’s opinion, no less than my own, was anon to the con- 
cession demanded by Austria; nor did I conceal my belief that: M. de Titoff's 
pretension to make common cause with Count Stirmer, notwithstanding the 
separate agreement which he had signed and sealed, was a mere demonstration, 
not resting on positive instructions, 1 assured them that our friendly counsels 
were by no means offered in a spirit of dictation, but founded, 05 I had clearly 
shown already, on distinct views of the Sultan's permanent interests, dignity, 
and independence, of which however they were 8 je to judge themselves, | 
adeed that, as far as 1 knew, they were not bound either by treaty or hy any 
other kind of engagement, to yield the point in dispute. 

‘he Grand Vizier and Aali Pasha acquiesced in these remarks. They 
also assured me that the Russian Envoy had not declared the protocol to be a 


aa7 


fovidional afféement, and the} moreover expressed a persuasion that his 

‘cellency, in making the resumption of his official intercourse with the Porte 

to depend upon Count Stirmer, was not acting in obedience to any specific 
orders from his Court. . 

With respect to the squadrons, which had’ been the express object of 
Reshid Pasha’s message to me, I thought it advisable to avoid any Aistingt 
declaration; and this I was able to do without difficulty, as his Highness only 
alluded to the question, and appeared to be satisfied when I remarked that the 
danger, whatever it might have been, had ceased with the relinquishment of 
the original demand; that the succeeding questions had been treated on 
diplomatic grounds; and that the squadrons had continued within reach only 
to give a certain degree of moral support to the Turkish Government in its 
negotiations with the Russian and Austrian Envoys. 

Our interview closed with an understanding that another proposal, drawn 

up in terms more agreeable to Austria, though still reserving the Siritari's 
ie should be submitted to Count Stiirmer, and that M. de Titeff should be 
called upon to declare his intentions as to the execution of the protocol and the 
renewal of diplomatic intercourse in the event of a fresh reference to Vienna. 
. On leaving the ‘Turkish Ministers I went to see General Aupick, whom I 
found more than ever anxious to hasten the departure of the squadrons, and 
inclined to look upon the remaining point of difference between the Porte and 
Anstria through the medium of his last very urgent instructions on that head. 
He agreed with me however in thinking that it would be premature to come to 
any'final determination until the intentions of M, de Titoff were more com- 
pletely ascertained, which could hardly fail to oceur within a very few days. 

With a faint hope of accelerating the completion of the desired sotilamiest: 
and removing every contingent obstacle to a thorough agreement between the 
French Representative and myself respecting the early and simultaneous 
retirement of the squadrons, I sought an interview with Count Stirmer and 
subsequently with M, de‘Titoff also, My visit appeared to be taken. in good 
part by each of them; and though I cannot boast of any ostensible suc- 
cess, | found no difficulty in obtaining a courteous and friendly attention to 
my remarks and arguments, 

To the Internuncio I made a frank avowal of my opinions as to the point 
at issue. I denied his having any treaty stipulation or other kind of engage- 
ment wherewith to make good his demand. i affirmed that he had no reason to 
mistrust the intentions of the Porte, and no right to require that kind of security 
against any futare machinations'of the Hungarian refugees, which the Sultan 
could not accord without an embarrassing surrender of what was due to his 
dignity and character as an independent Sovereign. Isubmitted that it was not 
more the interest of Austria than of England to manifest any disregard of those 
considerations which were the Porte’s most natural barriers against the encroach- 
ment of a too powerful neighbour, and I concluded by giving Count Stiirmer to 
understand that if he wished to obtain the assistance of those who might be 
supposed to exercise some degree of influence at the Porte, and to re-establish 
relations of confidence with the Turkish Government, he would not persist in 
requiring that single concession which it would be unwise in the Porte to make, 
and- unfair in its friends to recommend, - The principal objections urged by 
Count Stirmer were the engagement contracted, as he said, by M. Musurus at 


- Vienna, the importance to Austria of having a real security against the pre- 


mature enlargement of the refugees, and the milder feeling adopted of late by his 
Government with respect to those who had been compromised in the recent 
revolutionary conflicts. He stated, moreover, that his instructions were peremp- 
tory; that he had shown his good-will by making every coucession in his power; 
and that the only remaining point of difference was one as to which he had 
positively no discretion to exercise. 

To the Russian Envoy | offered my congratulations on the conclusion of his 
separate agreement with the Porte, ant submitted how greatly it would redound 
to hia credit if he were to complete the work of accommodation by overcoming 
the scruples of his Austrian colleague, and closing the breach unfortunately made 
in those relations between the Porte and its more immediate neighbours, which 
tend 90 powerfully to maintain the peace of the East. M., de Titoff did not give 
me the idea of attaching any great importance to the success of his colleague's 
pretension; but he argued in favour of it as Count Stiirmer himself had argued, 


147 


278 


and left on my mind a confirmation of the impression I had previously entertained 
as to the motives of his perseverance in so vexatious a course of conduct. ; 

It remains to be seen whether the last conclusive step to be taken by Aali 
Pasha will produce any gia ile result, According to present appearances 


it-is most likely that another 


rence to Vienna will be found unavoidable. . 
I have, &c. 


(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING:

No. 218. 
Str Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston,—(Receiwed January 18, 1850,) 
(No, 389,) 
My Lord, Therapia, December 29, 1849. 


I HAD an audience of the Sultan to-day and presented Her Majesty's 
congratulatory letters on the birth of the two Princes who have lately been 
added to the Imperial family, with such expressions of interest as | thought best 
suited to the occasion. 

The Sultan availed himself of the opportunity to repeat his thanks for the 
support which he had received from Her Majesty and from Her Majesty's 
Government, under the late trying circumstances of disagreement with Austra 
and Russia. His Highness was pleased to make his acknowledgments in 
very emphatic terms ; and he seems to feel sincerely what he owes to England, 
not only under recent circumstances but on former occasions also. He was 
more particularly anxious that I should convey the expression of his gratitude 
and confidence to Her Majesty the Queen, 

The opening thus afforded for reverting to the urgency of strengthening 
the defenses of the empire, particularly those of the Bosphorus, and carrying 
out the principles of administrative improvement with more activity, was not 
to be neglected; and I had the satisfaction to observe that. the Sultan appeared 
to receive with approbation my suggestions respecting those objects. 

Thad the honour on this occasion to present the Earl of Lincoln and other 
English gentlemen to His Linperial Majesty, who was pleased to give them a 


-pracious reception.

THE city of Jassy is laid under contribution for military quarters, cach 
house paying in proportion to its extent, from three dueats to twelve piastres 
monthly, with option of providing quarters in lieu of payment. Itis a prevalent 
belief of the Russian officers, that orders will be received in the spring for the 
advance of theirtroopsinto Turkey. Galatzis free from a Russian garrison, but 
at Ibraila a regiment of Russian pontooniers 1500 strong is at present cantoned. 
In some of the district towns large quantities of provisions and forage are 
collected. The district towns, thirteen in number, have hitherto had a Starast 
or Consular Agent of Austria in cach of them, appointed by the Austrian agency. 
Their nomination is now made by the Minister at Vienna, and their functions 
have become more important; Austria in fact exercises a police surveillagce 
over the country, which is at the same time occupied by the forces of Russia. 

A new levy of recruits has been ordered in the Bucovina and Gallicia as in 


Russia. ‘This information had however previously reached us, and it 1s a. 


measure to which the Government have recourse annually. 

The Government of the Principalities is yursuing the path traced out for it,

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston—(Received January 14, 1850.) 


(No. 391.) 


My Lord, Therapia, December 31, 1849. 

IT is with the liveliest feclings of satisfaction that I find myself authorized 
at length to inform your Lordship that the long-pending and vexatious dispute 
between Russia and the Porte is finally set at rest by the open resumption of 
M, de ‘Titoff’s official relations with the Turkish Government. Another inter- 
view between the Russian Envoy and the Grand Vizier is to take place at noon 
to-day in his Highness’ house expressly for that purpose, which is to be accom- 
Bea by a formal delivery of the protocol signed, as your Lordship already 
knows, on the 25th instant. 

The tenacity with which this negotiation has been drawn out on the side of 
Russia, and its conclusion sought to be invested with formalities and ceremony, 
is not a little remarkable. 

The remaining difference with Austria is reduced to a mere point, the 
Sultan's ultimate right to determine at what period the Hungarian refugees may 

202 


150 | 


284 


be safely dismissed, independent of Austria’s consent, being alone reserved. 
Another reference will consequently be made to Vienna with a fair prospect of 
settlement favourable to the Porte’s view, and the Internuncio will have to decide 
whether his official relations with the Porte may be provisionally resumed during 
the interval. 

This state of things, imperfect aa it 1s with respect to Austria, has not been 
obtained without some additional exertions on behalf of the Porte. Such as it 
‘s 1 cannot hesitate to consider it as fully authorizing the application of your 
Lordship’s eventual instructions to Her Majesty's sera at Mosconissl, which 
‘s the more desirable, as the simultaneous retirement of the two squadrons, 
British and French, may be thus secured, agreeably to the desire of both 
Governments. 

A proper understanding already exists between General Aupick and myself 
on this subject, and the French steamer “ Prony,” which is appointed to convey 
his Excellency’s correspondence to Vourla and Toulon, will also take charge 
of this despatch to your Lordship’s address. 

I propose to forward by an express under British colours, my communica- 
tions to Sir William Parker, informing him that his continuance on the coasts 
of Turkey is no longer required. The performance of this duty will only be 
delayed until I shall have received an official confirmation of M. de Titoff’s 
reconcilement with the Porte, and apprized the Turkish Ministers of my inten- 
tion respecting the squadron. | 

It is doubtful at this distance from town whether T shall be able to receive 
my interpreter’s report of the intended meeting at the Grand Vizier's house in 
time to forward its contents by the present opportunity. I do not however 
apprehend any fresh delay or difficulty; and one of the Queen’s messengers 
being still at my disposal, | shall not have to detain my next i to your 
Lordship for the means of a safe and expetce conveyances to England.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston. —(Received January 14, 1850.) 


(No. 392. Private and Confidential.) 
My dear Lord, Therapia, December 31, 1849. 


IT is solely with a view to your Lordship’s information that I forward the 
copies inclosed herewith of a correspondence which took place yesterday between 
the French Minister and myself respecting the immediate retirement of the twa 
squadrons. | 

I had scarcely completed my reply to General Aupick’s letter when o 
message from Aali Pasha arrived to inform me that the Russian Envoy had 

ed to resume Without further delay his official relations with the Porte. This 
intelligence placed the matter under our consideration on a far clearer and more 
substantial ground than before; and it was a real gratification to me that | was 
thereby enabled to meet, without a shade of difference, the wishes and intentions 
of my French colleague, believing them to be founded on the anxious desire of 
his Government to call its squadron home with the least: possible delay. 

My previous communications with General Aupick on this subject suffi- 
ciently explain any slight appearance of abruptness that may strike your Lordship 
in his manner of announcing an intention which, with reference to the conside- 
rations stated in my reply, seemed rather premature. 

I lost no time in acquainting him with my decision, as suggested by the 
improved aspect of our question, and a copy of my last confidential note is inclosed 
herewith, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 2,°1850. 

IN consequence of the port of Odessa being frozen, the Turkish post now 

through the Prineipalities, and the communication with Constantinople 
is very tedious. : . 

ount Neselrode, whom I have just seen, informed me that the only 

intelligenee which had arrived from M. Titoff, since I last called on him, is an 
acknowledgement of instructions sent from hence, and the announcement that 
he had made a communication to the Porte which he hoped would be the pre- 
cursor of the renewal of diplomatic relations. re 

Count Nesselrade seemed to be so much vexed at not having received the 
intelligence he expected, that 1 apprehend he may have had some greater 
reason for dissatisfaction than the mere delay of the post; but he said that he 
was without news; and upon my inquiring of his Exoellency if there had been 
an indication of any unwillingness on the part of the Porte to close the affair, 
he replied that until M. Titoff reported the resumption of his official intercourse 
he should not consider the matter at an end, because the mass of intriguers, 
especially Frenchmen and others in the interest of France who infested Pera, 
Raat the usual course of diplomatic negotiations impossible, as every com- 
‘munication which was made to the ‘Turkish Government transpired five minutes 
afterwards; “therefore,” be said, ‘LT am unable to make any calculation on 
the subject, and it is the fault of the Porte for not having given greater powers 
to Fuad Effendi, who might have closed the whole affair at St. Peters urgh 
for we were ready to abide by the original terms which he had recommended to 
the acceptance of his Government, whereas now the details of the affair were a 
subject for the discussion of all the busy politicians of Constantinople.”

No. 225. 


Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received January 19.) 


(No. 3.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 2, 1850. 

I HAVE reason to believe that previous to the departure of General de 
Lamoriciére from St. Petersburgh he had several conversations with Count 
Nesselrode upon the expulsion of refugees, and that the French Minister 
listened with much favour to the Chancellor's arguments that it would be 
ae for the European Powers to come to a general understanding on the 
subject. 

General de Lamoricitre will doubtless carry these impressions to Paris; but 
I am at a loss to understand in what way the question can possibly, or with 
any chance of success, be brought forward for discussion with the French 
Government. 

[ inquired of Count Nesselrode, with whom I lately exchanged a few words 
on the subject, whether the rumour which had reached me was true, that the 
Russian Government were desirous to open negotiations with foreign countries 
for establishing a general system of extradition or expulsion of refugees; and 
was told by his Excellency that he thought an arrangement of the kind would 
be very useful, and greatly contribute to the happiness of the well-disposed 
portion of the population of Europe; but he said, “We must not now talk of 
extradition, because we have had enough of that word for a long time to come, 
and must content ourselves with expulsion, if even that can be obtained.” 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Inclosure in No. 226, 
Viscount Ponsonby to Prince Schwarzenberg. 


Fienna, January 7, 1850, 
THE Undersigned, &c., has the honour to subject to the knowledge of his 
Highness Prince Schwarzenberg, an observation upon the memorandum com- 
municated by the Sublime Porte to the foreign Missions at Constantinople in 
the month of February 1845, and which professes to lay down the rule for the 


» admission of foreign vessels, whether vessels of war or merchantmen, into the 


Straits of the Dardanelles and Bosphorus, | 

The Undersigned takes the liberty to direct the attention of his Highness 
the Prince to a fact which he will certainly find recorded in the correspondence 
of the Imperial Government with the Austrian Internuncio; namely, that the 
British Ambassador at Constantinople, upon receiving the communication 
above adverted to, applied to the Ottoman Ministers for a modification of the 
rule, and obtained it. The modification desired and obtained was to the 
effect that any British merchant-vessel or vessel of war should be allowed to 

ap ff) 


153 


290 


come within the outer castles of the Dardanelles at once, as far as Barbers’ 
Point, by night as well as by day; and further, the Ambassador, carly in 
October 1845, applied to the Porte for permission to be granted to vessels to 
pass up at night from the Black Sea and anchor in the Bay of Buyukdery, 
which jission was granted. 

The Undersigned thinks it unnecessary to trouble his Highness with a 
recapitulation of more facts connected with this matter, as his Highness will 
no doubt be in possession of full information respecting it in the correspondence 
of the Austrian Internuncio with the Foreign Office of the Imperial Govern- 
ment, and the Undersigned will conclude with the statement, that it is the 
opinion of the British Government, “That it would be a forced construction 
of the regulations of the Porte to apply them toa squadron of line-of-battle ships, 
and that the proper construction of the Treaty of July 13, 1841, and the construc- 
tion for which Great Britain will contend, excludes such a squadron both from 
the anchorage within the castles of the Dardanelles and from the anchorage 
within the outer castles of the Bosphorus.” 

The Undersigned, Xe. (Signed) PONSONBY.

No, 228. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston —(Received January 20, 1850.) 


(No. 402.) 
My Lord, Therapia, December 31, 1849. 

IN consequence of assertions which have been hazarded in the public prints 
and elsewhere during the course of our late transactions here, I have thought it 
advisable to obtain a clear declaration from the Ottoman Secretary of State for 
Foreign Affairs respecting two points of leading importance. 

‘or this purpose I directed M. Pisani to put the two following questions to 
his Excellency ;— 

1. Have the Turkish Ministers ever been seriously admonished, either by 
the Internuncio or by the Russian Envoy, that the approach of the squadrons 
prevented or retarded the final adjustment of the pending differences and the 
renewal of diplomatic relations f 

2, Did Aali Pasha, in reply to a formal inquiry addressed to him by those 
Ministers, ever deny officially or positively, that the Porte had authorized the 
entrance of the British ships of war under Vice-Admiral Parker within the outer 
custles of the Dardanelles ? 

To the former of these questions Aali Pasha is reported by M. Pisani to 
have replied, that M. de Titoff and Count Stlirmer had remarked to him, on 
learning the arrival of Her Majesty's squadron and its entrance within the outer 


291 


castles at the Dardanelles, that if the circumstance had been known when the 
Emperor of Russia first gave a favourable answer to the Porte, it might have 
raised new difficulties in the way of arrangement. 

To the second question he replied that when the two Representatives had 
made inquiry as to the entrance of the squadron, his answer to each of them 
had been that the ships had entered in consequence of bad weather; that there 
had not been time for soliciting a formal permission ; that as ships of war had 
been habitually allowed to come to the same anchorage, the Turkish commandera 
did not think it necessary, even had there been time, to receive instructions from 
the Porte; and that a continuation of bad weather had detained the ships. In 
short, the Pasha declared that not knowing if the squadron had been called in, 
he had neither affirmed nor denied the itioveation of the Porte. ~ 

The fact is, that the Turkish Minister, not knowing what to expect under 
the intimidating circumstances of the moment, from the resentment of Russia 
and her Austrian confederate, had no doubt secretly prepared their officers at 
the Dardanelles for the eventual passage of the squadron, and those officers did 
not therefore require any further eerie to Constantinople for the mere 
entrance of the ships within the outer castles according to the regulations 
applied to other vessels of war. 


I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

My Lord, Therapie, January 5, 1850. 


THE curiosity of the public at Constantinople was excited two.days ago by 
the arrival of an Austrian officer with despatches for the Internuncio, 

Count Stirmer having visited Aali Pasha at his house in the couree of 
yesterday, M. Pisani saw the Ottoman Minister at a later hour and was informed 
by hee Excellency in what manner Count Stirmer had explained the officer's 
arrival, 

It appears from what he stated, that the officer in question had been sent 
from the frontier with a packet of despatches which had been accidentally left at 
Vienna, and was subsequently forwarded too late to overtake the post. | 

It appears further that Count Stirmer communicated to Aali Pasha a 
despatch from Prince Schwarzenberg, announcing that the Court of St. Peters- 
burgh had instructed M. de Titoff to finish his question with the Porte, and 
repeating that he considered the entente préalable between Austria and the Porte 
as an indispensable condition of the resumption of their official relations. 

A new list of about fivescore Hungarians designed for detention in Turkey 
has been sent under instructions from Vienna by the Austrian Consul at Rust- 
chuk from Shumla, where he is residing at present; and Count Stirmer in 
communicating it to Aali Pasha expressed his readiness to strike out some of the 
names as being too insignificant to interest his Government, while he proposed 
that the remainder should be added to the list of thirty-six individuals already 
given in, whose intended mode of conveyance to Kutaya was reported in my 
preceding number, 

I have reason to believe that another question personal to Count Sturmer, 
and not mentioned by Aali Pasha, was the principal cause of his Excellency’s 
visit to that Minister. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

Sir, Foreign Office, January 25, 1850. 

I HAVE to state to your Excellency, with reference to your despatch 
No. 4 of the 5th instant, that you were quite right in not advising the Porte to 
consent to make the duration of its detention of the Hungarian refugees depend- 
ent on the good-will and pleasure of the Austrian Government. The Porte 
had already gone in the way of concession to Austria, to the full extent of what 
is consistent with a due regard to the independence of the Sultan, if indeed it 
may not be said to have in some degree overstepped that limit ; but the demand 
that the Porte should go further was entirely wnreasonable.

WITH reference to my despatch of the 15th instant, and by which | 
had the honour to bring to the knowledge of your Excelleney the confidential 
communication which had been made to me by M. Bardi, it is my duty now to 
acquaint your Excellency that » French merchant residing in Varna called upon 
me yesterday ; and, totally unawere that I was in any degree already aware of 
the subject of his communication, he stated to me that he had heard from a 
Croat residing in Varna, that his countrymen, the other Croats, who had arrived 
by the Austrian steamer, had proceeded to Shumla in the intention of assassi- 
nating one or more of the refugee chiefs who were in Shumla, and whose persons 
would be pointed ont to them by the agent who bad accompanied them from 
Constantinople. One of the Croats who arrived from Constantinople had remained 
in Varna as the cavass of the Austrian Vice-Consul, ond it is from him the 
informant of the gentlemen who called upon me heard what he related. [am 
informed that some remonstrance has been made by the Pasha of Varna against 
this cavass and the others who accompanied him bearing arms, as they ure

Shumla. The ostensible motives assigned for the arrival of these Croats, us

places. But it would appear unnecessary that eight of their number should 
have been landed at Bourgas, if such be the object of their arrival.

Sir, Therapia, January 1, 1850, 

IN pursuance of instructions addressed to me for eventual execution by 
Her Majesty’s Principal Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, I have the honour 
to inform you that the presence of Her Majesty's Mediterranean squadron in 
the neighbourhood of the Dardanelles being no longer required with a view to 
the negotiations at Constantinople now happily concluded between the Porte 
and one of the Imperial Governments, and in progress towards an amicable 
adjustment with the other, you are at liberty to quit your present station and to 
proceed elsewhere with the ships under your command, according to such other 
instructions as you may receive from the Lords of the Admiralty. 

A communication of similar purport is addressed by my colleague, the 
French Representative at the Porte, to the Admiral in command of the French 
squadron at Vourla; and 1 have reason to believe that the squadron will get 
under sail immediately on the arrival of the “ Prony” with General Aupick’s 
despatch. 

That vessel left the port of Constantinople about 8 o'clock yesterday 
evening.

Inclosure | in No, 238, 
Sir Stratford Canning to M, Pisani. 


Sir, Therapia, December 28, 1849. 

AS the time for removing the unfortunate refugees from Shumla appears to 
be at hand, well knowing to what privations and hardships they must be exposed 
in this country and at this season, while proceeding, whether by land or by sea, 
to their respective destinations, | hope to be excused for shine to draw the 
Porte’s attention emphatically to the subject of their wants. Persons cireum- 
stanced as they are, must no doubt be content to endure many severe trials with 
fortitude, They cannot expect that degree of indulgence which would enable 
them to evade the vigilance of those who are responsible lor their safe custody. 
There must also be some kind of limit to the charge which their maintenance 
imposes on the State in whose territory they have taken refuge. But a5 soon as 
due provision is made for these indispensable restraints, the duty of supplying 
their wants with liberality, and alleviating the rigours of their detention, 
commences, and ought not to cease while any unnecessary suffering calls for 
relief. 

The Turkish Government cannot be justly reproached with insensibility to 
these duties. In more respects than one, and on several occasions, the Porte has 
displayed a degree of generosity which might serve for an example to other 
Powers. ‘The Government, however, cannot exercise an immediate superin- 
tendence over numerous refugees Getethed at a distance from the capital, The 


h 
») 


298 


enforcement of its commands must depend on the obedience, good will, and 
humanity of those on the spot. It is easy to imagine how much unnecessary 
annoyance and distress may be occasioned by the carelessness, the avarice, the 
impatience, and natural coarseness of subaltern agents in authority, and to what 
a dee their vices may embitter a painful situation, and defeat the benevolent 
intentions of the Porte. Among the refugees there are no doubt some whose 
personal resources save them from much of the privation and annoyance to 
which they would otherwise be exposed. By far the greater number of them, 
however, are destitute of such advantages, and must be altogether dependent 
upon the local authority and its subordinate officers and soldiers. It may there- 
fore be expected that the Porte will take measures to impose a strict attention to 
its orders, and secure their full execution by means of judicious regulations and 
4 careful selection of responsible agents. The superintendent, in particular, 
should be a man of intelligence, steadiness, and humanity. Warm clothing, 
wholesome food, clean lodging, medical assistance, and supplies to provide for 
petty wants are indispensable, Liberty of religious worship, occasional privacy, 
access to the means of cleanliness, and free exercise in the open air, ought also 
to be allowed. In short, the Turkish Government cannot better consult its own 
interests and honour than by attending carefully to these humanities, and thereby 
securing the attachment of men who have thrown themselves on its protection, 
and who at no distant period may discharge the debt of gratitude by devoting 
their lives and talents to its service. 

You will explain the contents of this instruction to the Grand Vizier and 
Aali Pasha, leaving a Turkish translation in the hands of the former. 


Lam, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 16, 1850, 
FUAD EFFENDI received a messenger a few days ago from Constanti- 
nople. His Excellency informed me at the time of the arrival of his despatches, 
that the only communication of importance which had reached him, was the 
authority to return home whentver it suited his convenience, as the object of 
his embassy had been obtained; but he said that previously to taking leave of 
the Imperial Government, he was ordered to direct their attention to the ques- 
tion of reducing the Russian force in the Danubian Principalities, 
The ‘Turkish Ambassador has communicated with Count Nesselrode on this 
subject, and been informed by his Excellency that orders to this effect had 
already been given, 


299 


This intelligence was confirmed to me yesterday by the Chancellor, who 
assured me that the Minister of War had sent the necessary instructions to 
General Liiders to reduce the Russian occupying force to 10,000 men, and on my 
inquiring in what part of the Empire the troops that were withdrawn would 
be stationed, his Excellency said that he believed they would be scattered along 
the frontier. 

In fact, it is evident that Russia has recalled her troops out of deference to 
her engage-rents with the Porte, but she has done so in the expectation that it 
will not be long before their services may be again required, and therefore places 
them in such a position that they may be available at a moment's warning. 

The season of the year is nevertheless so unfavorable for the dislocation of 
troops, that one may be surprised at this early decision ; and the Chancellor, in 
mentioning the fact to me, said that the original intention had been to leave 
them in the Principalities till the spring. ‘ 

Fuad Effendi purposes setting out for Constantinople in about a fortnight. 
He will stay some little time at Bucharest on his wa 2 cee capital.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received February 7.) 
(No. 36. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 23, 1850. 

WITH reference to Viscount Ponsonby’s despatch No. 276, a copy of which 
was transmitted for my information in your Lardehiy's despatch No. 67 of the 
22nd ultimo, respecting the influence which the Russian Government is supposed 
to have acquired over the inhabitants of Transylvania, I have the honour to 
state that intelligence of the same tendency has reached me here from quarters 
generally well informed; and I think it cannot be doubted, although the Em- 
peror of Russia may have no intention of taking advantage ot the present 
moment of the favourable impression which has been made by his army on the 
inhabitants of Transylvania, that the Imperial Government will not lose sight of 
the influence which has been thus established on the Slavonic population of that 
country and of other parts of the Austrian Empire. 

I have lately conversed with several officers of the staff of the Russian army 
who were employed in the Hungarian war, and all have given a like account of 
the good fooling with which the Russian forces were generally received in that 
kingdom. They have described the peasantry as welcoming them as liberators 
from the tyranny of the Magyars, affording them the most willing assistance, and 
giving them supplies of every kind. 

One of these officers mentioned to me, as a proof of the good feelings which 
existed towards them, that a deputation had waited upon the Grand Duke Con- 
stantine, and actually proposed to him to accept the Crown of Hungary. M 
informant said likewise that similar proposals had been made in several districts ; 
that they not only caused the greatest annoyance to His Imperial Highness, but 
were totally disregarded by him, for he had come to Hungary from no other 
motive than that of acquiring military experience; and the immediate conse- 
quence of these unsought-for deputations was, that it was found expedient to 
remove him, without loss of time, from the scene of more active duty in which 
he was at first employed, to places where his presence was scarcely known, and 
where he had to his great sorrow much less chance of distinguishing himself. 1 
heard from the same: officer that whilst General Georgey was in the Russian 
camp, he had expressed his disapproval of these proceedings of the Hungarian 
peasantry, and censured them most severely, | 

A circumstance connected with the submission of General Georgey has 
lately come to my knowledge, and I beg leave to mention it, as it may possibly 
be unknown to your Lordship, When the reply to the first communication 
of his surrender was received from Vienna by the Russian Commander-in-chief, 
it seemed evident that the wish of the Austrian Government was, that 
Georgey and the principal officers who had acted under his commands should 
be brought to court-martial and shot, To this an answer was immediately 
returned that, according to the terms of the capitulation, such a proceeding 
would be unjustifiable, and the Emperor Francis Joseph was requested to 
reconsider the matter. The Austrian Government still insisted, and it was 
only on the Emperor of Russia declaring that unless he received the most 
positive assurances that Georgey’s life would be spared, and that the only 
punishment inflicted on him would be a removal to some distant spot in the 
Austrian dominions, where, though placed under the surveillance of the 
volice, he would still have his liberty, he should give him an honourable exile in 
Russia. Upon the arrival of this communication the Austrian Government at 
length agreed to the Russian suggestion; but so much delay again occurred in 

forwarding their reply, that the Emperor actually sent off a feldjiger to 


403 


oscow, with orders to the Governor-General to prepare apartments for the 
reception of «distinguished Hugin Lorie whom he should place under 
to his special care and attention. ; | 
a spre murtt it ight to mention this anecdote to your Lordship, as it 
serves to demonstrate the character of the Emperor of Russia, and to explain 
at the same time the just reasons of dissatisfaction which he had with the 
istrian | rment. Hesle cae 
ae ake be assured that the total loss of men killed in battle in the 
Russian army during the war in Hungary last year, did not exceed 700 men ; 
and that the expenses incurred by the War Department for this campaign, 
amounted to about forty millions of roubles, or about six and three-quarters 
illions sterling. 
ke. have of late had frequent occasion in my correspondence to allude to 
the supposed objects of Russia in the Hast, and of the opinion which exists 
generally in this country, that Turkey must infallibly, sooner or later, be 
annexed to the Russian Empire; and the ‘only doubt which exists in the minds 
of many Russians sin fe suetop appears to be the period at which this 
ation is to be effected. ie 
Ee his: subject is in fact one upon which I may say that the nation is 
united; and I have reason to believe that the only two persons who at this 
present moment are aware of the folly of entertaining this project, and are 
desirous to restrain all expressions of public feeling on the subject, are the 
Emperor and Count Nesselrode. They see the impossibility of attempting

‘ork in the hands of future generations. 
a “With reference to the Hanearlan deputations which were sent to the Grand 
Duke Constantine, it may not be irrelevant to allude also to a circumstance 
which happened ae years ago upon the oceasion of His Imperial Highness 
isl tinople. ae 
pe Gackt canal thers he was surrounded by a mob of the Christian popula- 
tion of that capital, and naturally by all who professed the Greek religion. The 
unanimous feeling of this mob, as described to me, was to rise in favour of the 
Grand Duke, their conviction being that he had not come there on a merely 
complimentary visit to the Sultan, but for the purpose of feeling his way as to 
the means of planting the Cross again at Constantinople. So great indeed 1 am 
assured was the enthusiasm expressed by all the Christian inhabitants of the 
city and of the Turkish Empire generally, at that time, that the Russian Minister

ong the populace, | ; 
aie These facts are probably all known to your Lordship, but it may not be 
without interest to repeat them at the present moment, for they show the power 
, possessed by Russia of extending her influence in the countries on her south- 
eastern frontier, and the care which appears to be devoted by those who now 
direct her policy to prevent too early an explosion which might mar her projects. 
At the same time we may arrive at another conclusion, which cannot fail to be 
satisfactory to Her Majesty's Government, that they have by their late measures 
at all events arrested the progress of Russian power, and gained time so as to 
enable the Porte to give a greater development to her system of reform, and to 
raise further barriers against inroads from this country.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston,.—(Reeeived February 7.) 


(No. 87. Confidential.) 

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, January 24, 1850, 
FUAD EFFENDI had an audience of the Emperor of Iussia at | o'clock 

this day, when he took leave of His Imperial Majesty ; and the following is the 

account which his Excellency has given me of what passed upon this 

occasion. 


160 


304 


After a few civil expressions from the Emperor, the Turkish Ambassador 
endeavoured to explain the difficult position in which the Sultan was placed at 
the commencement of the differences that had arisen between the two Courts, 
and attempted to excuse the conduct of the Porte, stating that the honour of the 
Sultan was at stake, and would have been seriously compromised if the Emperor 
had insisted on the fulfilment of the stipulations of the Treaty of Kainardji; and 
that be had been charged with the mission of appealing entirely to His Imperial 
Majesty's friendship to waive his rights in the matter. 

The Empcror appears at these words to have interrupted Fuad Effendi, 
who was probably going to deliver a speech which he had prepared for the 
oceasion, and to have said that he did not wish to reopen a question which he 
considered closed, and that he had only to observe thereupon, that he should 
expect the Porte in future to adhere more strictly to her treaty engagements, 
especially to those concerning the Dardanelles; for if any misunderstanding 
might have once existed as to the spirit of the Treaty, all doubt as to its true 
meaning was now removed, and no other interpretation could ever again be put 
on it than that which resulted from the late explanations of the British Govern- 
ment on the subject. 

The Emperor gave Fuad Effendi the assurance, in his usual emphatic 
manner, of his desire to maintain the most cordial and friendly relations with 
the Sultan, and trusted that the lute events would not cause any estrangement 
of that good understanding which he wished always to cultivate with the Porte ; 
adding that he was most anxious for the welfare of the ‘Turkish Empire; that he 
should be ever ready to co-operate with the Sultan in the Danubian Princi- 

alities, or in whatever part of his dominions he had.a right by treaty to inter- 
fere, for the maintenance of the sovereign rights of the Sultan; and he wished 
it always to be borne in mind that he should do this solely with a view to 
inerease and strengthen the Sultan's means of Government, and not for any 
purposes of his own. 

His Imperial Majesty then remarked to Fuad Effendi that he had just 
given a proof of his desire to meet the wishes of the Sultan on the question of 
the military occupation of the Principalities, by ordering General Liiders to retire 
from them with all the troops exceeding 10,000 men, which would soon be the 
whole amount of the Russian forces in Moldavia and Wallachia. 

The Emperor seems to have male but one allusion to the question of the 
refugees, when he expressed his dissatisfaction at the manner in which they had 
been treated by the Turkish authorities at Shumla, where he understood they 
had been received with honours that ought not to haye been showm to persons 
under the surveillance of the police. 

Fuad Effendi declared to me that he had every reason to be pleased with 
the Emperor's reception of him, and that His Imperial Majesty's assurances of 
good will to the Porte were given in a tone which left no doubt on his mind as 
to their perfect sincerity, 

The language of the Emperor to the Turkish Ambassador has so much 
resemblance to that held to myself by His Imperial Majesty five weeks ago, 
that one cannot entertain. the least doubt as to the truth of his present inten- 
tions: and indced it appears to. me impossible, after these solemn declarations, 
and the pledging of his Imperial word, that he can depart from them unless the 
Porte gives just cause of provocation ; and therefore 1 think we may reasonably 
expect that at all events during the reign of the Emperor Nicholas, no attempt 
will be made by Russia to subvert the Ottoman Empire. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received February 9.) 


(No. §. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, January 17, 1850. 

AFTER the repeated communications by which General Aupick had 
manifested his amxiety to hasten the return of the French Mediterranean 
squadron to Toulon, and our joint understanding, on the resumption of official 
relations between Russia and the Porte, that we should concur without further 
delay in releasing the two squadrons from their continued presence on the coast 
of Turkey, by writing respectively in that sense to each of the Admirals in 
command, I was not prepared for learning by & despatch from Her Majesty's 
Consul at Smyrna, that the entire French squadron was at anchor on the 10th 
instant in the bay before that city, with the appearance of meaning to remain 
there. se 

On the receipt of this intelligence 1 addressed a few lines of inquiry to the 
French Minister, and on the following day received from his Excellency an 
answer in explanation of the incident to which I had invited his attention. 

The want of provisions mentioned by General Aupick may be sufficient to 
account for any change in the plans of the French Admiral, but 1 do not 
remember to have heard a syllable of it in any of my previous communications 
with that Minister; and it is not unworthy of notice, that the “ Tmpartial 
newspaper published at Smyrna, states in its last number, that two French 
vessels with provisions on beard, which had been detached from Toulon, were 
subsequently countermanded by orders from the squadron. 

Copies of Mr. Brant’s despatch, of my letter to General Aupick, and of his 
Excellency’s reply, are inclosed herewith for Oe Lordship’s more complete 
information, It is not impossible that the allusion made in the last to Sir 
William Parker's supposed destination for Greece, may furnish a clue to the real 
motive of Admiral Parseval-Deschénes’ detention at Smyrna. 

To prevent the possibility of any misunderstanding founded on this unex- 
pected difference in the proceedings of the two squadrons, notwithstanding the 
efforts which | made to produce Hae ane simultaneous departure, I have

communicated confidentially to Aali Pasha and the Grand Vizier the letters which 
had passed on that subject between General Aupick and myself. The answer 
which T have received from those Ministers, contains an assurance that they 
had received no other information respecting the French squadron either from 
the authorities at Smyrna or from the French Legation here. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

Inclosure in No. 257. 
Colonel Neale to Sir Stratford Canning. 


Sir, Varna, January 9, 1850. 

WITH reference to the subject of the arrival here from Constantinople of 
the Croats who had proceeded towards Shumla, as detailed in my despatches 
Nos. 41 and 44 of last month, I have to acquaint your Excellency that I am 
informed, upon good authority, that they had been summoned to Shumla from 
Yonoskoi, the village where they were stationed, by Halim Pasha, in order to 
yemove the alarm, well or ill-founded, which their presence on the road to 
Shumla had occasioned to travellers coming from or roceeding to that place. 
Lam also informed that since their arrival in Shumla they were acting as guards 
to the Austrian Vice-Consul, who is for the present resident there. 

During the course of last week Colonel Talli, one of the Hungarian refugees 
who had arrived in Varna some days before, was sent back to Shumla under the 
following circumstances. Colonel Talli, upon his arrival here, having been 
arrested by the Turkish authorities, claimed the protection of the Austrian Vice- 
Consul, stating that he was one of the officers included in the capitulation of 
Comorn, and therefore considered himself entitled to his liberty ; and that he 
anticipated no danger even in returning to Austria. But the Austrian Vice- 
Consul declined to take any steps on his behalf, or to receive him in the 
Consulate under restraint, as Colonel ‘Talli proposed, until the correctness of his 
statement was ascertained. 

Upon the arrival of the last steamer, however, from Constantinople, the 
Pasha of Varna, as it is resumed, acting upon instructions he had received by 
that occasion, see to Colonel Talli that he must immediately return to 
Shumla; whieh was eflected in the midst of some resistance and much altercation 
and remonstrance on the part of Colonel Talh. 

It is understood that cavalry videttes are now placed at intervals on the 
roads round Shumla to prevent for the future the eseape of the refugees, among 
whom, however, a rumour prevails, in consequence of letters received from Con- 
stantinople, that a portion of them would very shortly be removed to some other 

lestination, 
cy beg to add, for the information of your Excellency, that the Austrian 
‘agent who accompanied the Croats from Constantinople, and alluded to in my 
previous despatches upon that subject, has returned to Varna, and proceeds to 
Constantinople by the present steamer. This agent, upon his arrival here from 
Constantinople, declared his intention of proceeding to Rustchuk ; but it is now

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston—(Received February 14.) 


(No. 24.) 


My Lord, Therapia, January 21, 1850. 
IN your instruction No. 307 of November the 30th, there is a jee 

wherein it is stated that Christians who embrace the Mahometan faith in Turkey, 

become thereby subjects of the Sultan. Respecting this proposition, I think it 


my duty to submit a few remarks for your Lordship's mature consideration. 

The pretension of the Porte is no doubt such as your Lordship has 
described it, and there are two Articles in the Capitulations which appear to 
warrant its application to British subjects. But the pretension is founded on 80 
monstrous a principle, that it may be doubted whether anything short of an 
express engagement could fairly bind a Christian Government to its observance. 
A mere change of creed is held to cancel the obligations of natural allegiance, 
and the Communder of the Faithful virtually claims every orthodox Mussulman 
for his subject. Now the Glst and 71st Articles of the Capitulations provide 
for the cuse of a British subject turning Turk, and taking advantage of his 
apostacy to keep possession of property belonging to his countrymen. The 
arrangement clearly implies that the renegade has ceased to be amenable to 
British jurisdiction ; but no such admission is distinctly expressed, and a tacit 
acquiescence, the result most probably of commercial interest or political expe- 
diency, may surely cease without a breach of good faith, when those motives no 
longer operate. 

Exclusive of what is exceptionable and contrary to English law in the 
principle, objections of practical importance are not wanting. A large Mussul- 
man population is now placed under British jurisdietion, and individuals so cir 
cumstanced in faith and allegiance not unfrequently come into this country. 
According to Turkish principles, any person of that deseription would forfeit his 
right to British protection on passing into the Sultan's dominions. Russia, too, has: 
Mussulman subjects, and they probably would not look in vain to any Russian 
Consul in this country for protection. A continued compliance on our side 
would therefore be attended not only with injustice to those who might claim 
our protection, but also with the Hae of yielding what another Govern- 
ment is pep to maintain. ‘The point would seem to be conceded by the 
Treaty of Kainardji, but there the concession is reciprocal, and stronger for 
Russia than the Porte, as the doctrines of Christianity afford no plea for the 
counter-claim. 

Though 1 would not willingly raise an idle question, or exaggerate the 
importance of one already mooted, | cannot lose sight of the bearing which too 
much respect for the remains of Turkish pretension, manifested by a Government 
like that of England, may have upon the progress of Administrative improvement 
in this empire. We have now reached a point where progress is too likely to be 
ata stand, In order to move forward, the forms and maxims of an old exclusive 
system of bigotry and arrogance, rotten at the core but hardened externally, must 
be made to give way. But this will never be done while foreign Governments 
show more respect for those absurd pretensions, than for their own enlightened 
principles and the rightful interests of their subjects. The question of Chris- 
tian evidence is an instance in point. ‘The Turkish law in that respect is a 
perfect barrier against the further amalgamation of Turks and Christians. It is 
so understood and secretly condemned by the leading Turkish Ministers. Its 
religious character, nevertheless, continues to sustain it, and the greatest interests 
of this empire, whether social, administrative, commercial, or political, stagnate 
in its shade. ‘The question in whieh this despatch originated is not indeed of 
the same magnitude, but it belongs to the same class. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Lord Bloomfield to Viscount Palmerston.—( Received February 16.) 


(No. 41.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 30, 1850. 


IN my despatch No. 37 of the 23rd instant, I reported that Fuad Effendi 
had had an audience of the Emperor. He has since received from His Imperial 
Majesty a diamond snuff-box, and each of the persons composing his suite have 
received some mark of Imperial favour. 

To-day the Turkish Ambassador took leave of Count Nesselrode, and 
to-morrow he sets. out for Jassy, by the way of Moscow and Kieff. He is to 
be accompanied by a feldjager, and will be shown every possible attention by 
the Russian authorities on his journey to the Principalities. 

Fuad Effendi has just called on me for the purpose of taking leave, when, 
after thanking me for the support 1 had given him during his mission to this 
Court, he told me that nothing of any importance had occurred at his interview 
with Count Nesselrode, except that his Excellency had delivered to his care a 
letter which the Emperor has addressed to the Sultan in answer to the one of 
which he had been the bearer; and on my inquiring if be knew the purport of 
this communication, Fuad Effendi said that it contained the usual professions of 
friendship for the Sultan, and of readiness to meet his wishes, and to establish 
the most cordial relations with his Government ; but that the Emperor had 
warned His Majesty not to permit the interference of foreign Powers in the 
affairs of Turkey, and that this was the only point worthy of remark in the 
whiole letter. : 

{ asked his Excellency if he had had any conversation with Count 
Nesselrode about the Prineipalities, and he told me that he had not; that he 
expected to meet that portion of the Russian troops who are to retire from them, 
on their march homewards ; that General Duhamel would immediately proceed to 
Jassy, where he probably should find him ; that his chief business in the Princi- 
palities would be to examine the report of the Commissioners of Revision ; and 
that what he had most at heart in terminating his connection with those pro- 
vinces was to establish some system by which their future government would 
insure the gradual improvement of the concdition of the peusantry, for which 
surpose it was essential that the corvées should be removed as far as possible ; 
wut that there were many difficulties to contend with in effecting this and other 
improvements, and none greater than the necessity under which the Porte found 
itself of not granting too much to Wallachia and Moldavia, in order hot to raise 
a Spirit of disaffection in Bulgaria and the provinces south of the Danube, which 
would have a right to be dissatisfied, if concessions of a similar kind were 
refused them. 

Fuad Effendi added that after he had settled the appointment of the 
Council of Government, and prepared instructions for his successor, whom he 
expects to find at Bucharest, he shall proceed to Constantinople, and enter upon 
his new duties; and that he hopes to be on the shores of the Bosphorus in the 
month of March. 

I have, ke. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Inclosure 1 in No. 260, 
Statement by Mr, Longworth. 


Constantinople, January 26, 1850. 


ON Sunday the 6th of January two persons paid a visit to General 
Guyon, and in the course of conversation alluded at some length to a report 
then in circulation that a party of Croatians bad been dispatched from the 
Austrian Chancery to Shumla for the purpose of assassinating M. Kossuth and 
other chiefs of the Hungarian emigration, I was not then acquainted with the 
names of cither of the individuals in question, but taking some interest in the 
subject I asked one of them, a respectable-looking man apparently about the age 
of five or six-and-twenty, if he really believed these reports, as they seemed to 
me incredible from their atrocity. ‘To this he replied that he not only believed, 
but knew them to be true; that to his certain knowledge these Croatians had 
been hired and brought here in the steamer from Trieste for the purpose of 
trepanning and assassinating the Hungarian refugees; that he had spoken to 
them himself, and entertained in consequence not the slightest doubt as to the 
nature of their errand; that they were twelve in number, and were placed 
under the orders of a certain Gabriel Sazmadgi, a person of this country but 
now it) the employment of the police at Vienna, and who had come out with 
them from Trieste. The second in command was a man of the name of 
Davidovitch, and they were accompanied by a woman of disreputable character, 
who passed for the wife of one of these emissarics; she was to be used he 
believed as a decoy to ensnare the refugees, and it was reported she had been 
formerly kept by General Perczel, one of the détenus at Shumla. All these 
Croatians, with M. Sazmadgi at their head, had heen embarked in an Austrian 
steamer bound to the Black Sea, and six of them landed at, Bourgas and six at 
Varna, This is in substance what was communicated to me by one of the 
persons who visited General Guyon on the 6th of January, and whose name | 
learnt on his departure was M. Turassi, an employé of the Austrian Chancery 
of this place. 

To these particulars I may perhaps be permitted to add some further 
information which has come subsequently to my knowledge, ind may not be 
deemed altogether irrelevant. ‘The nae Sazmadgi above referred to, after an 

2532

316 


absence of some weeks, and baffled it appears in his attempts by the vigilance of 
the ‘Turkish authorities, returned to Constantinople, leaving his accomplices at 
Varna. He has since, | understand, made a formal complaint through the 
Austrian Chancery to the Porte against the conduct of the Government fune- 
tioneries, whom he accuses of thwarting and persecuting his agents while 
carrying on his business, which was of a commercial nature, in the interior, | 
cannot say what the effect of these representations may have been, but it is 
certain that only a few days ago M. Sazmadgi took a second trip in the Austrian

Grand Vizier he could not undertake to execute the commission entrusted to 
him, if it was to be shared with such an associate. It was in consequence 
probably of this declaration of Ahmed Effendi that M. Sazmadgi returned alone 
to Varna, in order I presume to pursue his commercial operations in that 
neighbourhood. (Signed) J, A. LONGWORTH.

BY a despatch which reached me the day before yesterday, I learned from 
Her Majesty's Acting Consul at Bucharest, that General Liiders, accompanied by 
M. de Kotzebue, had called on Omer Pasha, and remonstrated with him on 
account of the number of Austrian subjects eeeneyy enlisted into the Ottoman 
army under his command. Mr. Grant describes the Russian Commander-in- 
chief as having declared to the Pasha that his Sovereign the Emperor Nicholas 
would not tolerate a continuance of that proceeding; and he adds, om the 
authority of a traveller, that an Austrian detachment at Cronstadt was preparing 
to march into- Wallachia, | 

T lost no time in cOnveT this intelligence to Aali Pasha, affording him 
thereby an opportunity of telling me whatever he knew and thought of the 
matter in question, His Excelleney's reply, as reported to me by M. Pisani, 
amounts in substance to what follows :— 


The Russian Envoy had sent him a message announcing that he had 


received despatchesby an express from M. de Kotzebue, apprizing him of his having 
complained to Omer Pasha of the large number of Austrian subjects disposed to 
embrace Islamism and to enter the military service of the Porte under the com- 
mand of General Bem, and of his haying remarked that as the Emperor of Russia 
was the protector of Christianity in the Principalities of the Danube, an end 
must be put to the practice ; for although the recruits were neither Moldavians 
nor Wallachians, proselytism was evidently encouraged in those provinces. It 
was further stated that Omer Pasha had denied his having endeavoured to make 
proselytes ; that the Mahometan religion did not warrant the rejection of volun- 
tary converts ; that indigence and misery were the real causes of apostacy ; and 
that he should propose to the Austrian Consul to check the tendency complained 
of by supplying means of relief to his destitute dependents. 

Aali Pasha appears from his own statement to have added in reply to M. de 
Titoff, who pressed for an immediate answer, that the Porte had hitherto received 
no direct intelligence of what had occurred in Wallachia; that the conduct of 
Omer Pasha as described would be approved by the Porte ; and that he would 
be instructed to require the presence of some one from the Austrian Consulate, 
as often as an Austrian subject should of his own aecord announce his wish to 
embrace the faith of Mahomet. 

Any attempt to make proselytes received as strong a disclaimer from the 
Ottoman Sceretary of State as from the Commander of the Turkish army in 
Wallachia.
