Inclosure 1 in No. 263. 
Mr. Grant to Sir Stratford Canning: 
Sir, Bucharest, January 18, 1850. 


FOR some days past great numbers of young artisans and workmen to 
various trades have presented themselves before the Turkish military autho- 
rities here, requesting to be allowed to embrace Islamism and to be enrolled 
in the Turkish service. 

Omer Pasha called on me a few days sinee, and communicated to me the 
application of these individuals, who are principally Hungarians and Germans 
under the protection of the Austrian Agency here, and told me that be had 
informed M. Timoni officially of the fact, and requested him to send a delegate 
from his Agency, to persuade himself that these proposed proselytes acted of 
their own free will. 


I understand M. Timoni feels confident that these persons, many of 


whom he declares to be minors, have been induced by the glittering promises 
held out to them through M. Kossuth’s emissaries here to take this step, 
under the belief that a fresh rise will shortly take place in Hungary and 
Transylvania; and that Turkish agents have likewise seduced them with pro- 
mises of rapid promotion, &e. This opinion, however, is not that of the 
Russian or French Agents, who, like myself, acquit Omer Pasha on this score 
of conversion of anything like inissionary efforts. 

Vet I confess it is difficult to imagine what can have thus suddenly induced 
these persons to desire to abjure their faith. Ihave endeavoured to ascertain 
whether any premium has been offered to or received by these individuals; but 
I cannot learn that any other sum has been given to them, than what may be 
considered as bounty-money granted to voluntary recruits, and equivalent to 
about 2. sterling. Now this to persons guining at the minimum that amount 

er month when working at their trades and employments, surely cannot be the 
allurement. . 

I told Omer Pasha frankly that I regretted the steps taken by these 
individuals, and that I felt sure their conduct would be severely censured 
in Europe; and that moreover I considered the incident in itself would 


16 


9) 
i) 


a20 


ereatly tend to retard the renewal of the friendly relations between Austria and 
the Porte. 

Omer Pasha remarked that he had not ee to effect these conversions, 
but that when these persons addressed themselves to him, desiring to be 
received into the faith of the Prophet, he could not refuse to. comply. 

Up to this day 1 learn that upwards of 150 have been sent across the 
Danube. | 

(Signed) EFFINGHAM GRANT.

William Parker's entrance within the outer castles of the Dardanelles, I had 
concurred with the Porte in thinking it necessary that an answer should be 
iven to the instruction previously addressed by Count Nesselrode to M. de 
‘Titoff, and communicated by the latter to Aali Pasha, The Ottoman Minister, 
after consulting me upon the subject, prepared the draft of an answer in the 
form of a circular to the Sultan's Representatives at St. Petersburgh, Vienna, 
Berlin, London, and Paris. On my i'd as a preferable course, that an 
T 


dae 


‘natruction explaining the circumstances of the case, and repelling the preten- 
eion of Russia's right to send a squadron into the Bay of Buyukdery, should be 
addressed to Fuad Effendi for communication to Count Nesselrode ; and that 
the two instructions should be transmitted to the Turkish Representatives in 
the four last-mentioned capitals, for communication to the respective Ministers 
there, Aali Pasha preferred an official note to M. de Titoff, on the ground of 
Fuad Effendi’s presumed departure from St. Petersburgh; and I had only just 
succeeded in persuading him to desist {rom a mode of proceeding so unneces- 
sarily formal, when the receipt of Count Nesselrode’s declared withdrawal of his 
pretension removed the only motive for replying at all to the instruction 
received from him by M. de Titoff; and consequently T recommended that the 
question should be allowed to drop without further correspondence between the 
two Governments. 

To this suggestion Aali Pasha and the Grand Vizier, who were much 
gratified by the purport of Baron Brunnow’s communication to your Lordship, 
were willing enough to assent ; but they found themselves obliged to give some 
kind of answer to the Russian Envoy here, in consequence of his having obtained 
from them a promise to that effect some time before. 

Such being the state of the case, [recurred to my previous suggestion,

Effendi, such as it was finally adopted alter the admission of some of the 
amendments which I thought it advisable to propose. 

I trust that the Porte’s declaration will now appear to your Lordship, both 
in form and substance, as little objectionable as the delicate circumstances of the 
case conid possibly allow. 

The circular to be addressed to the Turkish Ministers at the Courts of the 
other Powers immediately concerned in the Treaty of 1841, will be limited to a 
few words, merely authorizing the communication of the two instructions, 

{ learn from the Grand Vizier that no intelligence has yet been received of

remain there some weeks longer. ;

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received February 24.) 
(No. 39.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 5, 1850. 


THE Ottoman Secretary of State and the Austrian Internuneio have 
received answers from Vienna, the one to his instruction acquainting M. 
Musurus with the remaining points of difference concerning the Hungarian 
refugees, the other to his report of the latest discussions at Constantinople on 
the same subject. Both are in substance the same, Prince Schwarzenberg 
accepts the Porte’s last version of the note to be addressed to Count Stirmer, 
but insists upon the blank being filled wp with at least five years af unrecon- 
sidered detention, instead of a few months. Your Lordship is already in posses- 
sion of the amended draft to whieh I allude®. Inclosed herewith is a copy of M. 
Musurus'’s despatch to Aali Pasha. The Internuncio ina conference which he 
had some days ago with that Minister and the Grand Vizier, began by demanding 
a term of twelve years. He gradually came down to five, with an opening for 
reconsideration during that period ; and the difference thus reduced awaits the 
decision of the Council. 

The ‘Turkish Ministers have meanwhile applied to me for an opinion, and 
1 have uot hesitated to advise a firm resistance to any pretension exceeding the 
ample measure of deference already offered to the wishes of Austria. The 
Porte is bound neither by treaty nor ce the rules of good neighbourhood to go 
further. Already indeed she has offered to pledge herself to more than the 
obligations of any treaty imposed upon her, and by so doing, she has unnecessa- 
rily incurred the hazard of much future embarrassment. Prinee Schwarzenberg s 
yresent demand, if meant to be really stringent on the Porte, is | concelve 
inadmissible on grounds of humanity with respect to the refugees, and on those 
of honour, of prudence, and of national independence, with respect to this 
empire ; and if ‘lusive, serving uo purpose but that of humiliating the Porte and 
complicating the terms of agreement. After all that has passed, the Sultan's 
Ministers ave fairly entitled to say that they have reached the final point of 
concession, that they are ready to redeem the pledge already given, but that, if 
more be insisted upon, however they may regret the groundless dissatisfaction of 
Austria, they are content to abide the consequences. 

It would then remain for them to consider whether it would be more

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.— (Received March 8.) 
(No. 50.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 16, 1850. 


THE Ottoman Council has deliberated on the only remaining point of 
difference with Austria respecting the Hungarian refugees; and in virtue of its 
decision the Minister for Foreign Affairs has proposed to the Internuncio to 
insert a term of twelve months as the period of their detention, subject to the 
contingency of public tranquillity being completely re-established in Hungary. 

ili Pasha had received a conditional authority to extend the eriod to 
two years. He consulted me upon the subject, and I told him that 1 did not 
feel myself at liberty to depart from the opinion which | had already expressed ; 
namely, that the Porte would best consult its own dignity and interests by 
adhering to the last proposition which had been offered to Count Stiirmer at the 
oe of December. ‘That proposition involved a question of months, and not 
of years. 

I am informed that Count Stiirmer’s dissatisfaction on this account has 
been strongly declared to Aali Pasha, by means of a written instruction to his 
interpreter ; that he urges a fuller compliance with his present demand of five 
years’ detention, and that he intimates the possibility of some further diminution 
of the period being accepted at Vienna. 

His Exeellency’s relations with the Porte offer little apparent prospect of 
being immediately resumed. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Receiwed March 8.) 


(No, 51. Confidential.) 


My Lard, Constantinople, February 16, 1860. 
A COPY of the Internuncio's instruction mentioned in my despatch No. 
50 is inclosed herewith. Should neither party make any further concession, 
the Porte will cither proceed to execute its proposed, though unaccepted, 
agreement without further delay, or it will adopt the course which would have 
been preferable from the first, of sending the Hungarian, in like manner as the 
Polish, refugees out of the Sultan's dominions. Judging from the Grand Vizier’s 
language when I last saw him, the Porte 1s at present inclined towards the latter 
mode of proceeding. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

M. de Titoff to M. Chirico. 


ic Janvier, 1850. 
EN renouvelant aujourd'hui la demande ge le Gouvernement Impérial 
m'a chargé de poursuivre auprés de la Sublime Porte relativement a l’expulsion 
des Sieurs Czaykowski et Lenoir, vous voudrez bien rapneier a son Excellence 
Aali Pacha les explications verbales oi: je me flatte de lui avoir fait apprécier 
le bon droit et les motifs de notre réclamation. 


Quant aux motifs, les Ministres Ottomans sont trop clairvoyans pour en 
récuser la gravité et la justesse. Dés leur apparition en Turquie ces deux indi- 
vidus n'ont point exerce d’autre profession que l'intrigue politique. Ils n'y 
mettent surtout depuis quelque tems ancune réserve. Ghia ces intrigues révo- 
lutionnaires sont hostiles & la Russie et nuisibles ila Turquie elle-méme, c'est 
notoire; et indépendamment de la certitude morale, les preuves matérielles ne 


manqueraient point, si, pour les produire, il ne nous répugnait d’inculper des | 


tiers et de multiplier des compromis facheux, 

Quant au droit, je tiens 4 répeter ici comme je |l’ai dit en conférence, que: 
Article I du Traité de Kainardji, qui sert de base & notre demande, n’impose 
aux Parties Contractantes aucun devoir de prouver la culpabilité des transfuges 
dont elles auraient 4 requérir l'extradition ou l'expulsion. Czaykowski et Lenoir 
(Zwarkowskt) sont natiis des Etats Russes, par conséquent sujets de l'Empereur, 
Cela suffit 4 rendre lapplication du Traité obligatoire a leur égard, vi que 
l'Article précité, sauf le cas du changement de religion, s'applique a tous les 
Bujets respectifs qui pour quelque cause que ce soit, passeraient d'un empire 
dans l'autre, dés une réquisition en sera faite; et cela, dit le méme Apticle, afin 
que pour de tels malfaiteurs il ne s'éléve aucun refroidissement ou contestation 
inutile entre les deux empires, 

La Sublime Porte reconnaitra que loin de marcher au but salutaire du 
Traité en évitant les contestations gratuites, e’est leur donner une source perpé- 
tuelle que d'établir un précedent d'aprés lequel chaque fois que le Gouvernement 
Imperial invoquerait |'Article Il du Traité de Kainardji A legard de l'un de gea' 
sujets réefugié en Turquie pour se soustraire aux lois, il suffirait dune Ligation 
ou méme & un Consul étranger de déclarer cet individu son protégé, moyennant 
la simple signature d'un passeport. 

Le Cabinet Impérial ne saurait se resigner & croire qu'il entrit dans la 
pensée de la Sublime Porte et d'aucune Puissance bienveillante pour le bon 
ordre et le repos dans |'Orient, de vouloir ainsi réduire av néant nos légitimes 
réeclamations, et convertir en lettre morte nos stipulations consacréés par nos 
‘Traités avec la'Turquie, 

Czaykowski et Lenoir, selon leur origine, n'ont d'autre nationalité légale 
que la nationalité Polonaise. A Vappui de cette assertion, plus amplement 
développée dans nos entrevues avec Aali Pacha, je prendrai la liberté de lui 
communiquer la notice ci-jointe, résumant ce que l'on sait d'essenticl sur les lois 
en miaticre de naturalisation. Je dois abandonner & la sagesse de M. le 
Ministre le parti a tirer de ces données. Mais je ne saurais dissimuler combien 

ee serait manquer ala dignité et aux intéréts de la Sublime Porte, si, contre 
toute justice, on voulait, au moyen d'une protection prépotente et arbitraire, 
empécher lexécution de ses traités avec une Puissance amie et limitrophe, 


Veuillez, Monsieur, placer la présente sous les yeux de M. le Ministre des _ 


Affaires Etrangéres, et en laissant copie 4 son Excellence.

No, 279. 


Viscount Palmerston to Sir Stratford Canning. 


(No. 80.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, March \1, 1850. 

1 HAVE received your Excellency’s despatches Nos. 50 and 41 of the 
16th ultimo, reporting on the discussions still pendirg between Austria and the 
Porte in regard to the disposal of the Hungarian refugees ; and I have to observe 
to your Excellency that if the state of the negotiation should leave the Porte at 
liberty to choose the last of the two alternatives mentioned by your Excellency, 
namely, that of sending the Hungarian, in like manner as the Polish refugees, 


out of the Sultan’s dominions, such a course would no doubt be the best, as it 


would preclude all further discussion as to subsequent proceedings with respect 
to these refugees. 

This observation applies of course to these among the Hungarians who are 
desirous of leaving Turkey, and who are in the list presented by the Austrian 
Minister. ‘T'o expel the others who are poor and without means of subsistence, 
and who Wave not been named by the Austrian Government, would be a harsh 
measure, and not required by any uneasiness expressed by the Austrian Govern- 
ment with respect to those persons. 

I have further to state to your Excellency that Her Majesty's Government 
approve of your having recommended the Porte, as stated in your despatch 
No. 50, to adhere to the last proposal which it had made to Austria in December 
Inst. as to the period for the detention of the Hungarians, 

am, fe. 


(Signed) PALMERSTON.
